method.prereg: Families (sector-neutral percentile ranks → average within family → average across families, equal weights): - Q Quality: gross profit/assets, ROE (TTM), operating cash flow/assets, accruals (−), leverage (−), asset growth (−), net share issuance (−) - V Value: earnings yield (TTM), free-cash-flow yield, EBIT/EV, book/price - M Momentum: 12-1 month total return - S Earnings momentum: SUE (latest quarterly diluted EPS YoY change ÷ std of prior 8 YoY changes) Composite = mean(Q, V, M, S). Rebalance monthly; signal at month-end t uses only data filed ≤ t; 10 bps one-way costs. Variants reported (not selected on results): QVM only; each family alone; v3 conviction proxy; v2 composite. Risk (volatility) is a constraint, not a return driver. Live-only overlays (analyst revisions, NTM valuation) are tie-breakers/red flags only because no point-in-time history exists for them.

glossary: Index fund (UCITS, Irish-domiciled)
a fund that simply owns all S&P 500 companies. The Irish legal wrapper keeps it outside US estate tax and halves the US tax on its dividends.
T-bill
a short-term US government IOU (3–12 months). It is the closest thing to risk-free cash in dollars and currently pays about 4% a year.
Satellite / sleeve
the small part of the portfolio held in individual stocks, next to the index core.
Backtest
replaying a rule on past data to see how it would have done.
Point-in-time
using only what was knowable on each past date: the companies actually in the index then, and the accounts filed by then.
Look-ahead and survivorship bias
the two classic backtest cheats. Look-ahead uses information that was not yet public. Survivorship tests only today's winners and forgets the companies that shrank, were bought or went bust.
Pre-registered
the model was written down and frozen before any test was run, so it could not be tuned to the answer.
Pts/yr (percentage points a year)
the difference between two annual returns, e.g. 12.5% vs 15.1% is −2.6 pts/yr.
t-stat
how many standard errors a result sits from zero. Between −2 and +2 means "could easily be luck".
95% range (confidence interval)
the band that would contain the true value in 95 of 100 repeats of the experiment.
Volatility
how much a price typically swings in a year (one standard deviation, as a %).
Tracking error
how far a portfolio's yearly return typically strays from the index, in either direction.
Beta
how much a stock or portfolio tends to move when the index moves 1% (a beta of 0.8 means about 0.8%).
Drawdown / worst fall
the largest fall from a previous high to a later low, before recovering.
Stress replay
re-running today's holdings through a past crisis (e.g. 2008, 2020) on daily prices.
Stationary bootstrap
a simulation that builds thousands of possible futures by stitching together random blocks of real past days. It keeps the real clustering of good and bad days.
Scenario (bear / base / bull)
an assumed long-run market return of 2% / 6% / 9% a year. The odds in this report are conditional on the scenario.
Calibrated odds / base rate
how often something actually happened historically to stocks like this one (same score band and volatility). It is not a forecast for the specific stock.
NTM P/E
share price divided by the next twelve months of expected earnings per share. Lower means cheaper per dollar of profit.
P/FFO
the REIT version of P/E. FFO (funds from operations) adds back property depreciation, which overstates real costs for landlords.
P/B and justified P/B
price relative to book value (net assets), used for banks and insurers. The justified P/B is what the return on equity supports.
Reverse DCF
instead of forecasting cash flows to get a price, start from today's price and solve for the growth the market is assuming. Then ask whether that growth is plausible.
Own-history percentile
where today's valuation sits within the company's own past range (0 = cheapest ever, 100 = dearest).
Kill criterion
a measurable condition, written in advance, that means the investment case is broken and the stock is sold.
INCLUDE / INCLUDE-SMALL
the diligence verdict. INCLUDE is held at full weight (up to 10% of the sleeve). INCLUDE-SMALL is investable with a named reservation and held at half weight (up to 5%).
US-situs
an asset the US treats as located in the US for estate tax (US shares and US-domiciled ETFs). Irish UCITS funds are not US-situs.
Withholding tax
tax taken at source from dividends before you receive them: 30% for a UAE resident on US shares, 15% inside an Irish fund.

facts: US estate tax on US-situs assets
Non-US persons get a $13,000 credit ≈ $60,000 exemption (not indexed); rates 18–40%; Form 706-NA above $60k. No US–UAE estate treaty. Illustrative tax: $80k → $5,200; $100k → $10,800.
30% for UAE residents (no US–UAE income-tax treaty; W-8BEN does not reduce it). Capital gains generally not US-taxed.
No personal income tax; Cabinet Decision 49/2023 keeps personal investment income outside UAE Corporate Tax.

CSPX / VUAA / SPY5 (physical, 15% withholding inside the fund) and SPXS (swap, ~0% withholding, counterparty risk) are not US-situs. All-in annual tax drag at a 1.11% yield: VOO 0.36%, CSPX/VUAA 0.24%, SPY5 0.20%, SPXS 0.12%.

IBKR: US stocks ~$0.005/share (min $1); LSE ETFs 0.05% of value; no inactivity fee. Vested: 0.25% per trade (max $35), US stocks/ETFs only, clears via DriveWealth (US-situs), and appears to onboard only Indian-origin (PAN/NRI) clients — check eligibility (R3).
Which IBKR entity holds a UAE account

UAE residents are onboarded by Interactive Brokers (U.K.) Ltd, DIFC Branch (DFSA Category 4, an arranging broker); custody sits with Interactive Brokers LLC in the US, so SIPC protection applies (not FSCS). Verified on IBKR's own pages, 26 Sep 2026 (R3).
Open items only a broker or adviser can settle

Marked permanently open, each with a workaround. (1) Estate-tax situs of idle cash at a US broker: keep the reserve in T-bills or a UCITS T-bill fund such as IB01, not as a large broker cash balance. (2) Fractional units of CSPX/VUAA at IBKR: the order ticket shows whether "cash quantity" is offered; otherwise buy whole units (VUAA about $149 a unit at its 24 Sep NAV). (3) IBKR market-data fees: optional; delayed quotes are free.
The Securities and Commodities Authority (SCA) became the Capital Market Authority (CMA) on 1 Jan 2026 (Federal Laws 32 and 33 of 2025). Sarwa is regulated by the ADGM FSRA (R3).
Individual US stocks cannot be wrapped in UCITS, so a stock-picking sleeve is US-situs; keeping it near or below ~$60k limits estate-tax exposure, while the index core can sit in a UCITS fund.
rules: Hold broad US exposure in an Irish-domiciled UCITS S&P 500 fund (not US-situs, 15% fund-level dividend withholding) and the v4 stocks as a satellite. The satellite is where the research can add return; the core is where the 90%-over-10-years confidence actually lives.

Buy in three equal tranches about three weeks apart. Use limit orders near the last close and never buy a stock in the two trading days before its earnings date. In Dubai time the US market is open 17:30–00:00 while US daylight saving applies (early March to early November) and 18:30–01:00 otherwise.

Re-run the model each quarter. Sell a holding only if it falls out of the top quarter of the ranking or a kill criterion fires. Trim any position above 1.5× its target weight. Most weeks the right action is no trade.

Each holding has 3–5 measurable exit triggers in its dossier (for example, a guidance cut plus a >10% fall in next-year EPS estimates, leverage above a stated level, or a thesis-breaking event). If one fires, exit at the next review; if none fires, price moves alone are not a reason to sell.

A −10% portfolio fall triggers a review of every thesis; −15% a review of the equity/reserve mix; −20% means the stated tolerance is reached. Stop orders are not used: gaps can fill far below the trigger.
Know what would change the view

Fold the satellite into the index if it trails the S&P 500 by more than 20 points over 24 months (about a 1-in-8 outcome if it has no edge, given its 13% tracking error). Revisit the design if a quarterly re-run replaces more than half the names or a data audit finds a material error.
weekly: Open the dashboard: note the week's moves for the portfolio, the S&P 500 and each holding (2 min).
Check whether any holding reported earnings or issued guidance this week; compare with its kill criteria in the dossier tab (10 min).
Check the news list for holdings for M&A, regulatory action, management changes or accounting issues (5 min).
Check weights against targets: act only if a position exceeds 1.5× target or a kill criterion fired (3 min).
Record the decision, including "no trade", in the decision log with the date and reason (5 min).
Quarter-end weeks only: re-run the model and review the replacement list before trading (extra 30 min).

hero.title: Your all-stock portfolio: 20 researched companies chosen from the whole S&P 500.
hero.lede: You asked for an all-stock portfolio chosen from the whole S&P 500. Every company got a quick research pass; 500 got full SEC-filing research so far. The 20 stocks held are the best of 205 that passed every test: good businesses whose price does not assume more growth than the evidence supports. That rule keeps out Microsoft, NVIDIA, Alphabet, Amazon, Meta and Apple at today's prices. Honest odds: no rule tested here beat the S&P 500 over 2012–2026, so treat beating it as a coin flip, not a promise. The price of going all-stock is risk: the 20 fell −38% in the 2007–09 replay.
tiles: chance of a gain over 5 years (base case)
chance of beating the S&P 500 over 5 years (no assumed edge)
independent bets, once co-movement is counted

answer.v: Hold the 20 stocks at the weights in the table, with no index fund or T-bills. In past crises they fell −38% in the 2007–09 replay (S&P 500 −55%), −35% in the COVID crash and −13% in 2022. Base case: 78% chance of a gain over 5 years, a coin flip to beat the S&P 500, and 88% chance of a fall worse than 20% at some point. Fewer than 12–15 names adds single-company risk. Direct US shares count toward the ~$60k US estate-tax threshold for non-US persons. 30% of US dividends is withheld: about 0.48% of the portfolio a year on its 1.6% yield. Research, not advice.

answer.k: If you want less risk later: what to own
answer.v: An S&P 500 UCITS fund (e.g. CSPX or VUAA, Irish-domiciled: no US estate tax, 15% dividend withholding) as the core; T-bills or a UCITS T-bill fund as the reserve; the stock satellite at no more than 15–20% of the total (any part of the satellite the caps cannot fill also goes into the index fund).

answer.k: If you want less risk later: how much in each
answer.v: This depends on your drawdown limit. Moderate 55/15/30: 87% chance of a gain over 5 years, 48% chance of a fall worse than 20% at some point. Cautious 35/10/55: 95% and 10%. Index only: 80% and 81%. In a 2008-style crash even the Cautious mix fell −24%; a limit that must hold then needs about 37% or less in equities. Defensive 15/10/75 (the equity budget of Codex's release v005): over 99% and under 1%; it fell −12% in the 2008 replay. Your call; this is scenario analysis, not advice.

answer.k: What to expect from the stocks
answer.v: Roughly index-like returns, give or take about 13% a year. The honest odds for each name: 65–70% chance of a gain over a year, 43–46% chance of beating the index. Every holding has written exit triggers.

A satellite that trails the S&P 500 by more than 20 points over 24 months (fold it into the index); a kill criterion firing on a holding; a new quarter's model re-run replacing more than half the names.

port.note: Weights are shares of the stock sleeve. Sleeve rules were fixed before the diligence verdicts were read: official point-in-time score in the top 70, 1-year volatility ≤ 45%, no pending takeover, valuation attractive or fair versus the company's own history, diligence INCLUDE (full) or INCLUDE-SMALL (half), ≤ 2 names per sub-industry, inverse-volatility weights of 3–10% (full conviction) or 1.5–5% (half conviction), sectors ≤ 25%; sleeve capacity the caps cannot absorb is held in the S&P 500 index fund. * Calibrated odds are empirical frequencies for S&P 500 stocks in the same score decile and volatility band, 2011–2025.

bt.lede: We froze a model built only from well-replicated research (quality, value, momentum, earnings surprise) before running any test, then tested it month by month from 2012 to August 2026 on the stocks that were actually in the S&P 500 at each date, with as-filed SEC data and trading costs. A second agent rebuilt it independently and matched it within 0.04 points a year. It did not beat the S&P 500: the top 30 returned 12.5% a year against 15.1% for the index (t = -1.12), and a higher score did not mean a higher return. Every variant told the same story, including the v1, v2 and v3 models. Tested the way v3 was tested (on today's survivors), the same model shows 18.6% a year instead of 12.5%: a 6.0-point illusion.

stats.name: Sleeve rule as pre-committed (top 20, vol ≤45%, inverse-vol, quarterly)

bt.notes: Point-in-time S&P 500 membership (D1/D2), total-return prices (D2), as-filed SEC XBRL fundamentals filed before each month-end (D3); 10 bps per trade; Newey–West t-statistics. Residual survivorship (delisted names without free price data) flatters every strategy by about 0.9% a year versus the real equal-weight ETF (RSP); it cannot turn the negative result positive. Full detail: v4/outputs/b1_report.md, independent replication v4/outputs/b1x_report.md.

risk.lede: All stock, the 20 holdings have a 88% chance of a fall worse than 20% at some point within 5 years (base case). If you later want less risk, allocation is the lever. The index alone has a 81% chance of a fall worse than 20% at some point within 5 years; adding a 30% T-bill reserve cuts it to 48%, and 55% cuts it to 10%. The 20 stocks fell harder than the index in the COVID crash and held up far better in 2022.
risk.worst: The worst fall to plan around. Over the full daily history (2005-01-04 to 2026-09-25) at today's weights, the stock sleeve's worst fall was −41.3% (peak 2007-12-10, trough 2008-11-20, recovered 2009-11-16). The S&P 500's worst fall over the same days was −55.2% (2007-10-09 to 2009-03-09). The crisis replays above use the S&P 500's own peak and trough dates, so they can show a smaller figure for the sleeve (GFC: −37.8%). Treat −41% as the sleeve's tail-risk anchor. In the Moderate mix the 2007–09 replay cost −38.0% and in the Cautious mix −24.3%; set those against your 15–20% tolerance.
risk.divers: Diversification. The 20 stocks behave like about 17 independent positions once their tendency to move together is counted (17 if only the weights are counted). About 41% of the sleeve's day-to-day risk comes from the market as a whole (its sensitivity to the S&P 500, beta, is 0.61); the rest is specific to the companies. The largest company-specific risks are BR (12%), ACGL (10%), GDDY (10%). Per dollar invested, the riskiest holdings are GDDY, INTU and SYF: each adds 1.4–1.4 times as much of the sleeve's risk as its weight alone would suggest. Measured over the last three years of daily prices, the sleeve's volatility is 14.6% and it strays from the S&P 500 by about 12.7% a year. An independent re-computation and the method are in Appendix A.
risk.notes: Scenarios: Bear 2% / Base 6% / Bull 9% a year (R1, sourced from 12 institutional forecasts); T-bills 4%. 20,000 stationary-bootstrap paths of 2005–2026 daily returns (B2 module). Sleeve alpha assumed zero. Scenario analysis, not advice.

findings.topic: A hard 15–20% loss limit needs a small equity share
findings.v005: Maximum 25% equity (15% index + 10% direct, at least 75% reserve); a hypothetical tail shock (index −60%, stocks −75%, reserve −2%) loses 18.0% at full deployment.
findings.v4: Daily-data replay of 2007–09 with quarterly rebalancing: staying within −20% needed ≤37% in equities, within −15% ≤29%. The Defensive mix (v005's budget) fell -11.6% in that replay.
findings.effect: v4 adds the Defensive 15/10/75 mix to every allocation table, with simulated odds on the same engine as the other mixes.

findings.topic: Whether 15–20% must hold in every crash
findings.v005: Treats 15–20% as the design objective for the whole portfolio, hence 75–81% reserve.
findings.v4: Shows the trade-off instead. Base case, median 5-year return +4.9%/yr for Defensive vs +6.0%/yr for Moderate; P(fall > 20% within 5 yrs) 0% vs 48%. The 15–20% figure comes from the earlier Codex review notes; to Claude the owner described his risk appetite as 'not very risk-averse, not extremely risk-taking'.
findings.effect: v4 does not override v005: the owner chooses which sentence describes his limit (the one next step).

findings.topic: Irish UCITS index core and a short-Treasury reserve
findings.v005: VUAA (IE00BFMXXD54) for the index; IB01 (IE00BGSF1X88, 0–1 yr Treasuries) plus cash for the reserve.
findings.v4: CSPX or VUAA for the core; directly held T-bills or a UCITS T-bill fund for the reserve. IB01 is such a fund; both keep the reserve outside US estate tax.
findings.effect: v4 names IB01 as one eligible reserve fund, alongside direct T-bills.

findings.topic: Dividend withholding and US estate tax
findings.v005: 30% withholding on direct US dividends; Irish funds 15% internally; direct US shares are US-situs.
findings.v4: Same facts, re-verified against IRS and issuer pages on 26 Sep 2026 (R2, R3).

findings.v005: Ranks only the original fourteen v3 candidates and says so ('not a claim to have found the best fourteen investments in the entire market').
findings.v4: v3's candidate list rested on biased evidence: its momentum result falls from 29.1%/yr to 18.1%/yr once stocks count only after joining the index, and its conviction filter failed out of sample. v4 screens all 503 point-in-time members with pre-registered rules plus primary-source diligence. The only overlap is HIG.
findings.effect: v4's satellite is not built from v3's list. v4 also found no stock-selection edge, so neither workstream's picks should be expected to beat the index.

findings.topic: AMP and PAYX as first purchases
findings.status: AMP CONFIRMED (eligible, not held); PAYX CONFIRMED as buyable (eligible, not held)
findings.v005: BUY NOW at ≤ $500 (AMP) and ≤ $101.80 (PAYX), 2% slots each, base 3-yr IRRs 12.8% / 12.2% after withholding.
findings.v4: Once v4 extended research to every S&P 500 company, its own full diligence (F21) first rated AMP INCLUDE at full conviction (cut to INCLUDE-SMALL, half conviction, in the 6 October re-assessment RA10), fairly priced at under 10x forward earnings. AMP passes every v4 test but is not held: eligible, but outside the best 20 (conviction, margin of safety, base-case return). PAYX was researched in full in wave 2 (F37): INCLUDE-SMALL (half conviction), with the price implying about 0.7% a year of cash-flow growth against management's own guided 7–9% earnings growth, and a base-case return of about +9.8% a year. It passes every v4 test but is not held: 20 names outranked it under rule (j). Its named reservation is a slowdown in the Management Solutions unit (75% of revenue) and an April 2026 data breach.
findings.effect: Both names now pass v4's own full diligence, so v005's judgement that they are sound purchases at those limits is confirmed; v4 keeps both on its bench of eligible names (neither is in the current 20). PAYX closed at $101.37 on 25 Sep 2026, just under v005's $101.80 limit. X1 reproduced both v005 base cases to the cent from SEC filings. AMP's 13x exit multiple sits near its 10-year average P/E. PAYX's 20x sits below its whole 10-year P/E range (about 24–34x): conservative, but v005 does not say so. The AMP gap between v005 (13–14% IRR, cash-flow model) and v4's valuation model (+6.5%/yr, price-to-book relative to peers) is a method choice, not an error on either side.

dossiers.A:
Agilent Technologies (A) - standard-depth diligence, agent F160

1. Verdict

WATCH (reason: a high-quality, recovering instruments franchise, but the 25 Sep 2026 close of $172.79 implies about 12% annual FCF growth for ten years versus a base case near 8%). Horizon 12-36 months. This agrees with the quick triage that did not advance it; the triage's cited basis ("general knowledge") is replaced here by filings. Would become INCLUDE-SMALL below about $150 (base-case 3-year return above 10%) or on a durable core growth beat above 7%.

2. Business in plain English

Agilent sells lab instruments (chromatography, mass spectrometry), the consumables and service contracts that keep them running (CrossLab, about 40% of revenue, 34.3% segment operating margin in Q3 FY26), and diagnostics products (Biocare pathology added 24 Jun 2026). Customers are pharma, biopharma, chemical and environmental labs. The installed base and recurring service annuity are the moat; instruments are cyclical.

3. Why the model likes it, and durability

b1 family scores: momentum 0.46, quality 0.22, value 0.22, sentiment 0.49 (momentum and sentiment drive it; earnings yield 3.0%, FCF yield 2.6%, SUE 0.29). Durable part: three consecutive quarters of beats and raised guidance. Not durable: Q3 FY26 non-GAAP EPS includes a $0.06 one-time tariff-refund benefit and an approximately 110 bps margin benefit (Q3 FY26 release, 0001090872-26-000062).

4. Results, last seven quarters (consolidated; fiscal year ends 31 Oct)

Q2 FY25 (Apr 2025) 1,668 18.0% 0.75 1.31 107

Variance, Q3 FY26 vs Q3 FY25: revenue +$140M (+8.1%; core +7.3%), GAAP operating income $444M vs $360M (+23%, +290 bps margin), GAAP EPS +8%, non-GAAP EPS +18%. GAAP EPS lags non-GAAP because the effective tax rate was 18.5% (82/444) versus 8.2% a year ago (30/366). Margin drivers per the Form 10-Q (accession 0001090872-26-000064) MD&A: volume, price, tariff refund, lower restructuring, partly offset by higher variable pay. Segments Q3 FY26: LDG $746M (+10% core), ACG $786M (+5% core), AMG $346M (+7% core). Source: Ex 99.1 accessions 0001090872-25-000070, -26-000015, -26-000052, -26-000062; Q1-Q3 FY25 from the same releases' comparative columns and 9M FY25 cash flow.

5. Guidance track record (FY26 non-GAAP EPS, versus prior range)

  • 24 Nov 2025 (0001090872-25-000070): "Fiscal year 2026 revenue is expected in the range of $7.3 billion to $7.4 billion, representing a range of up 5% to 7% reported and up 4% to 6% core(1). Non-GAAP EPS(3) is expected in the range of $5.86 to $6.00." Initial.
  • 25 Feb 2026 (0001090872-26-000015): "Non-GAAP EPS(3) is expected in the range of $5.90 to $6.04." Raised (midpoint $5.93 to $5.97); revenue range widened to $7.3-7.5 billion.
  • 27 May 2026 (0001090872-26-000052): "Non-GAAP EPS(4) is now expected in the range of $6.00 to $6.10, an increase of 8 cents at the midpoint." Raised.
  • 26 Aug 2026 (0001090872-26-000062): "Non-GAAP fiscal year 2026 EPS(4) is now expected in the range of $6.18 to $6.21, an increase of 15 cents at the midpoint (including $0.06 net benefit from tariff refunds in the third quarter) versus our prior guide." Raised; ex-refund the raise is about $0.09.
  • Q4 FY26: "Non-GAAP EPS(4) is expected in the range of $1.71 to $1.74 per share. This guidance does not include any future benefit from tariff refunds." Q3 was guided $1.48-1.50 (May release) and delivered $1.62 including $0.06 of refund. Four raises or confirmations in a row; the quality of the latest raise is lower than the headline.

6. Earnings quality and balance sheet (consolidated unless stated)

  • FCF: TTM OCF about $1,609M (FY25 $1,559M less 9M FY25 $1,014M plus 9M FY26 $1,064M) less capex $342M = about $1.27B, versus TTM non-GAAP net income about $1.72B: about 74% conversion. 9M FY26 OCF carried a $295M outflow in "other assets and liabilities" and $376M cash taxes. SBC $105M for 9M FY26 (about 1.9% of revenue).
  • Balance sheet at 31 Jul 2026 (condensed consolidated, Ex 99.1 0001090872-26-000062): cash and cash equivalents $1,758M; short-term debt $304M (2026 senior notes, 3.05%, due 22 Sep 2026, per the 10-Q); long-term debt $3,645M; consolidated stockholders' equity $7,363M. Consolidated net debt about $2.19B (carrying debt $3,949M less cash $1,758M), about 1.1x TTM EBITDA of about $2.08B (Yahoo cross-check). Undrawn $1.5B unsecured revolver (to June 2028) and $1.5B commercial paper program per the 10-Q.
  • M&A: Biocare acquired 24 Jun 2026 for $950M net, funded by $600M 4.90% senior notes due 2032 issued 25 Jun 2026 plus cash; goodwill +$549M, intangibles +$520M; stock deal, not tax-deductible (10-Q, 0001090872-26-000064).

7. Valuation and V1 reconciliation

Verdict: INCLUDE-SMALL (half weight) — 12–36 month thesis horizon. [Corrected 2026-10-06: verdict changes to WATCH: implied growth is above the base case, which fails the INCLUDE/INCLUDE-SMALL rule; see Correction DV01] One-sentence reason: a 2.5-billion-device installed base is monetizing better than ever (Services at a record run-rate, gross margin at an 8-quarter high), but the current iPhone-17 supercycle plus Services re-acceleration has pushed the price to imply more growth than this analyst's steady-state base case, so it is a hold-with-a-reservation, not a full-conviction add.

1. Business in plain English

Apple sells premium hardware (iPhone ~50% of revenue, Mac/iPad/Wearables the rest) to a large, loyal, high-income-skewed installed base, then monetizes that base through Services (App Store, subscriptions, advertising, Apple Care, licensing — notably Google's payment for default search placement). The moat is the hardware-software-services ecosystem and switching costs, not any single product's technical superiority. Growth increasingly comes from Services (higher margin, more durable) rather than hardware unit growth.

2. Why the model likes it / is it durable

b1 composite percentile 0.72 (second-highest of the four names after NVDA), driven by Value (fam_V 1.20 raw, ep/fcfp percentiles ~0.49–0.51) and a very high leverage percentile (0.79) reflecting Apple's large, deliberate net-debt capital structure rather than distress [Corrected 2026-10-06: Apple has net cash of about $62.2B at 2026-06-27 (cash and securities $146.5B vs debt $84.3B, 10-Q 0000320193-26-000020)]. The durability case rests on installed-base growth and Services mix shift, both verifiable below.

4. Guidance track record

Apple does not issue formal point/range revenue guidance (a long-standing practice), so a "raised/maintained/cut vs. prior range" comparison is not available; this is disclosed rather than omitted. 5. Moat and competition

  • Installed base: >2.5 billion active devices, up from 2.35 billion a year earlier (≈6.4% YoY growth) — the base that Services monetizes; management called it "a new all-time high...across all major product categories and geographic segments." [1]
  • Services: FY2025 Services revenue $109.16B — the first fiscal year Services exceeded $100B; Q1 FY26 Services hit a record $30.0B, +14% YoY. Services carries materially higher gross margin than products and is the more durable growth engine.
  • China — share recovering, but competitively contested: Apple held 18.1% of China's smartphone market in Q2 2026 (up from 13.9% a year earlier, +24.9% YoY shipment growth — one of only two top-10 vendors growing), but Huawei leads with 22.6% share, "the highest in five years." Apple used early price-hike warnings to pull forward iPhone-17 upgrades while holding its own price, a tactic that will not repeat indefinitely. [4]
  • Regulatory: Apple opened to third-party payments/app stores in the EU under the DMA; in China, 48 iOS developers petitioned SAMR for an antitrust investigation into App Store commissions (Jun-2026), and Apple pre-emptively cut its standard China App Store commission from 30% to 25% (Mar-2026) — a real, filed reduction in take-rate in at least one major market, with more regulatory pressure visible elsewhere. [4]
  • Apple Intelligence / AI features: sources reference "a more personalized Siri coming this year" — i.e., Apple's flagship on-device AI feature was still pending/rolling out as of the cutoff, later than competitors' generative-AI assistants; this is a genuine execution-timeline risk to the "AI upgrade cycle" bull thesis, not yet a proof point. [1]

6. Earnings quality & balance sheet

  • TTM (Q4 FY25–Q3 FY26) operating cash flow $146,724M, capex $10,041M, FCF ≈$136,683M, FCF margin ≈29.3% of TTM revenue — strong, typical of Apple's asset-light manufacturing model (contract manufacturers carry most fixed-asset intensity).

  • This analyst did not pull a precise current net-cash/net-debt balance-sheet figure from the sources gathered in this pass (time-boxed); Apple has historically run a large gross-debt, partially-offsetting-cash capital structure for tax and capital-return efficiency rather than distress — flagged as an item to verify against the FQ3 FY26 10-Q balance sheet directly rather than asserted here.   1. Huawei leads China smartphone share (22.6% vs. Apple's 18.1%) and Apple's recent China growth was partly a price-hike-avoidance pull-forward, not necessarily sustainable.

AbbVie is a global biopharmaceutical company. care here, detailed below) AbbVie's official guidance excludes future acquired-IPR&D/milestone expense because it "does not forecast" that item; it then pre-announces each quarter's actual IPR&D hit via a standalone Item 2.02 8-K roughly a month before the full earnings release, and republishes an "updated" guidance range that folds in the now-known charge. Q3 2025 (2025-10-31): FY2025 raised from $10.38–$10.58 to $10.61–$10.65 (adjusted EPS, excluding Q4 IPR&D). 2. 2026-01-07 8-K (pre-announcement): discloses Q4 2025 IPR&D/milestone expense of $1.3bn pretax (−$0.71/share) and restates the "including Q4 IPR&D" FY2025 range down to $9.90–$9.94. 3. Q4/FY2025 (2026-02-04): FY2025 actual adjusted EPS $10.00 — a beat versus the IPR&D-inclusive $9.90–$9.94 range, but a −1.2% YoY decline once the year's cumulative $2.76/share of IPR&D charges are counted. FY2026 initial guidance issued (excluding 2026 IPR&D): $14.37–$14.57. 4. 2026-04-03 8-K: discloses Q1 2026 IPR&D expense of $744m pretax (−$0.41/share), restates FY2026 (IPR&D- inclusive) to $13.96–$14.16. 5. Q1 2026 (2026-04-29): genuinely raised (on an apples-to-apples, IPR&D-inclusive basis) to $14.08–$14.28. 6. Q2 2026 (2026-07-31): updated to $13.87–$14.07, explicitly to absorb $0.14/share of dilution from the pending Apogee Therapeutics acquisition (partially offset by $0.10/share of operating overperformance) — a guidance change driven by a new deal, not an operating cut, but the headline range is nonetheless lower than the prior $14.08–$14.28. Net: guidance has been raised on an operating basis in every quarter reviewed once IPR&D and M&A dilution are adjusted for consistently — but the headline ranges alone, read naively, would look like an unexplained miss (FY25) followed by a cut (Q2'26) or a raise (Q1'26) depending on which two releases are compared. This dossier resolves that by reading the pre-announcement 8-Ks, per the wave-3 mandate.

6. Earnings quality & balance sheet (consolidated, GAAP, entity = AbbVie Inc. and subsidiaries; 10-Q period

2026-06-30, filed 2026-08-03, and 10-Q period 2026-03-31, filed 2026-05-08) - Stockholders' equity is NEGATIVE: total stockholders' equity −$5,935m at 2026-06-30 (−$6,656m at 2026-03-31), driven by treasury stock −$10,618m and accumulated deficit in retained earnings −$17,333m against additional paid-in capital of only $23,156m. This is a longstanding structural feature (large buybacks/dividends and Allergan- deal-related charges over several years, not a new single-quarter event) but it means AbbVie has no equity cushion: the balance sheet is supported entirely by ~$85bn of goodwill+intangibles ($35.5bn + $49.1bn at 2026-06-30) against $135.1bn of total assets and $141.0bn of total liabilities. - Leverage: total debt $70.8bn, cash $6.6bn, net debt $64.3bn (both at 2026-06-30). TTM EBITDA (sum of the last four quarterly EBITDA figures reconciled in the company's filings, Q3'25–Q2'26) ≈ $21.2bn → net debt/EBITDA ≈ 3.0x, consolidated. This is a moderate, investment-grade-consistent level for large pharma but leaves no room for a leverage surprise given the zero equity cushion above. [Corrected 2026-10-06: stale: after 30 Jun 2026 AbbVie issued $10.0bn of notes and closed the $10.9bn Apogee cash acquisition (3 Sep 2026); pro forma net debt about $75bn, about 3.5-3.6x EBITDA] - Recurring "one-off" item: acquired IPR&D/milestone expense was $2.76/share for FY2025 (~$4.9bn pretax at ~1.77bn shares) and continued at $0.41/share (Q1'26) and further amounts in Q2/Q3 2026 — i.e., AbbVie has incurred a large IPR&D charge in every recent quarter. 7. Valuation snapshot & reverse DCF (own build; no V1 row exists for ABBV — not previously a top-70/lane name)

Adjusted NTM P/E on FY2026 guidance midpoint ($13.97): 264.34/13.97 = 18.9x. EV (mktcap $467.1bn + net debt $64.3bn) / TTM FCF ($19.68bn) ≈ 27.0x; FCF yield on equity market cap ≈ 4.2%. Reverse DCF (2-stage, 10-yr + Gordon terminal; terminal growth 3.0%): given AbbVie's low reported beta (0.281, FMP) understates its true risk (patent-cliff/litigation/negative-equity risk are not well captured by historical beta for a company mid-transition), I ran two WACC scenarios rather than picking one: at WACC 7.5%, implied 10-yr FCF/share growth ≈ 5.0%/yr; at WACC 8.5%, implied growth ≈ 7.7%/yr. A reasonable evidence-based base case — mid-single-digit revenue growth (immunology deceleration as Skyrizi/Rinvoq mature, partially offset by neuroscience and an early obesity pipeline) translating to high-single-digit EPS/FCF growth via margin and buybacks — sits at roughly 6–8%/yr, i.e., inside the WACC-sensitivity band, not clearly below it. Verdict: implied_vs_base = "in_line." [Corrected 2026-10-06: restated implied growth about 10.5% (WACC ~8.9%, FCF $17.2bn after SBC, EV incl. Apogee) vs 6-8% base: implied_vs_base = above] This is a fair, not a cheap, price for a business whose two biggest growth drivers (Skyrizi, Rinvoq) are still compounding but will mechanically decelerate as they scale.

8. Bull case

  1. The Humira patent-cliff bear case is now largely played out and visible in the numbers: Humira was $756m of revenue in Q2 2026, versus $4.54bn for all of FY2025 and far larger before — the worst of the erosion is behind, confirmed by four quarters of reported data, not a projection.
  2. Immunology ex-Humira (Skyrizi + Rinvoq) grew revenue 14.6% operationally in Q2 2026 on an already-large base ($8.0bn combined in the quarter) — genuine, large-scale, currently-realized growth.
  3. Dividend raised 5.5% with FCF coverage comfortable (TTM FCF ≈ $19.7bn vs. TTM dividends paid ≈ $11.9bn implied by the quarterly cash-flow statements), supporting the income case even if growth decelerates.

9. Bear case

  1. Zero equity cushion (negative $5.9bn stockholders' equity) plus ~3.0x net debt/EBITDA leaves no room for a negative surprise (an adverse litigation judgment, a failed pipeline bet, or a large dilutive deal) without raising real balance-sheet-risk questions, unlike most other large-cap pharma peers with positive equity.
  2. The recurring, large acquired-IPR&D/milestone expense line ($2.76/share FY2025) is excluded from "adjusted" EPS every year; if treated as a normal, recurring cost of maintaining AbbVie's pipeline (which the multi-year pattern suggests it is), normalized earnings power is lower than the headlined adjusted EPS implies.
  3. Reverse DCF shows the current price already embeds a base-case-level growth assumption — there is little room for the Skyrizi/Rinvoq deceleration (both are large, maturing franchises) to arrive faster than modeled without the stock re-rating down.

10. Key risks & kill criteria (measurable triggers that would invalidate the thesis)

  1. Consolidated net debt/EBITDA (per the 10-Q's own reconciliation) exceeds 3.5x in any quarter.
  2. Combined Skyrizi + Rinvoq operational revenue growth falls below 8% YoY for two consecutive quarters (vs. 14.6% in Q2 2026).
  3. Acquired IPR&D/milestone expense exceeds $3.00/share on a trailing-12-month basis (vs. $2.76/share in FY2025), signalling an accelerating, not one-off, drag.
  4. Adjusted diluted EPS guidance is cut on an IPR&D-and-M&A-adjusted, apples-to-apples basis (i.e., excluding the effect of newly disclosed IPR&D charges and disclosed acquisitions, which are not true operating cuts).
  5. An adverse final judgment or settlement in the Allergan opioid MDL or Biocell breast-implant litigation materially exceeding the current $1.7bn litigation accrual.

dossiers.ABNB:
ABNB — Airbnb, Inc.

1. Verdict

INCLUDE-SMALL (half weight) — thesis horizon 12–36 months. Genuinely strong, primary-source-verified operating momentum (revenue/GBV/margin guidance raised or beaten in each of the last four quarters, ~10% reduction in diluted share count since 2022 from buybacks [Corrected 2026-10-06: the Q4 2025 release says approximately 9% (acc 0001193125-26-048670)], a $12bn net-cash balance sheet [Corrected 2026-10-06: net cash is $9.6bn: cash and short-term investments $12.07bn less $2.48bn long-term debt (10-Q 0001559720-26-000027, 2026-06-30)], 37% TTM FCF margin) is offset by a valuation that is not statistically cheap (26.3x NTM P/E against peers that are not fully comparable) and by spreading, city-by-city short-term-rental regulation that is a genuine and event-driven — not merely theoretical — risk to the core listings business. Investable at reduced size given the balance-sheet quality and cash generation; the named reservation is that the base case requires further multiple re-rating from an already-premium starting point, offering limited margin of safety.

2. Business in plain English

Airbnb operates the world's largest marketplace connecting people who want to rent out a home or room ("hosts") with travellers who want to stay in one ("guests"), and — increasingly — travellers who want to book an "experience" (a local activity) or, via a newly launched initiative, a hotel room. Airbnb owns no real estate; it earns a service/commission fee (an "implied take rate," revenue ÷ Gross Booking Value) on each booking, which has run 9%–18% quarter to quarter (the swings are driven mostly by the timing mismatch between when a guest books and pays vs. when they stay, not by a change in pricing — see §4). It competes with Booking.com/Vrbo/Expedia for the room-night, and — where regulators restrict short-term rentals — increasingly with hotels directly, which is why it has begun listing boutique/independent hotels itself in supply-constrained cities.

3. Why the model likes it — and is it durable?

B1 composite is top decile (live_rank 40/~2,300; [Corrected 2026-10-06: live_rank is 40 of 503 (b1_live_scores.csv)] composite percentile ~92%; only 3 of 4 factor families computed — no reliable SUE/earnings-momentum signal exists yet given ABNB's short public history. Gates: the composite carries no disqualifying-red-flag gate — see §11 for the separate legal/regulatory red-flag check.) Family drivers: Momentum (fam_M ≈0.97, extremely high) — the stock has re-rated hard off strong, repeated guidance beats; Quality (fam_Q ≈0.91, very high) — strong gross-profit/assets, ROE and operating-cash-flow/assets, low leverage (net cash); Value (fam_V ≈0.23, weak) — ABNB is expensive on every value sub-metric, which is the honest counterweight to the other two families. [Corrected 2026-10-06: the file shows fam_Q 0.971, fam_M 0.909, fam_V 0.247: the momentum and quality values quoted above are swapped]

Durability check: the momentum is real and corroborated in primary-source releases — Q1, Q2 2026 revenue both exceeded the high end of prior guidance, and full-year 2026 Adjusted EBITDA-margin guidance was raised three times running (Q4-2025 "stable YoY" → Q1-2026 "at least 35%" → Q2-2026 "at least 35.5%"). [Corrected 2026-10-06: that is an initial guide followed by two raises, not three raises] But the mechanism of margin expansion is cost discipline (customer-support cost per booking down ~10–16% YoY on AI-driven efficiency) and operating leverage on GBV growth — not take-rate/monetisation expansion (take rate has been flat-to-down YoY in three of the last four quarters once the RNPL booking-timing effect is stripped out). A growth algorithm that depends on continued GBV volume growth is more exposed to a regulatory/supply shock than one where pricing power is doing the work. [Corrected 2026-10-06: the Q1 and Q2 2026 releases expect the simplified 15.5% single fee and guest-insurance revenue (+60% YoY in Q2) to lift the full-year take rate]

Every quarter's actual result in the table above met or exceeded the high end of the prior quarter's guidance range (explicitly stated by management each time: "exceeded the high end," "exceeded our outlook across every key metric"). Full-year revenue-growth guidance has also accelerated through the year: "at least low double digits" (Q4'25) → "low to mid teens" (Q1'26, raised) → tracking mid-to-high teens actual by Q2. This is a clean, verifiable four-quarter beat-and-raise pattern.

6. Earnings quality & balance sheet

  • FCF conversion: very strong — TTM FCF margin 37%, well above the ~19–22% net-income margin, reflecting genuine operating leverage plus the (non-repeatable-forever) benefit of a growing, negative-working-capital deposit float.
  • SBC: materially high, 9.7%–15.8% of revenue every quarter over two years — this is the real, recurring, dilutive cost the retail/asset-light playbooks warn against adding back uncritically. The offsetting, verifiable fact: diluted weighted-average share count has fallen from 626m (Q2 2025) to 597m (Q2 2026), a genuine ~4.6% YoY reduction, and the company states fully-diluted shares are down ~10% since buybacks began in Q3 2022 — buybacks are more than absorbing the RSU dilution on a net basis, which is a legitimate, evidenced rebuttal to the naive "add back SBC and ignore dilution" critique. Cumulative cash spent on buybacks + RSU tax withholding since Q3 2022: $13.6bn (per Q4 2025 release) — a very large capital-allocation commitment relative to the company's size.
  • GAAP vs adjusted: ABNB's own EPS is not separately XBRL-tagged (see §4 note) and diluted EPS/NI both benefited from a $60m uncertain-tax-position release and favourable FDII tax treatment in Q4 2025 disclosed by the company itself; long-term effective tax rate is guided to decline into the "mid-to-high teens" from 2026 due to the One Big Beautiful Bill Act (OBBBA).
  • Net debt/capital metrics: net cash (cash + STI − total debt) ≈ $9.6bn per V1's latest snapshot; even after the March-2026 $2.5bn note issuance, ABNB remains net-cash, not net-debt. Capex is immaterial (~0.3% of revenue) — a genuinely asset-light model, so leverage/coverage ratios are not a constraint here.
  • M&A: none pending or recently closed; the "hotels" initiative to date is a distribution partnership, not an acquisition.

7. Valuation snapshot — reconciliation with V1

V1 verdict: fair (score 0.10/1.0, near the boundary). NTM P/E 26.3x vs. ABNB's own only 53-month trading history (flagged by V1 itself as a "short/limited history" caveat — appropriately so; 53 months is not enough to establish a reliable own-history percentile through a full cycle) — currently the 23rd percentile of that short history. Peer median cited is 13.1x across BKNG/CCL/EXPE/HLT — I flag this peer set as heterogeneous per the sector playbook's own warning against blending owner/lessee/OTA/franchisor business models in one multiple: HLT is an asset-light hotel franchisor (structurally deserves a premium multiple of its own), CCL is a capital-intensive cruise operator, and EXPE is a lower-growth, lower-margin OTA — only BKNG is a close structural peer to ABNB. The 13.1x blended peer median is therefore less informative than it looks; I would not lean hard on the "ABNB trades at ~2x peer median" framing without unbundling the peer set first.

Reverse-DCF implied 10-year growth is +26.5% (using TTM EBIT margin 20.8%) against consensus FY1 growth of only +11.6% — the market is pricing continued mid-20s%/year growth for a decade. V1's own historical-CAGR fields are null (no 5/10-year delivered-growth comparison is possible — again a function of ABNB's short history as a public, post-pandemic-ramp company), so the "priced-for-vs-delivered" cross-check that anchors DG and DRI's valuation reconciliation is simply unavailable here — a genuine limitation, not an oversight. V1 base case: revenue growth 13.6%/yr, margin expanding to 22.5% (above the current TTM 20.8%, consistent with the margin-guidance raises in §5), exit multiple 33.7x — i.e., re-rating further up from today's already-premium 26.3x → base annualised 3-yr return +18.8%; bear −20.3%/bull +78.9% (an unusually wide bear/bull spread, reflecting genuine two-way uncertainty). Street 12-month target range $135–$220 (mean $184.35); V1's base 3-year value exceeds the Street 12-month high (same street_flag caveat as DG, less concerning given the different horizons).

My view: consistent = true, dossier_view = fair. I do not have a primary-source basis to call ABNB "cheap" — take rate is not expanding, the peer comparison is soft, and the base case's own math requires the multiple to expand again from an already-rich level, which is a materially weaker margin of safety than DG's setup (re-rating from a trough toward a historical norm). I also do not see grounds to call it "expensive"/"full" — the cash generation, balance sheet, and four-quarter beat-and-raise record are real. "Fair," with two-sided risk, is the right characterisation, and I agree with V1.

8. Bull case / bear case

Bull (3): 1. Four consecutive quarters of beating the high end of its own guidance on revenue, with Adjusted EBITDA margin guidance raised in three of the last four releases (28% Q4'25 trough → "at least 35.5%" current FY26 guide) — genuine, verifiable operating momentum. 2. $12.1bn net cash, 37% TTM FCF margin [Corrected 2026-10-06: $12.1bn is gross cash plus short-term investments; net cash is $9.6bn], and a demonstrated willingness/ability to shrink the diluted share count (−4.6% YoY) despite heavy RSU issuance — a rare combination of growth and capital-return capacity. 3. The direct-hotel-booking initiative in supply-constrained/regulated cities (NYC, LA, Madrid, San Francisco) is a credible, already-launched hedge against the regulatory risk in the bear case below, and the 2026 FIFA World Cup is a disclosed near-term demand catalyst.

Bear (3): 1. Short-term-rental regulation is spreading, not stabilising: Spain's Constitutional Court upheld Barcelona's decision not to renew any of its 10,101 tourist-apartment licenses (expiring Nov-2028); Spain separately fined Airbnb €64 million in December 2025 for advertising unlicensed listings; [Corrected 2026-10-06: per the 10-Q the fine is about EUR65M (reduced in Sept 2025 from EUR110M), disputed, suspended by a EUR70M surety bond, and no loss is accrued] and Budapest, Athens and Houston added new restrictions in 2026 alongside the already-restrictive NYC and Barcelona regimes. This is a real, monetised, geographically-widening risk to the core listings business that is not obviously reflected in a take rate that has not expanded. 2. Take rate itself has been flat-to-down YoY in three of the last four quarters — the margin story is 100% cost/leverage-driven, which is more fragile than a pricing-power-driven margin story if growth decelerates. 3. The DOJ filed an amended federal housing-discrimination complaint against Airbnb in March 2026 alleging a pattern-or-practice of discrimination (broader than the single-host allegation the case began with) — an active, escalating federal legal matter with headline and financial-liability risk.

9. Key risks & kill criteria (measurable)

  1. FY revenue-growth or Adjusted EBITDA-margin guidance is cut versus the immediately prior quarter's guidance (four straight raises/holds to date).
  2. Take rate (revenue ÷ GBV) falls for two consecutive quarters on a YoY basis by more than 100bps, stripped of the disclosed RNPL/FX timing effects — i.e., a genuine, explained monetisation deterioration.
  3. Diluted weighted-average share count rises YoY for two consecutive quarters (buybacks failing to offset RSU dilution — currently falling, −4.6% YoY at Q2 2026).
  4. Net cash (cash + STI − total debt) falls by more than $3 billion in a rolling 12 months outside of a disclosed, board-approved acquisition.
  5. A new city/national regulatory action (license non-renewal, platform-wide ban or a fine) is disclosed that management itself identifies as covering a "material" market, or cumulative disclosed regulatory fines exceed $150 million on a trailing-12-month basis (calibrated off the December-2025 Spain fine).

10. Catalysts & calendar

  • Next earnings: Q3 2026 results, estimated early November 2026 (historical pattern: Nov 1/6/7 in 2023–2025; not yet confirmed by the company).
  • FIFA World Cup 2026 (June–July 2026, US/Mexico/Canada) — disclosed demand catalyst already partly in the Q2 2026 numbers; full effect should show in Q3 2026 results.
  • Any ruling or settlement in United States v. Airbnb (DOJ housing-discrimination suit, amended complaint March 2026).
  • Expansion pace of the direct-hotel-booking initiative beyond its four initial cities.

11. Red-flag scan

  • DOJ housing-discrimination lawsuit: United States v. Airbnb, Inc., N.D. Cal., an active federal civil-rights case; DOJ filed an amended complaint in March 2026 broadening the allegation to a pattern-or-practice theory across multiple cities. Unresolved as of this dossier.
  • Spain fine: €64 million (~$70m), announced December 2025, for advertising unlicensed short-term rentals — a direct, monetised regulatory penalty (not merely a market restriction).   • Shareholder viewpoint-discrimination suit: Alliance Defending Freedom sued Airbnb (Delaware federal court, filed June 2025) over exclusion of a conservative shareholder proposal; a February 2026 ruling allowed the core claim to proceed. Lower financial materiality, a governance/proxy-process matter rather than a core-business risk.
  • Prior discrimination settlement: a 2024 class-action discrimination settlement included a $6m guest-compensation fund — already resolved, noted for completeness.
  • No auditor change, restatement or going-concern language identified in the filings reviewed. Insider Form-4 activity is high-frequency but consistent with routine RSU-vest sell-to-cover under 10b5-1 plans across a large Section-16-officer roster; no unusual acceleration in net insider selling was identified within the scope of this review.

1. Verdict

INCLUDE — thesis horizon 12–36 months. Diversified specialty P&C/reinsurance/mortgage insurer with an industry-leading underwriting record. The reinsurance/property-cat pricing cycle is softening (confirmed in primary filings, not just triage), but Arch's core combined ratio remains excellent (82–84% ex-cat/PYD), ROE is still 15–18% on an operating basis, and — unlike the triage note's qualitative "already prices in the cycle turn" claim — my own reverse valuation shows the price implies declining normalized earnings, i.e. the market is pricing in more cyclical deterioration than the evidence in the last two quarters supports. 2. Business in plain English

Arch Capital underwrites property & casualty insurance, reinsurance and mortgage insurance globally through three segments (Insurance, Reinsurance, Mortgage). It makes money from the spread between premiums collected and losses/expenses paid out (underwriting profit) plus investment income earned on the "float" (premiums held before claims are paid). Competitive position: management is widely regarded (and its own results confirm) as one of the most disciplined underwriters in the sector — it shrinks lines when pricing is inadequate and grows when pricing is attractive, rather than chasing volume.

dossiers.ACN:
ACN — Accenture plc

1. Verdict

INCLUDE-SMALL — the world's largest IT/management-consulting franchise, priced at 12x NTM earnings (a deep discount to its own 25–30x historical norm) for a business that is genuinely decelerating (revenue growth down to mid-single digits, new bookings down YoY, a real U.S.-federal headwind) but is not broken: margins are still expanding, free cash flow is enormous, and the balance sheet is net cash. Named reservation: bookings turned negative YoY this quarter and the GenAI-disintermediation risk to the core staff-augmentation model is real, not hypothetical, so this is a "priced-for-pessimism" holding, not a clean compounder. Horizon: 24–36 months.

2. Business in plain English

Accenture is the largest global IT and management-consulting firm: it helps large companies and governments redesign business processes, migrate and run IT systems (cloud, ERP, data/AI platforms), and increasingly build and run generative-AI applications, billing mostly on a time-and-materials or managed-services (outsourcing) basis. Revenue splits roughly evenly between project-based Consulting and longer-duration Managed Services; its moat is scale, deep client relationships across every major industry, and the switching costs of ripping out a multi-year outsourcing/systems-integration relationship.

3. Why the model likes it — durable or artefact?

b1 factor scores: composite percentile 0.90 (top decile), live_rank 50, quintile 5, decile 9 — genuinely strong across families. Quality is excellent and not an artefact (pct_gp_a 0.94, pct_roe 0.73, pct_leverage 0.91 — very low leverage, pct_asset_growth 0.96 — disciplined balance-sheet growth) and Value is strong (pct_fcfp 0.92, pct_ebit_ev 0.97, pct_bp 0.95 — cheap on cash flow, EBIT/EV and book value). Momentum (pct_mom_12_1 ≈0.74) is [Corrected 2026-10-06: wrong: pct_mom_12_1 is 0.135 (bottom quintile); also pct_gp_a 0.73, pct_roe 0.59, pct_asset_growth 0.35, pct_bp 0.74 per b1_live_scores.csv] positive despite the growth deceleration, likely reflecting the stock's re-rating discount bottoming. The quant score is a genuine value-and-quality signal, not a momentum chase; it is durable in the sense that it correctly identifies Accenture as statistically cheap for its quality, but it does not by itself resolve whether the growth deceleration is cyclical (federal budget noise) or the start of secular GenAI erosion — that judgment is made below.

6. Earnings quality & balance sheet (Accenture plc — single consolidated reporting entity; no bank/insurer-style

subsidiary capital metrics apply) - FCF conversion: OCF for the nine months ended 2026-05-31 was $9,267.9M against GAAP net income of $6,375.8M for the same period (10-Q XBRL) — FCF/NI (after $492.5M of nine-month capex) is comfortably >1x, i.e. cash earnings exceed accounting earnings, a genuine quality signal (deferred-revenue growth from Managed Services contracts is a contributor). - GAAP vs. adjusted gap: Accenture's own "adjusted" EPS excludes discrete FY25 business-optimization (restructuring) costs; FY26 guide is now GAAP $13.38–13.50 vs. adjusted $13.78–13.90 — the two have converged versus FY25 (which had a larger one-off drag), consistent with the FY25 restructuring program winding down. - Balance sheet (consolidated, 10-Q, 2026-05-31): cash and short-term investments ≈$10,171.6M; total long-term debt (senior notes) $5,029.4M plus $112.8M current portion (commercial paper + other) ≈$5,142M total debt → net cash ≈$5,029M, i.e. Accenture could retire all its debt with cash on hand roughly twice over. No restatement, going-concern, or investigation language found.

7. Valuation snapshot and V1 reconciliation

V1 systematic valuation (v1_valuation_table.csv): verdict "attractive," score 0.98. NTM P/E 12.01x (own-history percentile 56.5th — mid-range, i.e. not at a historic low multiple despite the "cheap" label, because Accenture's own multiple has structurally compressed over the cycle); peer median 11.93x (essentially in line with peers); V1's P/E-implied growth is -5.5% (the price implies the market expects revenue/earnings to shrink); V1's bear/base/bull 3-year annualized returns are 11.6% / 30.2% / 49.7%. V1 also flags its own base case as internally suspect: street_flag = "base 3y value exceeds Street 12m high target" — V1's base-case re-rating (to ~30%/yr for 3 years, implying the price roughly doubles) would put Accenture above even the highest analyst 12-month price target ($275 vs. current $176.11), which V1 itself surfaces as a red flag. I do not fully agree with V1's base case: a full re-rating back to Accenture's mid-2010s–2020 25–30x multiple looks too aggressive given the bookings deceleration and negative YoY bookings this quarter; I use a more conservative reverse-DCF: NTM EPS ≈$14.66, ~5–7%/yr EPS growth (in line with the FY26 EPS guide's 10–11% this year, decelerating toward mid-single-digit consulting/managed-services growth longer term) with a modest re-rating to 14–15x (still below history, reflecting partial resolution of the federal/GenAI overhang) implies roughly base case ~11–13%/yr total return (including the 3.7% dividend and continued buybacks) — well below V1's 30.2%/yr but still comfortably positive and, crucially, below what I believe Accenture can deliver on a normalized basis if the deceleration stabilizes rather than compounds. Bear case: LC growth stays near 2–3%, no re-rating (multiple stays ~12x), federal drag persists longer than guided → roughly 3–5%/yr (mostly the dividend). Bull case: bookings reaccelerate as GenAI transformation work becomes a net new-demand driver rather than a cannibalization risk, multiple re-rates to 17–18x → roughly 20–23%/yr. valuation_view_vs_v1: dossier view cheap, consistent: true in direction (both V1 and I see the stock as statistically cheap) but inconsistent on magnitude — V1's base case is more optimistic than mine (reconciliation: V1's base-case re-rating assumption is not supported by the current bookings trend, and V1 itself flags this via street_flag).

8. Bull case / Bear case

Bull: (1) 12x NTM P/E against an 11.2% FCF yield and a net-cash balance sheet is priced for far more pessimism than a still-growing, margin-expanding franchise (GAAP operating margin +20bps YoY in Q3) usually receives; (2) generative-AI transformation bookings and large ($100M+) client deals are still growing (104 such bookings YTD, up 13%, per the Q3 release) — GenAI may be a net tailwind for large-scale reinvention work, not only a threat to staff-augmentation revenue; (3) $8.2B already returned to shareholders YTD (buybacks + dividends) provides a floor-like capital-return yield even absent a re-rating. Bear: (1) new bookings fell YoY in Q3 FY26 (-2% USD/-3% LC) for the first time in this two-year window — a leading indicator for future revenue, not yet a lagging one; (2) the U.S. federal segment is an acknowledged, guided-for drag (≈1% of FY26 growth) tied to government contract reviews/terminations, and could worsen with further budget actions; (3) the long-run risk that GenAI compresses demand and pricing for traditional staff-augmentation consulting is structural and not yet resolved one way or the other by the data in hand.

9. Key risks & kill criteria (measurable)

  1. Local-currency revenue growth below 3% (the bottom of the FY26 guide) for two consecutive quarters.
  2. New bookings YoY decline (USD) continuing for two more consecutive quarters (one quarter, Q3 FY26, already negative).
  3. U.S. federal segment drag exceeding the guided ~1% impact on full-year local-currency growth (i.e., realized federal drag disclosed at >1.5% in a future quarterly release).
  4. GAAP operating margin expansion stalling or reversing YoY (currently guided to 50–70bps of full-year FY26 expansion; any quarter of YoY margin contraction would break this).
  5. Consolidated net cash position (cash and short-term investments minus total debt, from the 10-Q balance sheet) falling below $2 billion, e.g. from debt-funded M&A (such as Dragos) rather than cash-funded.

  • Dragos/runZero/NetRise acquisition close (terms/timing not disclosed in the reviewed release) is a near-term item to confirm in the FY26 10-K or a subsequent 8-K.

11. Red-flag scan

No restatement, auditor-change, going-concern, or SEC/DOJ-investigation language found in the reviewed 10-Q (2026-05-31); the filing explicitly states no material change to the FY25 10-K risk factors. No material named litigation beyond the routine Commitments and Contingencies reference. dossiers.ADBE:
ADBE — Adobe Inc. (Application Software, Information Technology)

1. Verdict

INCLUDE-SMALL (half weight) — 12–36 month horizon. Adobe is priced by the market as if genAI will structurally erode Creative Cloud, but the reverse DCF shows the stock needs 10 years of shrinking free cash flow to justify today's price, while the company is actually growing revenue and FCF double-digits and buying back ~5–7% of its share count a year. Sized small, not full weight, because the core bear case (AI-native tools substituting for paid seats) is genuinely unresolved and the company just lost both its CEO and CFO within six months.

2. Business in plain English

Adobe sells subscription software: Creative Cloud (Photoshop, Premiere, Illustrator, and the Firefly generative-AI tools bundled into it) to designers, marketers, photographers and students; Document Cloud (Acrobat/PDF, e-signature) to every knowledge worker; and Experience Cloud (marketing/analytics platforms) to enterprises. Revenue is ~97% subscription, billed annually or monthly, so it is recurring and priced with high switching costs (file formats, muscle memory, team workflows). It makes money the way most SaaS companies do: high (~89%) gross margin, low incremental cost per seat, most of the cost base is R&D, sales/marketing and content-delivery infrastructure. Its competitive position is entrenchment in professional creative and document workflows against a wave of new AI-native point tools (Midjourney, Sora, Figma, Canva) that can each do a slice of what Adobe does, for less.

3. Why the model likes it — durable or artefact?

Adobe screens at the very top of the v4 quant model's composite (composite_qvm 0.885, decile 8/10, rank 118): quality (fam_Q 0.99 — gross-profit/assets 98th pct, ROE 84th pct) and value (fam_V 0.92 — FCF/price 93rd pct, earnings yield 92nd pct) are both exceptional, while momentum is in the bottom quintile (fam_M 0.166, 12-month momentum 17th pct) and the earnings-surprise/sentiment factor is also weak (fam_S 0.326, SUE 33rd pct). This is a classic contrarian value-versus-momentum split, not an artefact: quality and value are computed straight from filed financials that are, in fact, still growing (revenue +13% y/y, non-GAAP EPS +15% y/y in the most recent quarter); the weak momentum/sentiment factors are the market's real-time verdict on the AI-disruption narrative and the Q4 revenue guide landing a hair below consensus. Both readings are correct simultaneously: the business is executing, and the market is discounting it hard for a risk that has not yet shown up in the numbers.

1. Verdict

INCLUDE-SMALL (half weight) — 12–36 month horizon. Sized small, not full weight, because the reverse DCF shows the market has already priced in 10-year FCF growth (~9–14% depending on discount-rate assumption) that is at the upper edge of — and by some readings modestly above — a prudent through-cycle base case for an analog semiconductor company, and the stock is trading near its highest-ever revenue run-rate, which the sector's own playbook flags as exactly the point multiples look least trustworthy.

2. Business in plain English

Analog Devices designs and sells analog, mixed-signal and DSP chips — the components that convert real-world signals (voltage, temperature, motion, radio-frequency) into digital data and back — into industrial automation, automotive (EV powertrain, ADAS, in-cabin), communications infrastructure (including AI data-center power and connectivity) and consumer electronics. It sells through direct enterprise relationships and distributors, with long (5–10+ year) product design cycles once a chip is "designed in" to a customer's product, which makes revenue sticky but also slow to re-accelerate after a design loss. It earns money on high gross margins (~65–67%) typical of analog IP with long product lifecycles and low process-node intensity relative to logic/memory chips.

3. Why the model likes it — durable or artefact?

ADI's composite_qvm score (0.503, decile 7, rank 173) is unremarkable overall, but the composition matters: momentum (fam_M 0.683, 69th pct) and earnings-surprise/sentiment (fam_S 0.723, 72nd pct) are doing the work, while quality (fam_Q 0.399 — gross-profit/assets only 29th pct, ROE 25th pct) and value (fam_V 0.419, FCF/price 40th pct) are middling. This is the mirror image of ADBE: ADI is being re-rated on execution momentum during a cyclical recovery, not because it screens as statistically cheap or exceptionally profitable on trailing numbers. That is a durable but cycle-dependent reason — real (three consecutive quarters of guide-and-beat, an AI-data-center growth leg that did not exist at the prior cycle peak), but it will fade automatically once the base effect from the FY24 trough laps, so the momentum score should not be read as a standing quality signal.

8. Bull case / bear case

Bull (3): 1. Client-funds interest income is a structural tailwind as long as short rates stay above zero — a multi-year annuity ADP does not have to "earn" through sales effort. 2. New-business bookings and retention have both been resilient through a soft small-business hiring cycle, suggesting share gains against smaller competitors (Paychex, Gusto, Rippling) rather than market softness. 3. Margin expansion (+140bps in Q4 alone) shows real operating leverage still available in a business the market already treats as mature.

Bear (3): 1. Client-funds interest income falls mechanically if the Fed cuts rates faster than the curve currently implies — a real, quantifiable headwind to adjusted EBIT that is macro, not company-specific. 2. Well-funded, product-led challengers (Gusto, Rippling, Deel) are taking share in the smallest-employer segment where switching costs are lowest; ADP's own growth is concentrated in larger, stickier accounts. 3. At 23.7x trailing earnings for high-single-digit growth, there is little room for a guidance miss without multiple compression on top of any earnings miss.

1. Verdict

2. Business in plain English

Autodesk sells subscription software for people who design and build physical things: AutoCAD and Revit for architecture/engineering/construction (AECO), Fusion/Inventor for manufacturing, and Flame/Maya for media and entertainment. Customers pay annual or multi-year subscriptions; switching costs come from decades of files in Autodesk's proprietary formats, industry-standard certifications built around its tools, and deep workflow integration on large capital projects. With the August-2026 MaintainX acquisition (a mobile-first CMMS/asset- maintenance platform), Autodesk is extending from "design and build" into "operate," per its own August 2026 release.

The informative reverse calculation is market-implied deal probability: with deal value $15.00 and a no-deal reference price of ~$10.7 (the pre-rumour VWAP implied by the 40.3% premium), $14.87 implies about a 97% chance of closing (ignoring time value and dividends).
  • Spread: 0.87% to $15.00. If it closes Dec 31 2026 (97 days) that is ~3.3% annualised, or ~7.7% annualised including one $0.17595 dividend; for a Mar 31 2027 close (187 days), ~1.7% or ~4.0% including one dividend (dividends after Q2'26 not verified). Versus a 4.24% 3-month risk-free rate (V1 assumption) the excess return is small relative to a ~28% downside tail; break-even break-probability is about 4%.
  • Standalone fundamentals: EV/2025 Adjusted EBITDA is not computed because the press-release EV ($33.4B) is proportional while the $2,871M Adjusted EBITDA is consolidated (mixed basis). AES is a capital-hungry standalone (negative FCF, equity claims of ~$8B outside AES common), so my standalone base value is below the deal price: implied_vs_base = "above" (price embeds the deal, not fundamentals).
  • 3-year scenario returns (annualised, total return): bear -9.4%, base +4.9%, bull +7.4%. Basis: base = deal closes ~Jan 2027, holder receives $15.00 plus two quarterly dividends of $0.176, proceeds then earn a 4.2% cash rate for the remaining ~2.7 years; bear = deal fails, price ~$10.70 at year 3 plus ~$0.35 dividends (dividend cut); bull = deal fails or is re-bid and the standalone equity reaches ~$17 with four $0.35 dividends. Bull: (1) Shareholders, HSR, CFIUS and the Ohio regulator have all approved, removing the largest regulatory hurdles; financing is committed and not a closing condition; (2) large termination fees protect AES ($100M/$588M from Parent); (3) 2025 adjusted results beat the range "Adjusted EPS of $2.10 to $2.26" ($2.34 actual).   1. Termination of the merger agreement or an amended price below $15.00 (any 8-K Item 1.02 or amended Item 1.01).

dossiers.AFL:
Aflac Incorporated (AFL) - Fundamental Diligence Dossier (F128, standard depth)

Verdict: WATCH, 12-36 month horizon. Reason: a high-quality, well-capitalised supplemental insurer (adjusted return on equity excluding foreign-currency remeasurement 16.6%, Japanese solvency ratio 226%) that is priced for about +3% a year earnings growth when my base case is +1%; per-share growth in 2026 comes from buying back about 7% of the company a year with cash that exceeds earnings. Change condition: price near $98 (base-case present value, about 13% below 113.72), or evidence that Aflac Japan's underlying premiums stop shrinking and the yen strengthens. Triage (Q05, not advanced, "shrinking core Japan block") is confirmed on price, not on quality, and its -18.6% forward-EPS figure is largely a comparison artefact (below).

1. Business in plain English

Aflac sells supplemental health and life insurance (cancer, medical, accident, savings-type life) to individuals through agents and brokers. About two-thirds of adjusted pre-tax profit comes from Aflac Japan (premiums in yen, with persistency above 92%); the US business sells workplace voluntary benefits, plus group life, disability, dental and vision that are scaling. Earnings come from premiums less claims and expenses plus investment income on a $103B portfolio. Moat is agency distribution, brand and the locked-in block of in-force policies; the drag is that Japan's in-force premiums are shrinking (limited-pay policies reaching paid-up, reinsurance) and a weak yen (159.45 per dollar in Q2 2026 vs 144.60) cuts reported dollar earnings.

2. Why the model likes it / durability

b1 shows a financial-sector quality and value profile: Yahoo trailing P/E 12.3x on GAAP EPS 9.27 (inflated by investment gains), forward P/E 15.1x on 7.54, beta 0.58, payout 0.26, Street "buy" (mean target 118.5, range 99-138, 15 analysts). Durable: capital ratios are strong and buybacks are large. Artefacts: GAAP EPS (9.27 TTM) includes net investment gains and derivative and currency gains, so use adjusted EPS; FY2025 adjusted EPS of $7.49 includes a $0.76 boost from the Q3 2025 actuarial assumption update (Q3 2025 call), so FY2026 consensus of about 7.0 looks like a 6% decline but is about +4% on an underlying basis (7.49 - 0.76 = 6.73).

Aflac gives segment ranges on the CFO call (prepared-remarks transcript, Exhibit 99.3 to each 8-K), not an EPS range. (prior 2025 Japan range not opened). FY2025 segment outcomes were not retrieved. - Q4 2025 call (0001628280-26-005458), 2026 outlook: "For Aflac Japan, we expect underlying earned premiums to decline 1% to 2% in 2026, and we also expect the expense ratio to be in the 20% to 23% range. Japan's margin range is 2 points lower than 2025's 35%-38%: a guided step-down. - Q1 2026 call (0001628280-26-028396): no change to these ranges was stated in the prepared remarks (I searched the text). - Q2 2026 call (0001628280-26-054333): "we now expect to be at the high end of our guidance range of 60% to 63% for the full year of 2026, excluding the annual actuarial assumption review in Q3" (Japan benefit ratio: a worse outlook, year-to-date 63.4%) and "We expect our net earned premium growth rate for 2026 to be just below our guidance range of 3% to 6%, versus previous guidance for the low end of this range" (a trim).   • Reserve assumptions: 2025's Q3 actuarial review added $0.76 to EPS; the 2026 Q3 review (due with Q3 results) can move either way and is excluded from the Japan 60%-63% benefit-ratio range.
  • Stock-based compensation is not material to this analysis.

6. Valuation and reverse DCF (price 113.72; market cap about $57.0B on 501.3M shares; 25 Sep 2026 close)

V1 row: none exists for AFL in v1_valuation_table.csv or v1_valuation.json (insurers are not covered), so v1_verdict is null; this is the first valuation view. Multiples: 16.0x FY2026 EPS of about 7.10 (H1 actual 3.50 plus H2 about 3.60; consensus per Yahoo 7.02 current year, 7.54 forward), 15.0x TTM adjusted EPS of 7.56 (2.49 + 1.57 + 1.75 + 1.75), price to book 1.88x GAAP and 2.07x adjusted book ($55.01); dividend yield 2.1% ($2.44), total shareholder yield about 9% at the H1 pace. Reverse DCF (owner earnings = TTM adjusted earnings $3.9B, distributed in full as dividends and buybacks; cost of equity 9.0%; terminal growth 1%; ten years): the price implies +3.0% a year earnings growth (+1.1% with a lower 8.5% cost of equity and 2% terminal growth, +2.0% at 9.0% and 2%). Evidence-based cases: bear -2% a year (Japan premiums shrink 2%, benefit ratio above 63%, yen at 160+ for years, credit or cyber losses), base +1.0% (Japan underlying premiums -1% to -2% and margin 33%-36%, US premiums +3%-6% at a 17%-20% margin, about $50M a year of switch-trade income), bull +3.5% (yen recovery, reinsurance lifts ROE, Miraito and Anshin Palette sales growth). Present value per share: bear 79.3, base 98.2, bull 117.7 versus 113.72. Implied growth is above base. Scenario returns, 3 years annualised total return (start FY2026 adjusted EPS 7.10; dividend $2.44 growing 3/5/7%; exit P/E 11.5x/14.5x/16.5x): bear -7.8% (EPS flat at 7.10, 11.5x); base +3.7% (EPS +5% a year, made up of about +1% earnings and about -4% share count, to 8.22, 14.5x); bull +11.0% (EPS +8%, 16.5x).

7. Bull and bear

Bull: (1) capital is strong (ESR 226%, RBC above 600%, leverage 21.8%) and management is deploying it ("$983 million" of repurchases in Q2); (2) new Japan products are selling (H1 sales +7.0% to ¥37.3B, Miraito cancer, Tsumitasu savings life, Anshin Palette medical) and Japan's margin is up 270 basis points in H1; (3) a yen that strengthens from 159 lifts reported dollar earnings, and the reinsurance target widened to "up to 30% of FSA reserves" should raise ROE.   2. Aflac Japan pre-tax adjusted margin below 33% for two consecutive quarters, or the full-year Japan benefit ratio (excluding the Q3 actuarial review) above 63%.

1. Verdict

INCLUDE-SMALL — A genuinely improving specialty-insurance franchise (Connected Living volume growth, disciplined Global Housing underwriting, shrinking share count, rising holding-company liquidity) trading at a full-but-not-extreme valuation, with a real, company-disclosed EPS deceleration mechanism baked into H2 2026 that the market may not fully be pricing given persistent price-target raises. Thesis horizon: 12–24 months.

2. The Business

Assurant is a specialty insurance holding company operating two segments. Global Lifestyle (77.5% of FY2025 net earned premiums, fees and other income of $9,582.5M [FY2025 10-K, Global Lifestyle segment table, filed 2026-02-19]) sells mobile device protection/trade-in, extended service contracts, and credit/financial-services insurance through mobile carriers and retailers ("Connected Living," $5,378.7M FY2025, +11.9% YoY), plus vehicle and commercial-equipment protection ("Global Automotive," $4,203.8M FY2025, +1.1% YoY) [FY2025 10-K, filed 2026-02-19]. Global Housing (22.5% of segment revenue, $2,768.8M FY2025 [FY2025 10-K]) underwrites lender-placed homeowners/flood/manufactured-home insurance plus renters and specialty products — genuine catastrophe-exposed underwriting risk. Global Lifestyle is best analyzed as a capital-light, fee/administration-heavy business with a real but secondary loss-ratio component (its own Adjusted EBITDA margin is only ~8% of revenue [FY2025 10-K] because commissions to carrier/retail partners and cost of trade-in inventory dominate the cost base); Global Housing is the true underwriting business where combined-ratio-style economics and catastrophe exposure matter most. Assurant simplified its portfolio further in FY2025-26: a legacy run-off subsidiary holding fully-reinsured individual life, annuity and long-term-care blocks (reinsured to John Hancock) was classified held-for-sale in Q4 2025 and sold in March 2026 for an $11.2M cumulative loss on sale [FY2025 10-K Note 3; Q2 2026 10-Q Note 4, filed 2026-08-06] — following the larger 2021 Global Preneed divestiture to CUNA Mutual ($1.35B) [company press release, 2021-08-02, pre-dating this dossier's window but relevant context].

3. Why the Model Likes It

The 0.80 composite is driven by Quality (0.859) and Momentum (0.834) percentiles, with Value (0.711) more modest [lead_prelim_rank.csv]. Momentum is evidenced, not manufactured: revenue grew every quarter for the last six at +6.7% to +11.3% YoY [derived from 10-K/10-Q XBRL, see §4], adjusted EPS ex-catastrophes grew double-digits, and guidance has been raised three times in the last four releases with the raises subsequently validated by actuals (§5) — this looks like a genuine re-rating on improving fundamentals rather than a hot run into an air pocket, except that the improvement in Global Housing profitability (Adjusted EBITDA +28% FY2025 [FY2025 10-K]) is partly a function of $113.1M of favorable prior-year reserve development (PYD) in 2025 on top of $106.7M in 2024 [FY2025 10-K MD&A, filed 2026-02-19] — a two-year tailwind management itself says will not repeat in H2 2026 (§4, §6). Quality (ROE ~15.9% on a full-year-average-equity GAAP basis, rising from 13.4% FY2023 [ratios.py output on 10-K data]; OCF/NI of 2.10x FY2025) is real but partly inflated by that same reserve-development windfall and by two years of below-average catastrophe losses. Value at the 71st percentile is driven by a trailing P/E of ~13x-15x, not by a discount to book — on a P/B basis (~2.15x) the stock is fully valued for its current ROE (§7). Net read: momentum and quality are directionally real (Connected Living growth, buybacks, improving underwriting discipline) but a meaningful share of the last two years' earnings beats rode a fading reserve-development tailwind, not a permanent step-change in loss experience.
