dossiers.CIEN:
CIEN — Ciena Corporation (Diligence agent F95, wave 6)

1. Verdict

WATCH — 12–36 month thesis horizon. Ciena is the best-positioned pure-play optical/coherent-networking supplier to the AI-datacenter-interconnect buildout, and the fundamentals are real (37% revenue growth, raised guidance three quarters running), but the stock (+~163% over 12 months, triage data) already prices in roughly two more decades of AI-capex-grade growth. The implied 10-year FCF growth (~21%) is above a defensible base case (~15%), so this is priced for perfection, not a value opportunity today.

2. Business in plain English

Ciena designs and sells optical transport, routing/switching and network-automation software that lets telecom carriers, cloud/hyperscale providers and web-scale customers move enormous volumes of data between and inside datacenters. It makes money selling hardware (line systems, transponders) plus recurring software/services (network management, maintenance). Competitive position: the largest independent (non-Cisco/Huawei/Nokia-affiliated) optical-networking supplier, with deep incumbency at Tier-1 telecom and, increasingly, "cloud provider" (hyperscaler) customers building AI datacenter interconnects.

3. Why the model likes it / durability

Factor data flags very strong momentum and earnings-momentum (b1_live_scores: composite ~0.49, live_rank 253, mom_12_1 in the 90th+ percentile within tech) driven by a genuine, filed-and-verified acceleration: revenue growth 24%→31%→36%→37% YoY over the last four reported quarters. [Corrected 2026-10-06: actual YoY growth of the last four quarters is +20.3% (Q4 FY25), +33.1% (Q1 FY26), +39.5% (Q2 FY26), +37.0% (Q3 FY26); growth peaked in Q2 and eased in Q3] This is not a one-off — it is backed by a $2.5bn remaining-performance-obligation (RPO) balance (10-Q, Note on revenue) and management explicitly attributes it to hyperscaler AI-interconnect demand, not a single customer. The durability question is whether this AI-datacenter capex supercycle continues at this intensity for years (bull case) or normalizes once the current wave of hyperscaler buildouts matures (bear case) — this is a real, evidence-based debate, not an accounting artefact.

5. Guidance track record (last 4 releases, FY26)

  • Q1 FY26 release (Mar 5 2026): guided FY26 revenue $5.9bn–$6.3bn.
  • Q2 FY26 release (Jun 4 2026): raised to $6.3bn ± $100m (32% YoY at midpoint) and guided Q3 revenue $1.625bn ± $50m.

Three consecutive quarters of raised guidance, each cited directly from the exhibit 99.1 press releases (accessions 0001628280-26-015006, -040767, -060361 wrappers). No guidance cut in the period reviewed.

6. Earnings quality & balance sheet

  • Cash & debt (consolidated, from the Q3 FY26 10-Q balance sheet): cash $2,445.7m (Aug 1 2026) vs $1,091.95m at FYE (Nov 1 2025) — a $1.35bn jump. Long-term debt (noncurrent) $3,229.8m (Aug 1 2026) vs $1,524.2m at FYE — also a jump. Entity scope: consolidated Ciena Corporation, per the condensed consolidated balance sheet, Item 1.
  • Cause (Note 13, Short-Term and Long-Term Debt, consolidated basis): on June 11 2026 Ciena closed a private offering of $2.875bn 0.00% Convertible Senior Notes due 2031 ("2031 Notes"), together with a bond-hedge/warrant structure (paid $988.4m for the convertible bond hedge, received $873.4m from warrant sales — a standard capped-call overlay that raises the effective conversion price and caps near-term dilution). Proceeds were earmarked for refinancing an existing term loan, general corporate purposes and, explicitly, "investments to enhance supply chain capacity" — i.e., funding manufacturing capacity for the AI-interconnect buildout — plus a $140m ($~0.3m shares) opportunistic buyback. Net debt (gross LT debt $3,229.8m − cash $2,445.7m) ≈ $784m, modest relative to a ~$52bn market cap. Zero cash coupon on the new notes minimizes near-term interest-expense drag; the trade-off is potential equity dilution above the (higher, warrant-hedged) conversion price and reliance on convertible-market access.
  • FCF conversion: nine-month FY26 operating cash flow $683.6m, capex $194.9m → 9-mo FCF ≈ $488.7m. LTM (Nov25–Aug26 pieced from 10-Q/10-K) OCF ≈ $1,055m, capex ≈ $240m → LTM FCF ≈ $814m, i.e. FCF margin ~13.9% of LTM revenue (~$5.86bn) — solid and improving, though capex is rising (supply-chain investment) which will pressure FCF near-term even as revenue grows.
  • RPO $2.5bn (10-Q Note 3), most due within 3 years — a genuine forward-demand signal, but subject to the supply conditions the filing itself flags.
  • Share count: ~142.1m basic / ~146.0m diluted shares outstanding (Aug 1 2026 10-Q cover page and EPS note); modest increase YoY from equity comp, partly offset by the opportunistic $140m buyback.
  • Litigation: ordinary-course employment, commercial, tax, IP-indemnification claims (10-Q Note 20, incorporated into Item 1 Legal Proceedings) — no material litigation, no SEC/DOJ investigation, no restatement or material-weakness language identified in the reviewed filings.

7. Valuation snapshot and reverse DCF

No V1 systematic valuation row exists for CIEN (v1_valuation_table.csv was checked — no match); v1_verdict = null, per program rule. - Price (2026-09-25 close, per v4/data snapshot): $356.91. Trailing GAAP P/E ≈79.0x (TTM diluted EPS ≈$4.48, rebuilt from the last four quarters). Forward (NTM) P/E ≈35.9x on consensus NTM EPS $9.93 (d4 live snapshot). Analyst mean target $516.83 (range $347–$660, 19 analysts, consensus "buy"). - Reverse DCF (FCF-based): LTM FCF ≈$814m; enterprise value ≈$53.0bn (mkt cap ≈$52.2bn + consolidated net debt ≈$0.78bn). Solving a 10-year two-stage FCF DCF (WACC 9.0–9.5%, terminal growth 2.5–3.0%) for the growth rate that clears today's EV gives an implied 10-year FCF CAGR of ~21–23%. [Corrected 2026-10-06: FCF here adds back stock-based compensation (LTM ~$212m) and the 9.0-9.5% rate is not tied to the 5.17% 10-year Treasury plus a stated equity risk premium; restated implied 10-year FCF CAGR is ~25-27% at 9.0-9.5% and ~30% at an 11% cost of equity, still ABOVE the ~15% base case, verdict unchanged] - My base case: mid-to-high-teens FCF growth (~15%/yr) over 10 years — the AI-interconnect capex wave normalizes from its current intensity within 3–5 years even if it does not reverse, and rising manufacturing capex (the very capacity the new convertible funds) will compress the FCF margin before it expands it. Implied growth (~21%) is ABOVE this base case → the stock is priced for the current growth rate to persist for a decade, which is a demanding, not conservative, assumption. This is a great business at a price that leaves little room for the cycle to even partially normalize. - Peers (qualitative): Cisco (larger, more diversified, cheaper multiple — ~20x NTM per Q05/Q11 triage data), Lumentum/LITE and Coherent/COHR (higher growth, similarly extended multiples — see COHR dossier), Nokia (much cheaper, slower growth). CIEN's multiple sits between the "cheap incumbent" (CSCO) and "extreme momentum" (LITE) peers.

8. Bull case / Bear case

Bull (3 points): (1) AI datacenter interconnect spend is structurally multi-year, not a one-off refresh cycle, and Ciena's incumbency with both telecom and hyperscale customers is a genuine moat; (2) three consecutive guidance raises and a $2.5bn RPO show real, filed demand, not sentiment; (3) the 0%-coupon convertible funds capacity without near-term cash-interest drag, so operating leverage should show up in FCF as the new capacity utilizes.

Bear (3 points): (1) customer concentration risk — management itself flags that "a small number of [cloud] customers become a larger portion of our business" (10-Q MD&A, quoted) — a pause by 1–2 hyperscalers would hit growth hard; (2) capex intensity is rising (9-mo capex $194.9m vs $95.4m prior year, +104%) precisely because the company is racing to add capacity — if demand normalizes before that capacity is needed, margins and returns on the new investment suffer; (3) at 79x trailing / 36x forward P/E and an implied ~21%+ 10-year FCF CAGR, there is essentially no valuation cushion for a slower AI-capex year, a competitive share loss, or a supply-chain hiccup.

9. Key risks & measurable kill criteria

  1. Quarterly revenue growth decelerates below 20% YoY for two consecutive quarters (vs the current 33–39% run-rate) — signals the AI-interconnect cycle is normalizing faster than the base case assumes.
  2. RPO ($2.5bn as of Aug 1 2026) declines quarter-over-quarter for two consecutive quarters — a leading indicator of order softening ahead of revenue.
  3. Consolidated net debt (gross LT debt minus cash) exceeds $2.5bn — would signal the convertible-funded capacity buildout is burning more cash than the FCF ramp can support.
  4. Any single "cloud provider" customer disclosed (or inferable from segment concentration commentary) at >15% of revenue — the concentration risk management itself flagged crystallizing.
  5. A guidance cut (vs. the immediately prior quarter's range) — would break the three-quarter beat-and-raise pattern that currently underpins the bull case.

10. Catalysts & calendar

  • Next earnings: Q4 FY26 / full-year results, estimated mid-December 2026 (pattern: prior two fiscal-year-ends reported Dec 11 2025 and Dec 12 2024; not yet confirmed by an 8-K as of this writing — treat as an estimate).
  • Convertible-note conversion price and any capped-call unwind mechanics become relevant if CIEN trades materially above the (undisclosed in the excerpt reviewed) conversion price before 2031.

11. Red-flag scan

No auditor change, no material weakness, no going-concern language, no SEC/DOJ investigation, no restatement found in the FY25 10-K or the three FY26 10-Qs reviewed. The one flag worth naming explicitly is the debt/cash step-change in Q3 FY26 (Note 13) — fully explained by the June 2026 convertible offering, not a surprise or an accounting issue, but a first-time reader of the balance sheet alone (without the notes) could misread it as distress; it is the opposite — a proactive capacity-funding raise.

dossiers.CINF:
CINF — Cincinnati Financial Corporation — Fundamental Diligence Dossier

1. Verdict: INCLUDE-SMALL (half weight). Thesis horizon 12–24 months. Genuinely attractive valuation (cheapest of the three names on both peer and own-history basis) and a strong 2025 underwriting-improvement trend, but the most recent quarter (Q2 2026) shows real deterioration — a 100.8% consolidated combined ratio (an underwriting loss), driven by Commercial Lines at 104.1% and Ohio storm losses "nearly four times" the 5-year Q2 average — and current-accident-year ex-catastrophe losses are also rising YoY (85.1%→88.1%), so this is not purely a weather blip. Sell-side FY1/FY0 EPS revisions skew negative (6 down/1 up; 8 down/0 up). Cheap for a reason that needs one more quarter to resolve.

2. Business in plain English

Cincinnati Financial is a super-regional property & casualty insurer selling commercial lines, personal lines, and excess & surplus (E&S) lines almost exclusively through a network of independent agencies (under 3,000 agency relationships, expanding), plus a small life-insurance subsidiary. Its defining feature versus peers is an unusually large equity securities portfolio held for total return (~$13.2bn, ~40% of invested assets) rather than the bond-heavy mix typical of insurers — this makes GAAP net income swing with the stock market, which is why the company (and this dossier, per program instructions) reports on non-GAAP operating income, which strips out realized/unrealized investment gains, as the truer read of underwriting performance.

3. Why the model likes it — durable or artefact?

b1 composite 0.875 (decile 9), but live_rank 62 and live_top30 = False despite the decile-9 score — an internal inconsistency versus HIG (decile 10, rank 20) and MTB (decile 10, rank 35) that this dossier cannot explain from the data provided (flagged as a data conflict below, not silently accepted). Quant strengths: pct_roe 83rd pctile, pct_ocf_a 93rd, pct_sue 90th (strong earnings-surprise history: beats 7 of last 8 quarters, avg surprise +59% — inflated by the investment-gain volatility in GAAP EPS discussed below, so partly artefact: the model may be rewarding GAAP earnings surprises that are really equity-market beta, not underwriting skill). Momentum family in the CSV shows CINF was NOT among the ≤2-insurers cap in the old v3 CIO rule (v3 held AIZ+HIG as its two insurers, not CINF) — a genuinely new addition versus v3, not a re-underwrite.

Share buybacks were not disclosed/quantified in three of the four releases reviewed (Q1'26, Q3'25, Q4'25 releases state "not stated" for repurchase volume) — an information gap, not a finding of no buyback activity; diluted share count did fall slightly Q2'25→Q2'26 (157.8M→155.7M), implying some repurchase activity nets against option/incentive issuance.
  • No debt/leverage or capital-adequacy figures were surfaced in the press-release extracts reviewed (P&C-appropriate metrics — statutory surplus, RBC — sit in the 10-K/statutory filings, not pulled given the time budget). Disclosed gap, not a red flag.

7. Valuation snapshot (v1 pipeline, 2026-09-25 close)

P/B 1.52x vs. peer median 1.79x — 43rd percentile of CINF's own history: genuinely cheap on both axes, the most attractive of the three names on valuation alone. Justified-P/B implies a sustainable 10.8% ROE, vs. actual TTM (GAAP) ROE 20.0% — but TTM GAAP ROE is itself equity-market-inflated per §6, so the "cheapness" partly reflects the market correctly discounting non-recurring investment gains, not necessarily mispricing. V1 base-case 3-year annualized return +11.5% (bear +2.9%, bull +20.7%) — note bear case here is still positive, unusual among the three names, because book value has a large cushion of unrealized gains. V1 verdict: "attractive."

8. Bull case

  1. Cheapest of the three on both peer-relative and own-history P/B, with a bear-case scenario that still shows a positive 3-year return per V1 — a real valuation cushion.
  2. 2025 underwriting trend (Q1'25 113.3% combined → Q3'25 88.2% → Q4'25 85.2%) shows the franchise can produce excellent combined ratios when catastrophe experience is benign, and agency-count growth (355 new appointments in 2025, 220 more in 1H26, "still under 3,000... a lot of runway") is a genuine, quantified distribution-expansion story.
  3. Large embedded equity-portfolio gains ($8.9bn pre-tax) provide a capital cushion that a pure-bond-portfolio peer would not have in a rising-rate environment.

9. Bear case

  1. Q2 2026 combined ratio of 100.8% is an underwriting loss, with current-accident-year ex-cat losses also rising YoY (85.1%→88.1%) — the deterioration is not fully explained by catastrophe severity alone; Commercial Lines specifically weakened from 92.9% to 104.1% combined YoY.
  2. GAAP earnings and book-value growth are heavily equity-market-dependent (40% of the portfolio); a sustained equity drawdown would hit reported book value and GAAP income much harder than a typical bond-heavy P&C peer, even though underwriting is unaffected.
  3. Sell-side FY1 (6 down/1 up in 30 days) and FY0 (8 down/0 up) EPS revisions both skew decisively negative — consistent with, not contradicting, the Q2'26 underwriting miss.

10. Key risks & kill criteria

  1. Consolidated combined ratio stays above 100% for a second consecutive quarter (Q3 2026 report, ~Oct 26).
  2. Current-accident-year ex-cat combined ratio continues rising past ~90% (was 88.1% in Q2'26).
  3. Commercial Lines combined ratio fails to normalize back under ~95% within two quarters.
  4. A sustained broad-equity-market drawdown >20% that visibly impairs book value per share (given the 40% equity allocation).
  5. Net FY1 consensus EPS revisions remain negative for two more months without stabilization.

11. Catalysts & calendar

  • Next earnings: ~2026-10-26 (Q3 2026 — estimated/pattern-based, not company-confirmed, per d4 snapshot; historically CINF has reported late-Oct, e.g. Oct 27 2025, Oct 24 2024).
  • Annual dividend-increase announcement typically accompanies the Q4/full-year release (previous increases: $0.81→$0.87 for FY2025, i.e. +7%).

12. Red-flag scan

No auditor change, material weakness, restatement, going-concern language, SEC/DOJ investigation, or short-seller report surfaced in the four earnings releases reviewed. Scope limitation: full 10-K risk-factor diff, Form 4 insider-selling pattern, and litigation/contingent-liability notes were not pulled given the time budget — this is a genuine gap in this pass, not a clean bill of health, and should be completed before sizing any position.

2. Business in plain English

Colgate-Palmolive sells toothpaste, toothbrushes, personal-care and home-care products (Colgate, Palmolive, Softsoap, Hill's Pet Nutrition) in over 200 countries. CMCSA — Comcast Corporation

1. Verdict

INCLUDE-SMALL. Horizon 12–36 months. Named reservation: Comcast announced on 29-Jun-2026 that it will split into two public companies (a "Comcast" broadband/wireless RemainCo and an independent "NBCUniversal" that also absorbs Sky), targeted to close in ~12 months; the capital structure, dividend policy and exact NBCUniversal stake retained (up to 19.9%, to be sold down) are not yet finalized. The 25-Sep-2026 close ($21.91) already prices in roughly a 16–24%/year perpetual decline in free cash flow — far worse than anything in the last 5–10 years of delivered results — so the valuation gap is real, but realizing it depends on a binary corporate event executing cleanly, not just on the underlying cash flows. [Corrected 2026-10-06: the 16-24% a year range rested on V1's mismatched inputs (levered FCF against enterprise value at a 6.05% WACC, FCF before cash paid for intangible assets, SBC added back). On equity value of $77.75bn, TTM FCF after intangibles and SBC of $16.45bn and a 9.0% cost of equity, the price implies a decline of 14.1% a year for 10 years (12.5% on FY2026E, 9.6% on owner FCF). Still far below any base case, so the conclusion is unchanged. See Re-assessment (RA10).]

2. Business in plain English

Comcast sells broadband internet, video and wireless service to US households and businesses (Connectivity & Platforms, ~64% of Q2 2026 revenue) and, through NBCUniversal, makes and distributes films, TV and news (NBC, Telemundo, Universal Pictures, Peacock) and operates theme parks including the new Epic Universe (Content & Experiences, ~36% of revenue). It earns money from broadband/wireless subscriptions, advertising, content licensing and park admissions/spending. Its moat in cable/broadband is a regulated-adjacent local infrastructure duopoly; in media it is content IP and distribution scale, both now being reorganized into two separately traded companies.

3. Why the model likes it — durability check

b1 composite 0.656 (decile 7, quintile 4, live_rank 172). Driven by Value (fam_V 0.79) and Quality (fam_Q 0.56) — cheap on earnings/FCF yield (pct_fcfp 0.97, pct_ep 0.94) with reasonable ROE/OCF-to-assets — while Momentum is the weakest family (fam_M 0.42), consistent with a stock the market has been reluctant to re-rate. This is a genuine value setup, not an artefact: NTM P/E 6.16x sits at the 6.8th percentile of its own ~15-year history (own_history_percentile 6.8) — i.e. only 7% of history was cheaper. It is, however, above the Cable & Satellite peer median of 4.44x (peer set is now just 2 names, mostly CHTR, after Versant's spin removed a pure-play cable-network comp) — so the cheapness case rests on CMCSA's own history, not on a peer discount.

7. Valuation — reconciled against V1 (v1_valuation_table.csv / v1_valuation.json)

V1 verdict: attractive (score 0.96/1.00). V1's reverse FCFF DCF (WACC 6.05%, 10-year fade to 3% terminal, EV $154.8bn) finds the price implies FCF shrinking at −24.2%/year for 10 years — versus a 5-year delivered CAGR of +2.8% and a 10-year delivered CAGR of +5.1%. See Re-assessment (RA10).] V1's scenarios: bear +24.2%/yr, base +62.1%/yr, bull +89.5%/yr (3-yr annualised, including dividends), driven mostly by multiple re-rating (exit P/E 10.0x/17.2x/20.2x vs today's 6.2x) rather than by growth assumptions alone. I agree with the direction (cheap; implied growth is far below any reasonable base case) but not the magnitude. My own base case: low-single-digit FCF growth (0% to +3%/year) — Residential Connectivity is genuinely shrinking (−4.0% yoy) but Business Services (+3.7%), wireless (record adds), and the higher-margin, faster-growing Content & Experiences segment (+22.9%) are real, disclosed offsets. That is still dramatically above the priced-in −24%/year, so implied_vs_base = below, supporting inclusion — but V1's base/bull cases require the market to re-rate the P/E to 17–20x, which depends heavily on the NBCUniversal/Sky spin-off actually closing on favorable terms (clean investment-grade balance sheets for both entities, as management has stated as a goal but not yet delivered). A re-rating case is less certain than a pure cash-flow case, which is why I size this INCLUDE-SMALL rather than full INCLUDE.

8. Bull case

  1. Valuation is priced for a level of FCF decline (−16% to −24%/yr) that is far worse than anything Comcast has delivered even during the worst of cord-cutting (5y CAGR still +2.8%), leaving a large margin of safety if the business merely does not shrink. [Corrected 2026-10-06: the priced-in decline is 9-14% a year, not 16-24% (see section 7 correction). The margin of safety remains large: base-path value at 9.0% is $54 a share at 0% FCF growth on FY2026E FCF less SBC ($14.8bn), $43 at -4% and $61 at +2%, against $21.91.]
  2. The NBCUniversal/Sky spin-off is a disclosed, dated catalyst that management frames as unlocking two focused, investment-grade companies — sum-of-the-parts is a plausible re-rating path given the conglomerate discount visible in the 6.2x multiple today.
  3. Wireless (record 448,000 adds) and Peacock (first profitable quarter) are genuinely inflecting positive at the same time broadband erosion is decelerating (−167k vs −201k a year ago), i.e., the offsets are strengthening, not just theoretical.

Bear case

  1. Residential broadband is still losing subscribers every quarter with no evidence of an inflection to growth — this is the core cash-generating asset and the secular decline (fixed wireless, cord-cutting) is real and ongoing.
  2. The spin-off is announced but unexecuted: terms for splitting debt, the size/duration of Comcast's retained NBCUniversal stake, and each entity's dividend policy are all undecided as of this writing, and buybacks are already paused — a live example of the process constraining shareholder returns before it delivers any benefit.
  3. Q4 2025/Q1 2026 already show what separation costs and losing a profitable segment (Versant) look like in the numbers; the NBCUniversal/Sky separation is a much larger transaction and could produce a similar, or larger, transitional earnings air-pocket.

9. Key risks & kill criteria (thesis-invalidation triggers)

  1. The NBCUniversal/Sky spin-off is delayed beyond Q4 2027 (18+ months from announcement) or is restructured so either resulting entity is sub-investment-grade.
  2. Residential broadband net losses exceed 250,000 in any quarter (vs. −167,000 in Q2 2026), i.e., the recent deceleration reverses.
  3. Net debt/EBITDA rises above 3.0x ahead of the spin (from ~2.3–2.4x now), suggesting the balance sheet is being loaded to fund the separation.
  4. Wireless net adds fall below 300,000/quarter (from 448,000 record in Q2 2026), removing the main offset to broadband erosion.
  5. The dividend is cut or suspended in connection with the spin-off.

dossiers.CMG:
CMG — Chipotle Mexican Grill, Inc.

1. Verdict

WATCH — 12–24 month horizon. The operating story has genuinely improved (traffic turned positive for two straight quarters after a 2025 decline — triage's red flag is now partly stale), but at the current price the market is implying roughly 13% annualised FCF growth for 10 years [Corrected 2026-10-06: restated ~8-9% after correcting FCF, lease treatment and discount rate; see Correction section], well above what continued margin compression and a low-single-digit comp algorithm can plausibly deliver. This is the textbook case the addendum warns about: a good business priced for more than it can deliver is WATCH, not INCLUDE.

2. Business in plain English

Chipotle operates (and franchises internationally, minimally) fast-casual Mexican restaurants with an assemble-in-front-of-you format, digital ordering/Chipotlane drive-through pickup, and a highly standardized, capital-light unit economic model (~mid-40% restaurant-level margins historically). It makes money from high unit volumes and strong per-store economics rather than menu pricing power, and is expanding units domestically and, slowly, internationally through partner-operated stores.

3. Why the model likes it / durability

b1 factor data (v4/data/b1_live_scores.csv, as-of 2026-09-25): decile 5/10, quintile 3/5 — a mid-pack quant score, not a standout, driven by very strong profitability (roe percitle 89th, ocf_a percentile 95th) offset by weak recent value (bp percentile 18th, i.e., expensive on book) and mixed momentum. Triage's stated red flag — "three consecutive quarters of negative comps, driven by traffic/frequency declines" — was accurate as of when that triage ran (comps were negative in fiscal Q2–Q4 2025, per company releases: Q3 2025 comp +0.3% but transactions −0.8%; Q4 2025 comp −2.5% with transactions −3.2%; full-year 2025 comp −1.7%, transactions −2.9%). That has changed: Q1 2026 comp +0.5% (transactions +0.6%) and Q2 2026 comp +2.2% (transactions +1.0%) — two consecutive quarters of positive traffic, the company's own Q2 2026 release calling it the "second consecutive quarter of improving transaction comp." The triage's red flag is therefore partly overturned by more recent data, which is exactly the kind of update this dossier exists to catch — but margin has not recovered alongside traffic (see §4), so the "quality" score may be lagging a genuine profitability deceleration.

This figure should not be read as a leverage red flag in the way a term-loan balance would be; it is a real fixed obligation (store rent) but of a fundamentally different, less-refinancing-risk character than bank/bond debt. No dividend; capital return is via buybacks.

6. Red flags

  • 2026 multistate Salmonella outbreak: the first lawsuit tied to a 2026 multistate Salmonella outbreak was filed in Minnesota federal court in August 2026 (plaintiff hospitalized); Chipotle has said jalapeños are the likely vehicle but had not, as of the reporting found, identified the specific supplier. This is a live, ongoing food-safety/legal matter, not historical.
  • Prior securities-fraud class action (2024): a securities-fraud class action naming Chipotle and former CEO Brian Niccol (who departed for Starbucks in 2024) and food-safety officer Laurie Schalow was filed in November 2024 in the Central District of California, related to earlier food-safety-linked disclosures; this predates the current CEO/management team but is a live case to track for outcome/settlement risk.
  • Margin compression alongside the traffic recovery: restaurant-level margin fell 220bps and operating margin fell 250bps YoY in Q2 2026 even as comps turned positive — the "quality" score in the b1 factors may not yet reflect this; decompose whether it is wage/food inflation, marketing spend to drive the traffic recovery, or new-unit drag before assuming margins snap back with comps.
  • No restatement, no material weakness, no going-concern language found in the reviewed filings.

7. Reverse DCF and valuation vs V1

v4/outputs/v1_valuation_table.csv has no row for CMG — v1_verdict = null. Own reverse DCF: EV $45.25B (from d4_live_snapshot.parquet), TTM FCF $1.116B, 8.5% discount rate, 3% terminal growth ⇒ implied 10-year FCF growth ≈ 12.9% p.a. The market's implied growth is above that base case — valuation_view_vs_v1.implied_vs_base = "above" [Corrected 2026-10-06: restated to "in_line"]. This is consistent with the b1 value factors (bp percentile only 18th — expensive on book) even as quality/profitability factors are strong; the stock is priced for a full margin recovery and sustained double-digit growth simultaneously, which is a high bar given §4's margin trend.

8. Bull case

  1. Traffic has now inflected positive for two consecutive quarters (Q1 +0.6%, Q2 +1.0%) after three quarters of decline in 2025 — the "Recipe for Growth" initiatives (value perception, digital/Chipotlane throughput) appear to be working, and guidance has been raised accordingly.
  2. Unit growth ("350 to 370 new restaurant openings," quoted in §4, for 2026) continues at a high absolute rate on an already-large base, and ~80% of new company units will have a Chipotlane, historically Chipotle's highest-margin, highest-volume format.
  3. Balance sheet is essentially debt-free (ex-leases) with strong FCF generation, giving management flexibility to keep investing in the turnaround without financial strain.

Bear case

  1. Restaurant-level margin (25.2%) and operating margin (15.7%) both fell meaningfully YoY even in the "recovery" quarter — the market's implied ~13% FCF growth requires margins to stop falling and likely re-expand, which has not yet happened in the data.
  2. The 2026 Salmonella outbreak is an open legal and reputational risk with an unidentified supplier as of the last update found — Chipotle has prior, expensive experience (a $25M DOJ fine tied to earlier foodborne-illness cases) with food-safety events denting traffic for multiple quarters.
  3. Guidance was only raised to "low single digit" comps, not high-single or double-digit — management itself is not calling for the kind of growth the current EV implies over a 10-year horizon.

9. Key risks & kill criteria

  1. Comparable restaurant sales growth prints negative for any quarter (a reversal of the current two-quarter positive-traffic trend).
  2. Restaurant-level operating margin falls below 24% (i.e., more than 100bps below the Q2 2026 25.2% print) for two consecutive quarters.
  3. The 2026 Salmonella outbreak is linked to a Chipotle-controlled (not third-party supplier) failure, or the case count/lawsuit count materially expands beyond the single Minnesota filing found here.
  4. Full-year 2026 comparable-sales guidance is cut from the current "low single digit" range at the Q3 2026 report (2026-10-28).
  5. New-unit growth (openings) falls materially below the guided 350–370 range for 2026, signalling real-estate or capital-allocation strain.

10. Catalysts & calendar

11. Red-flag scan (summary)

Live 2026 Salmonella-outbreak litigation (first suit filed August 2026 in Minnesota federal court, supplier not yet identified) and a pending 2024-origin securities class action (Central District of California) are the two material legal items; no restatement, material weakness or going-concern language found in the reviewed 10-Q (accession 0001058090-26-000066) or 8-K (accession 0001058090-26-000063).

CMI — Cummins Inc. — Diligence Dossier (Agent F40, standard depth)

1. Verdict

WATCH (not REJECT — quality/moat are real; not INCLUDE — price already discounts more growth than the evidence supports). Thesis horizon: 12–36 months, revisit on a pullback toward a 13–15x NTM P/E or on two consecutive quarters of EBITDA-margin expansion into the guided range.

2. Business in plain English

Cummins designs and makes diesel/natural-gas engines, powertrains, and — increasingly — large stationary generators ("Power Systems") used for data-center backup and continuous power, plus filtration, emission-control and electrified components. Customers are truck OEMs (PACCAR, Daimler, Navistar), construction/mining equipment makers, and, in the fastest-growing segment, hyperscale data-center developers who need standby/prime power while grid capacity catches up to AI-driven demand. It earns money on engine/parts sales, aftermarket service, and a growing share of high-margin large-genset systems.

3. Why the model likes it — durable or artefact?

b1 composite flags CMI on quality (low leverage, strong ROE/ROIC) and momentum (+36% trailing). The durable part is real: Power Systems' large-genset backlog is capacity-constrained into late 2026/2027, with orders on the newest platform (QSK95) being taken through H2 2028 (Cummins CEO J. Rumsey, Q2-26 call). The artefact risk is that revenue guidance has been raised three releases running [Corrected 2026-10-06: FY26 guidance was raised twice (May, Aug); the Feb-26 release was the initial guide] mostly on volume/mix (data-center gensets, NA on-highway recovery, China construction), while EBITDA margin actually fell YoY in Q2-26 (17.5% vs 18.4%) on higher incentive comp and R&D — i.e., the market is paying up for a top-line story whose margin delivery hasn't yet shown through.

The guidance raises are genuine and primary-sourced, but they do not by themselves resolve the valuation question.

6. Earnings quality & balance sheet

FCF/NI ~1.24x (strong). SBC only ~$93M TTM (~0.27% of revenue, per V1/D3 — immaterial). Net debt $3.16bn / TTM EBITDA (~$5.01bn) ≈ 0.6x [Corrected 2026-10-06: debt at 30 Jun 2026 is $7,695M (loans payable 459, commercial paper 348, current maturities 151, long-term 6,737) less cash and marketable securities $3,924M = net debt $3,771M; TTM EBITDA $5,281M; leverage ~0.7x] — low leverage, matches triage's characterisation. No pending M&A disclosed. Share count essentially flat (138.5–142.1M, buybacks roughly offsetting modest issuance). Two large one-offs bracket the two-year window in opposite directions (Atmus gain, Q1-24; Electrolyzer charge, Q4-25) — both are flagged above so GAAP and "clean" trends aren't conflated.

7. Valuation snapshot — reconciled with V1

V1 (systematic reverse DCF, FCFF method, SBC not added back, 10y fade to 3% terminal, WACC 8.74%) verdict: "excessive." NTM P/E 16.19x is only the 48.6th percentile of CMI's own 177-month history (i.e., not rich on a simple multiple basis) and is a discount to peer median 20.06x (CAT/PCAR/WAB) — but the reverse DCF says the $525.06 close implies 15.66%/yr FCF growth for 10 years, versus consensus FY1 growth of 8.95%, 5y delivered CAGR 8.44%, and 10y delivered CAGR 6.67%. V1 base-case 3y annualised return is −3.9% (bear −25.1%, bull +19.4%). I agree with V1's excessive call: the structural data-center tailwind is real, but it would have to compound at nearly double its own trailing rate, for a decade, with margin expansion that hasn't shown up yet, to earn today's price. Unresolved conflict to disclose: sell-side consensus price targets (mean $746, low $530) imply the stock is already below the Street's most bearish target — i.e., analysts are more bullish than either V1 or this dossier. I read that gap as sell-side targets embedding continued guidance raises and multiple re-rating that the reverse DCF treats as already-priced.

8. Bull case / Bear case

Bull: (1) data-center standby-power backlog is capacity-constrained into 2027–28, a multi-year, non-discretionary buildout; (2) balance sheet (0.6x net debt/EBITDA) funds it without dilution; (3) three consecutive guidance raises show real operating momentum, not just estimate resets. Bear: (1) EBITDA margin fell YoY in the most recent quarter despite the raises — the market is paying for margin that hasn't arrived; (2) on-highway engines remain cyclical (Class 8 truck demand swings), a large share of revenue outside Power Systems; (3) the price already implies growth well above anything CMI has delivered in 5 or 10 years.

9. Kill criteria

  1. EBITDA margin stays below 18.0% for two consecutive quarters despite reiterated FY26 guidance (would break the "raises are backed by margin" thesis). [Corrected 2026-10-06: already met as written at Q2-26: Q1-26 17.7% excluding the special item (15.4% reported) and Q2-26 17.5% against FY26 guidance of 17.75-18.5% then 18.0-18.5%]
  2. Power Systems / large-genset book-to-bill falls below 1.0x for two consecutive quarters (backlog thesis breaking).
  3. Net debt/EBITDA rises above 1.5x (from ~0.6x) without offsetting FCF growth.
  4. NTM P/E re-rates above the 20x peer median without a corresponding upward revision to consensus 10-year growth.
  5. Follow-on shareholder/consumer litigation tied to the 2023–24 DOJ/EPA/CARB Clean Air Act settlement produces a material (>$200M) incremental charge beyond current accruals.

10. Catalysts & calendar

Next earnings: ~Nov 4, 2026 (Q3-26; date not yet formally confirmed by IR as of this write-up — estimate based on historical early-Nov reporting pattern).

11. Red-flag scan

  • Regulatory: $1.675bn DOJ/EPA/California Clean Air Act settlement (largest-ever CAA penalty), finalized April 2024, for defeat-device/emissions-certification violations in pick-up-truck engines; >$325M in required remediation spend; ongoing shareholder/consumer follow-on litigation (immaterial accruals disclosed to date, but unresolved).
  • One-offs: Q1-24 $1.3bn Atmus gain (positive); Q4-25 $458M Electrolyzer/Accelera charge (negative) — both must be excluded from any "clean" growth read.
  • Insider activity: routine, small (<$0.6M each) open-market sales by VP-level executives through 2026 (CIO, Treasury VP, HR/CAO); no CEO/CFO sales found this session — no unusual pattern identified.
  • No going-concern language, no auditor change, no disclosed pending acquisition.

dossiers.CMS:
CMS — CMS Energy Corp. — Diligence Dossier (Agent F40, standard depth)

1. Verdict

INCLUDE-SMALL (half weight), reservation stated explicitly: Moody's moved the outlook on CMS/Consumers Energy to negative (from stable) over the size of a $24bn five-year capital plan relative to regulatory cost-recovery timing, and the balance sheet is securitization-heavy, complicating a clean leverage read [Corrected 2026-10-06: securitization debt is only $525M of about $19.3bn total debt (2.7%); consolidated leverage is about 6.2x net debt/EBITDA]. Valuation is not demanding and the earnings-guidance track record is strong. Horizon: 24–48 months (regulated utility — this is a rate-of-return/dividend-growth thesis, not a re-rating trade).

2. Business in plain English

CMS Energy is the holding company for Consumers Energy, Michigan's largest combined electric-and-gas regulated utility, serving ~6.7M of the state's residents. It earns a regulated return on the capital it invests in generation, transmission and distribution, set by the Michigan Public Service Commission (MPSC). It is one of the more purely "regulated-utility" names in its peer set (minimal unregulated/merchant exposure since NorthStar Clean Energy is a small renewables developer segment).

3. Why the model likes it — durable or artefact?

Triage flagged CMS for a "cheap NTM P/E (15.4x) for above-average guided growth" and a multi-year 6–8% EPS-growth record. That growth record is durable and verified: 2024 adjusted EPS $3.34, 2025 adjusted EPS $3.61 (beat the $3.54–3.60 guide range — the 22nd/23rd consecutive year of meeting-or-beating guidance per company messaging), 2026 guide $3.83–3.90 (raised twice from an initial $3.80–3.87) [Corrected 2026-10-06: raised once (5 Feb 2026), then reaffirmed in April and July], and a newly introduced 2027 guide of $4.08–4.17 (+6.7% at the midpoint) — all consistent with the reaffirmed 6–8% long-term algorithm. The one thing that looks like an artefact at first glance is the Q2-2026 earnings "miss": adjusted EPS of $0.37 vs. $0.71 a year earlier and vs. a ~$0.76 consensus (a >50% shortfall). Management's own bridge (Q2-26 earnings call) attributes it to items already contemplated in the 2026 plan: an $0.08 unfavourable weather comparison, $0.19 of storm-related O&M, and $0.23 from non-repeating 2025 liability-management benefits — and the company reaffirmed full-year guidance the same day. I read this as a real quarterly print, correctly explained, not a data conflict with the multi-year growth thesis — but it is a reminder that CMS's quarters are lumpy and headline "misses" will recur.

Bull: (1) 20-year unbroken dividend-growth streak and a guidance record that has never been cut in the window checked; (2) FY27 guide (+6.7% at midpoint) shows the growth algorithm rolling forward intact; (3) valuation (16.3x NTM P/E, ~5.2% implied growth) does not demand anything beyond the guided range. The history is real (guidance withdrawn 1 Jul 2025, $6.7bn goodwill impairment Q3'25, 2025 adjusted EPS $2.08 vs $7.17 in 2024). Centene is the largest US Medicaid managed-care insurer (12.1m Medicaid members), plus Marketplace/ACA plans (3.5m, down from 5.9m a year ago after repricing ~95% of membership), Medicare Advantage and the largest standalone Part D (PDP) book (8.8m). V1 (v1_valuation_table.csv / v1_valuation.json): verdict "attractive" (score 0.96), implied growth -25.9%, base 3-yr +67.7% a year, bear -2.2%, bull +142%. We agree on direction (cheap) but V1's numbers are unusable: (a) its EV of $19.8bn uses consolidated cash net of debt (-$10.95bn), i.e. it counts regulated-subsidiary cash; parent-level EV is ~$44.8bn ($30.5bn market cap + $16.1bn debt - $1.8bn unregulated cash); (b) its base assumes 27% annual revenue growth and year-3 EPS of $12.62 (vs $7.17 at the 2024 peak); V1's own street flag says base exceeds the Street 12-month high target. Own reverse DCF (project conventions: rf 5.17%, ERP 4.14%, Blume beta 1.07 -> cost of equity 9.6%, 3% terminal, owner earnings = 70-80% of adjusted EPS because regulated capital must be retained): the $61.82 price (market cap $30.5bn) implies ~3% to 6% annual adjusted-EPS growth for ten years from a $5.0 base. Our base is ~8.6% a year to 2029 ($5.0 to $6.4, still below 2024's $7.17), worth ~$74 a share (+20%); bear ~$42; bull ~$97. Multiples: 12.7x our FY26E, 11.6x Street FY27E ($5.35), own-history percentile 7 (V1), peer median 15.5x (ELV, HUM, UNH; V1). Price implies LESS than base -> "below". CenterPoint Energy, Inc. (CNP) — Diligence Dossier

Agent: F109 (wave 7) | As of: 2026-09-25 close ($36.84, mkt cap $24.10bn per d4/b1 snapshot) | CIK 0001130310

1. Verdict

INCLUDE-SMALL (half weight), thesis horizon 24–36 months. Reason: a rate-regulated T&D utility with unusually strong, regulator-blessed load growth (Houston Electric) is priced for less growth than management's own long-range guidance implies, but elevated consolidated leverage and a lumpy near-term debt/refinancing calendar are a specific, named reservation that keeps this from full weight.

2. Business in plain English

CenterPoint Energy is a regulated electric transmission & distribution (T&D) and natural-gas distribution utility holding company. Its main earner is CenterPoint Energy Houston Electric, LLC (a wholly owned subsidiary, "Houston Electric"), which delivers (does not generate) electricity to ~2.9m metered customers in the Houston metro area under ERCOT; it also owns natural-gas LDCs in Indiana, Minnesota, and other states. It earns a regulator-approved return on a growing "rate base" (capital invested in wires, poles, pipes) — revenue and profit grow mainly by investing capital and getting it into rates, not by selling more volume at a margin.

3. Why the model likes it — durable or artefact?

b1_live_scores.csv: composite decile 5 / quintile 3, live_rank 268 (mid-pack, not a top-30 name), Quality family percentile ~0.45 (roe pct 0.34, ocf/assets pct 0.15 — modest), Value family higher (fcfp pct 0.79, ep pct 0.66) — the model likes it mostly on cheapness (low forward multiple, high nominal FCF-yield metric) more than on quality; the fcfp (FCF/price) percentile is high because reported operating cash flow is being compared against a market cap depressed by scale, but note the underlying FCF is deeply negative once capex is netted (see §6) — the model's "value" signal here is partly an artefact of how FCF-yield is computed pre-capex-netting for a heavy-capex utility, not a signal of cash-generative cheapness. The durable part of the bull case is the rate case pipeline: Houston Electric's capital plan is filed and largely pre-approved through settlements, which is a real, verifiable growth driver independent of the model's factor scores.

Capital One Financial Corporation (COF) — Diligence Dossier

Agent: F74 (wave 4) | As of: 2026-09-25 close (px $200.20, mktcap $122.82bn per b1_live_scores.csv 2026-09-25)

1. Verdict

WATCH. Thesis horizon 12–24 months. A genuinely improved franchise — Capital One closed its ~$35bn all-stock acquisition of Discover on 18 May 2025 and now owns a closed-loop card network (Discover Global Network/Diners Club) instead of renting Visa/Mastercard rails — but the stock's P/B has already re-rated to the 88th percentile of its own 10-year history (b1_live_scores.csv) while trailing return on equity (9.2% TTM) still sits at or below the 9–10% cost of equity the market is pricing in. Not a rejection: credit trends are improving and capital return is real. The condition that would move this to INCLUDE-SMALL: two more quarters of the current NCO/delinquency improvement trend without labor-market-driven reversal, confirming ROE durably above ~11%.

2. Business in plain English

Capital One is a US bank holding company. Three segments: Credit Card (Domestic Card $259bn loans + Discover's card book, now the largest chunk of earnings), Consumer Banking (auto loans ~$87bn + branch/online retail deposits), Commercial Banking (CRE + C&I lending, ~$91bn loans, the smallest segment). The Discover deal added a fourth, structurally different source of profit: network fees on the ~$190bn/quarter of volume now running over the Discover/Diners rails, comparable to how American Express earns both issuer and network economics (source: 10-Q period 2026-06-30, filed 2026-07-28, "Business Segment Financial Performance").

3. Why the model likes it / is this durable

b1_live_scores.csv (as_of 2026-09-25): composite decile 10 (top decile), live_rank 38/500, driven by Value (pct_bp/pct_ep high, P/B 1.09x vs peer median 1.56x per V1) and Quality families. Partly durable, partly an artefact. Durable: the vertically-integrated network is a structural, one-time change to the earnings model, not a cyclical peak. Artefact/noise: 2025 GAAP earnings were badly distorted by a one-time acquisition-accounting charge (see §4) — a screen reading "cheap on trailing P/E" off 2025 numbers would be reading noise, not signal. The triage red flag ("the data card's reported revenue-growth figure (11.11) appears to be a data anomaly") is confirmed as a symptom of this same distortion, not a separate data error.

7. Valuation snapshot & reverse DCF

V1 valuation (v1_valuation_table.csv, as of 2026-09-25): P/B 1.09x vs peer median 1.56x (COF trades at a discount in absolute terms) but at the 87.6th percentile of its own 10-year P/B history (i.e., rich vs its own past even though cheap vs peers today — a bank that historically traded at an even bigger discount). V1's excess-return model backs out an implied required ROE of 10.78% against a cost of equity of 10.12%, versus 9.24% delivered actual (TTM) ROE — this is why V1 tags the name "excessive" (verdict_score −0.52). My own reverse DCF (excess-return / justified-P/B framework): using the same COE (~10.1%), the market is pricing in a sustainable forward ROE of roughly 10.5–11%. I agree directionally with V1 but weight the P/B-vs- own-history percentile more heavily: even if ROE reaches ~11% (achievable if Discover network economics and credit normalization both continue), the stock has already re-rated most of the way there, capping upside. Implied growth is judged in line with my base case, not below it — the valuation reconciliation in §1 explains why this is WATCH rather than INCLUDE-SMALL despite improving fundamentals. Scenario returns (3yr annualized, my own build): - Bear (labor-market-driven credit cycle turn; card/auto NCO rates rise back toward 6%/2%; ROE compresses to ~7%; P/B mean-reverts toward 0.85x): −8%/yr - Base (credit normalization continues at the current pace; ROE settles ~10.5–11%; P/B roughly flat near current multiple given it is already at a rich own-history percentile): +5%/yr - Bull (Discover network revenue synergies materialize, cost synergies land, ROE reaches 12–13%, buybacks continue at pace, P/B re-rates toward peer median 1.3–1.4x): +15%/yr

8. Bull case

  1. Vertically integrated card network (Discover Global Network + Diners Club) is a structural earnings-model upgrade that Amex-style closed-loop peers have historically monetized well; purchase volume +26% YoY and Global Payment Network volume +156% YoY (Q2 2026, 10-Q) show real scale already flowing through.
  2. Credit quality is improving, not deteriorating, in the core Credit Card segment (NCO rate down 49bps YoY, delinquencies down 56bps YoY) even as the loan book grew nearly 50% with Discover.
  3. Aggressive, sustained capital return ($2.7bn buybacks in Q2 2026 alone) at a P/B below peer median, funded from a CET1 ratio (13.7%) still well above regulatory minimums.

9. Bear case

  1. Trailing actual ROE (9.24%) still sits below the ~10.1% cost of equity the market requires, and the stock's P/B is already at the 88th percentile of its own 10-year range — most of the "normalization" good news may already be priced in.
  2. Auto-loan and small-commercial-book NCO rates are both rising (+18bps and +20bps YoY respectively), a leading indicator consistent with the triage's flagged "near-prime consumer exposure in a slowing labor market" — Domestic Card is improving, but not every book is.
  3. $1.625bn of combined disclosed litigation reserves (below) sit against a still-integrating balance sheet; a Discover-integration misstep (systems, compliance, or the CFPB order below) is a real, underwritten-for risk that has not yet been tested through a full credit cycle under the combined entity.

10. Key risks & kill criteria (measurable triggers)

  1. Credit Card segment net charge-off rate rises above 5.5% for two consecutive quarters (vs. 4.71% today).
  2. CET1 ratio (Basel III standardized, consolidated) falls below 12.0% in any quarter without a stated, credible capital-plan explanation (vs. 13.7% today).
  3. Consumer Banking (auto) NCO rate exceeds 2.0% for two consecutive quarters (vs. 1.48% today).
  4. Any new, material CFPB or DOJ enforcement action against the combined entity (distinct from the two inherited, already-reserved matters in §12).
  5. Quarterly buyback pace falls below $1bn for two consecutive quarters with no stated reason (a signal management itself sees less value or needs the capital), reversing the current $2.7bn/quarter run-rate.

11. Catalysts & calendar

Next earnings: Q3 2026 results, estimated ~2026-10-21 (Q3 2025 earnings 8-K was filed 2025-10-21; not confirmed).

12. Red-flag scan

  • Litigation — Discover Card Product Misclassification (10-Q Note 14, inherited from Discover): on 2023-07-19 Discover disclosed it had misclassified certain credit cards into its highest merchant/acquirer pricing tier. Discover and DFS Services entered a Federal Reserve consent order (2025-04-18, civil money penalty paid pre-close) and separately reserved $1.2 billion for a merchant class-action settlement; a related shareholder securities class action is also pending. This liability was known and priced into the acquisition; it is disclosed, reserved and ongoing, not a new surprise.
  • Litigation — CFPB Order on inherited private student-loan servicing (10-Q Note 14): the CFPB order remains in effect until December 2030 for issues predating the sale/transfer of that servicing — a long-tailed but bounded, already-known compliance obligation.
  • Litigation — Savings Account Litigation (Capital One's own, E.D. Va., filed 2023-07-10): 360 Performance Savings customers allege breach of contract for not being offered a new, higher-rate product. An initial settlement was rejected by the court in November 2025 after 17 state attorneys general filed an amicus brief opposing it; a new settlement ($425 million fund) was reached in December 2025 and given preliminary approval 2026-06-09 — not yet final.
  • No material change to risk factors since the FY2025 10-K per Part II Item 1A of the Q2 2026 10-Q. No auditor change, restatement or going-concern language found. Insider Form 4 pattern and short-seller reports not checked in the time available (disclosed limitation).
  • Data conflict vs triage/b1: triage flagged an apparent data anomaly in a reported "11.11" revenue-growth figure; this dossier attributes it to the Q2 2025 GAAP loss distorting YoY comparisons, not a separate data error.

Cencora's fiscal year ends September 30 — one quarter offset from CAH (June 30) and three months offset from CCI (December 31); flagged because it affects any same-period peer comparison.

1. Verdict

INCLUDE. Thesis horizon 18–36 months. One-sentence reason: the same drug-distribution oligopoly economics as CAH with a slightly better specialty/oncology mix, a three-quarter-running adjusted-EPS guidance raise streak, and a reverse DCF implying only low-single-digit 10-year growth — against a real, recurring earnings-quality flag (two straight years of PharmaLex goodwill impairments and a business now "exploring strategic alternatives" for several sub-units) that is disclosed and sized, not hidden. [Corrected 2026-10-06: the phrase 'reverse DCF implying only low-single-digit 10-year growth' used EPS as cash; on after-SBC free cash flow at an 8.5% discount rate the implied 10-year growth is 3.5%, still below the re-based 6-7% base case, so the verdict stands with a thinner margin (see Re-assessment RA9)]]

2. Business in plain English

Cencora is one of the three dominant US pharmaceutical wholesalers (with Cardinal Health and McKesson), distributing branded and generic drugs to retail and hospital pharmacies on thin (~1.5–2%) gross margins earned on volume and working-capital efficiency. It has been building a specialty-oncology and now urology physician-services platform (RCA — Retina Consultants of America, acquired Jan 2025; OneOncology, equity stake stepped up to full consolidation in Feb 2026) inside its larger U.S. Healthcare Solutions segment, plus an International Healthcare Solutions segment (mainly World Courier and European distribution) and an "Other" bucket (MWI Animal Health, Profarma, U.S. Consulting Services, remaining PharmaLex units) that management is now exploring strategic alternatives for — i.e., a likely partial divestiture. [Corrected 2026-10-06: not just a likely divestiture: U.S. Consulting Services was sold in April 2026 and an agreement to sell MWI Animal Health (merger with Covetrus) was signed in Q2 FY26, with assets held for sale of $3,836.1m and liabilities of $869.7m at 30 Jun 2026 and an FTC second request received 20 May 2026 (10-Q 0001140859-26-000034, Notes 3 and 6)]]

3. Why the model likes it, and whether that's durable

Triage's framing (same oligopoly economics as peers, slightly better specialty mix, weak recent momentum despite 20% street upside) holds up. The durable part: adjusted diluted EPS grew 16.3% in FY2025 ($16.00 vs $13.76) and FY2026 adjusted-EPS guidance was raised at every quarterly release reviewed (see §5), driven by real segment operating-income growth, not one-off items — GLP-1 volume and the OneOncology/RCA specialty build-out are named, structural drivers in the company's own release language. The less durable / genuinely mixed part: FY2026 revenue-growth guidance was cut, not raised, over the same year — from "7% to 9%" (Q1 FY26 release) to "4% to 6%" (Q3 FY26 release) for both total company and the U.S. Healthcare Solutions segment — even as EPS guidance kept rising. That combination (revenue guide down, EPS guide up) is consistent with margin/mix improvement and a smaller "Other" segment base (MWI Animal Health reclassified toward held-for-sale), but it means the "growth" the model is scoring should be read as margin-driven, not volume-driven, and the two should not be conflated.

Adjusted EPS was raised (or held) at every checkpoint, never cut, across the year reviewed. Revenue growth guidance, however, was walked down from 7–9% to 4–6% over the same period — the company's own segment guidance table (Q3 FY26 release) shows U.S. Healthcare Solutions revenue growth cut identically, alongside International Healthcare Solutions (~8% growth) and Other (~6% growth, i.e., not being wound down as fast as the "strategic alternatives" language might suggest). This is a genuine, disclosed divergence between the top-line and bottom-line guidance tracks, not a data error.

6. Earnings quality & balance sheet

  • Entity scope: all figures are consolidated Cencora, Inc. (10-Q balance sheet/cash-flow statement, 2026-06-30), not segment or subsidiary figures unless stated.
  • FCF conversion: nine-month FY2026 OCF was $1,687.5m vs nine-month FY2025 OCF of $741.7m — but quarterly OCF is extremely lumpy (Q1 FY26 alone was −$2,305m, Q2 FY26 −$967m, before a large positive swing) driven by working-capital timing around drug-price cycles and the OneOncology consolidation; nine-month capex was $511.0m. Full-year FCF should be read off the eventual FY2026 10-K, not annualized from any single quarter.
  • GAAP vs adjusted gap: FY2025 GAAP diluted EPS $7.96 vs adjusted $16.00 — roughly a 2x gap, the widest of the three companies in this batch, driven by acquisition-intangible amortization, the PharmaLex goodwill impairments (§3), litigation/opioid items, and (in FY2026) the OneOncology remeasurement gain. Every reconciling line is itemized in the company's own non-GAAP tables (10-Q Exhibit 99.1), not a black box.
  • Leverage: total debt at 2026-06-30 = $11.72bn (long-term $11.44bn + current $0.28bn), up sharply from $7.92bn at 2025-12-31 — the increase is the debt-financed OneOncology step-up acquisition (closed Feb 2026), confirmed in the cash-flow statement ("Cost of acquired companies, net of cash acquired" $4.97bn nine-month FY26 vs $4.00bn prior year). Cash $2.82bn → net debt ≈ $8.9bn. FY2026 guided adjusted operating income ≈$4.2bn base × 1.13–1.14 growth ≈ $4.7–4.8bn, plus run-rate D&A (~$1.0–1.1bn annualized from the nine-month $779m figure) → approximate EBITDA $5.7–5.9bn, putting net debt/EBITDA at roughly 1.5x — moderate, and elevated versus FY2025 levels specifically because of the OneOncology deal financing.
  • Stockholders' equity is thin ($3.05bn at 2026-06-30 vs total assets $83.8bn) — the same buyback-driven capital structure as CAH; not itself a distress signal given the leverage above, but it means small absolute swings in retained earnings move book equity a lot.
  • Opioid litigation: accrued liability for the Distributor Settlement Agreement and related opioid litigation was $4.2bn at 2026-06-30 (down from $4.3bn at 2025-09-30), expected to be paid over the next 13 years, with $396.2m expected in the next twelve months. In Q3 FY26 the company recorded a net credit (income) of $88.6m from litigation/opioid items (a favorable accrual revision or settlement-cost reduction), a data point worth noting as the mirror image of CAH's ongoing net cash outflow.
  • Recurring impairments as an earnings-quality flag: a further $249.5m "impairment of assets, including goodwill" was booked in Q1 FY2026 (nine-month total, per the 10-Q income statement) — on top of the $723.9m PharmaLex impairment in Q4 FY2025 and $418.0m in Q4 FY2024. Three consecutive fiscal years (FY2024, FY2025, FY2026-to-date) with a material goodwill/asset impairment is a pattern, not a one-off, concentrated in the "Other" segment now under strategic review.

7. Valuation snapshot and reverse DCF

Price used: $306.92 (2026-09-25 close, d4 live snapshot). NTM P/E ≈15.5x (d4, calendarized), trailing P/E 22.8x (distorted by the Q4 FY25 GAAP loss quarter), FCF yield ≈3.5% (materially lower than CAH's, reflecting COR's lumpier working capital and larger recent M&A cash outlay), sell-side mean target $369.31 (+20%, matching the triage note). No V1 row exists for COR — v1_verdict is null.

Reverse DCF (2-stage, per-share, terminal growth 2.5%, FY2026 guided adjusted-EPS midpoint ≈$17.85 used as the owner-earnings proxy): at a WACC of 7.5–9.0%, the $306.92 price implies roughly +0.3% to +3.7% annualized 10-year earnings growth — modestly higher than CAH's implied range but still well below COR's own recent trajectory (adjusted EPS +16.3% FY2025, guided +11–15% FY2026). Analyst base case: high-single-digit (7–9%/yr) 10-year adjusted EPS growth, reflecting some deceleration from the current pace as GLP-1 tailwinds normalize and OneOncology integration matures, but above the market's implied ~1–4%. valuation_view_vs_v1.implied_vs_base = "below" (price implies less growth than the base case), though with a thinner margin of safety than CAH given COR's higher debt load and recurring impairment pattern. [Corrected 2026-10-06: the 'FCF yield ~3.5%' above is trailing GAAP free cash flow of $2.04bn after a working-capital outflow in H1 FY26; guided FY26 adjusted free cash flow is ~$3.0bn (5.1% of the $58.6bn market cap, 4.8% after stock compensation). The reverse DCF treated the $17.85 adjusted EPS midpoint as owner earnings and used a 7.5-9.0% WACC; corrected inputs: FCF/share $14.82 after SBC, 191.6m shares, 8.5% discount rate (5.17% Treasury + 0.71 x 4.75%), terminal growth 3.5%, giving implied 10-year growth of 3.5% (2.2% at 8.0%, 4.7% at 9.0%, 5.9% at 9.5%), not 0.3-3.7%. The 7-9% base case is re-based to 6-7%. implied_vs_base stays 'below']]

8. Bull case / bear case

Bull: (1) Adjusted EPS guidance raised at every checkpoint in FY2026, on top of 16.3% FY2025 adjusted-EPS growth, evidencing durable execution even as the revenue guide was trimmed. (2) OneOncology/RCA give Cencora a specialty-oncology and retina-care physician-platform business with materially better economics than core distribution, now fully consolidated and contributing to segment profit. (3) The reverse DCF shows the market paying for only low-single-digit growth in a company that has consistently delivered double-digit adjusted EPS growth.

Bear: (1) Three consecutive fiscal years of goodwill/asset impairments (PharmaLex primarily) is a genuine capital-allocation track record concern, not a one-off; the businesses now under "strategic alternatives" review (MWI Animal Health, Profarma, U.S. Consulting Services) could realize further losses on sale. (2) Debt nearly doubled in two quarters to fund the OneOncology step-up ($7.9bn → $11.7bn), and net debt/EBITDA at ~1.5x, while not high in absolute terms, is a genuine increase in financial risk versus a year ago. (3) Revenue-growth guidance was cut from 7–9% to 4–6% during FY2026 — the "raise" story is entirely a margin/mix and buyback story, not a volume story, and that is a narrower, more fragile basis for continued EPS beats if margin gains stall.

9. Key risks & kill criteria (measurable)

  1. Adjusted diluted EPS guidance is cut at any quarterly release (breaking the current raise streak).
  2. A further goodwill/asset impairment exceeding $150m is booked in any single quarter (a fourth consecutive year of the PharmaLex-style pattern).
  3. Consolidated net debt/EBITDA rises above 2.5x without a disclosed, value-accretive reason.
  4. U.S. Healthcare Solutions segment revenue growth falls below 3% for two consecutive quarters (below even the cut 4-6% FY26 guide).
  5. The "Other" segment strategic-alternatives review results in a divestiture loss exceeding $200m versus carrying value.

10. Catalysts & calendar

Next earnings: Q4/FY2026 (fiscal year end), expected ~2026-11-04 (d4 snapshot next_earnings_date; the FY2026 10-K would follow, typically ~3 weeks later based on the FY2025 pattern of a 2025-11-25 10-K filing). Watch for: FY2027 initial guidance at that release, and any announcement on the "Other" segment strategic-alternatives review (MWI Animal Health, Profarma, U.S. Consulting Services).

11. Red-flag scan

Recurring PharmaLex-related goodwill impairment (three straight fiscal years, $418.0m FY24 + $723.9m FY25 + $249.5m FY26-to-date) — the clearest, most persistent red flag in this dossier. Opioid litigation: $4.2bn accrued, payments over 13 years — disclosed and, unusually, saw a net credit in the most recent quarter. A $113.5m equity-investment impairment in Q4 FY25 alongside the PharmaLex charge. Debt roughly doubled in two quarters to fund the OneOncology acquisition. No auditor change, restatement or going-concern language identified in the sections reviewed. Insider Form-4 pattern and short-seller reports were not checked in this pass — disclosed gap.

dossiers.CPAY:
CPAY — Corpay, Inc. (fka FLEETCOR) — Diligence Dossier (Agent F41, Wave 2, Standard depth)

1. Verdict

INCLUDE-SMALL — real double-digit organic growth at a reasonable adjusted multiple, but a named reservation: leverage (2.55x, above the company's own historical comfort zone), a fresh $100.9m preliminary FTC settlement charge (pending approval), and a wide, growing GAAP-vs-adjusted earnings gap. Thesis horizon: 12–36 months.

2. Business in plain English

Corpay (ticker changed from FLT to CPAY in 2024) sells corporate-payments software: fuel/fleet cards for trucking and field-service fleets, virtual corporate cards and AP automation ("Corpay One"/"Comdata"), and cross-border B2B payments (formerly Cambridge/AFEX). Customers are mid-market and large businesses that pay Corpay a recurring transaction/interchange-like fee for every fuel purchase, invoice payment or FX transfer it processes. It grows mostly by cross-selling its existing ~800k+ commercial customers into more products and by bolt-on acquisitions, funded with meaningful leverage. Competitive position: #1 or #2 in US fuel cards (WEX is the main competitor), a smaller but growing challenger in cross-border payments (versus Western Union Business Solutions, Convera) and corporate card (versus Amex, Brex).

3. Why the model likes it — durable or artefact?

b1/triage flags: Quality (ROE 32%, gross-profit/assets 0.076–0.28th pct in one direction, high leverage percentile pulling composite down slightly), Value (moderate — 42nd EP percentile), Momentum strong (12-1m return ~40%, 79th pct), Earnings-momentum (SUE) very strong (94th pct). Triage: quality 4/5, growth 4/5, price_vs_growth 4/5; "revenue +22%, margin 23%, ROE 29% and 13.1x NTM P/E is a rare combination of real growth and reasonable price." This is partly durable, partly an artefact: organic revenue growth (double digits for 5 consecutive quarters per management) and ROE are real and confirmed in filings. But part of the reported "adjusted EPS" acceleration (+36% YoY in Q2 2026, +29% in Q1 2026) is inflated by (a) heavy share buybacks (diluted share count down 7.1% YoY in Q2 2026) funded by increasing leverage, and (b) a widening list of non-GAAP add-backs (see §6). The earnings-momentum (SUE) factor score is therefore flattered by a metric (adjusted EPS) that management, not GAAP, defines.

CPRT (Copart, Inc.) — Diligence Dossier

Agent: F36 · Standard depth · Prepared 2026-09-26 · Prices/market data as of 2026-09-25 close ($27.59; mkt cap ≈$25.5B)

1. Verdict

WATCH — overturns the triage advance. Thesis horizon if resolved favourably: 12–24 months. The triage read CPRT as "near-monopoly economics intact" with growth merely decelerating; primary-source work through the just-reported Q4 FY2026 (filed 10-Sep-2026) and the 10-Sep-2026 M&A announcement finds a materially different, more adverse picture: gross margin compressed ~350bps YoY in the quarter, operating cash flow is down year-to-date, the CEO abruptly departed with the founder returning mid-cycle, plaintiff law firms have opened securities-related "investigations," and the company has just committed $1.9B of cash to an antitrust-gated acquisition (ACV Auctions) that management itself says is EPS-neutral in year one. None of this is disqualifying on its own, but together it removes the margin of safety the triage assumed. Condition to move to INCLUDE: a quarter of stabilised-or-improving gross margin, HSR clearance and a credible integration update on ACV, and no material finding from the ongoing securities-law-firm inquiries. No V1 systematic valuation row exists for CPRT; v1_verdict = null.

2. Business in plain English

Copart runs the largest online salvage- and used-vehicle auction network in the US (with UK/international operations), taking vehicles on consignment mostly from insurance companies after a total-loss determination (and, on a smaller "purchase agreement" basis, buying some vehicles outright) and selling them via its own online auction (VB3/VB Advantage) to dismantlers, rebuilders, dealers and exporters. Revenue is mainly per-unit service/auction fees plus, on purchased units, the sale margin itself. The moat is largely a real-asset one — a nationwide land bank of storage/processing yards that is genuinely hard to replicate (permitting, capital, insurer-relationship lock-in) — layered under a software/marketplace business.

Sector routing note: GICS files CPRT under "Diversified Support Services" / "Auto & Truck Dealerships" adjacency, neither of which is a clean fit. Per the stock-analysis skill's routing rules, this is nearest to the retail-ecommerce.md marketplace framework (fee/margin on transaction volume — "GMV × take rate" analog), with the land-bank/permitted-yard asset base treated as a moat feature (analogous to the waste-environmental "permitted disposal asset" logic) rather than the primary profit driver. Explicitly rejected: auto.md (Copart does not manufacture, retail, or finance vehicles) and people-businesses.md (this is not a pure labour/fee brokerage — the yard network is a real capital asset).

3. Why the model likes it / is the reason still durable?

data/b1_live_scores.csv: live_rank 380, composite factor score driven by Quality (fam_Q, high gross-profit/ assets and OCF/assets — both computed on stale data: max_filed_used 2026-05-29, i.e. the Q3 FY26 10-Q, predating the Q4 FY26 results and the ACV deal). 8. Bull case / bear case

Bull (3): 1. The land-bank moat (permitted yard capacity, insurer relationships) has not gone away; margin pressure this quarter is explicitly framed by management as investment spend (new products, wholesale facilities), which could reverse once those investments mature. 2. Net-cash balance sheet funds the ACV deal without leverage; if antitrust clearance is obtained and integration goes to plan, management's own framing (accretive from FY28) implies a longer-run earnings step-up. 3. Founder Jay Adair's return as CEO could be read as a stabilising, execution-focused signal after a rocky stretch, by someone who built the business the first time.

Bear (3): 1. Margin compression (−350bps YoY in the reported quarter) plus a YoY EPS decline is a real earnings-quality deterioration, not merely a deceleration in an otherwise-strong story, and the stated causes (new-service investment, facility cost inflation) are exactly the kind of "temporary" explanation that deserves scepticism until at least one more quarter confirms the trend reverses. 2. An abrupt CEO exit (announced 29-Jun-2026, effective 31-Jul-2026, stock −8% same day) alongside multiple plaintiff-firm "securities fraud investigation" press releases is a governance yellow flag that should be tracked to resolution (these law-firm releases are frequently opportunistic and non-predictive of any finding, but the pattern coincided with a real, disclosed earnings deterioration and a leadership change, which raises the bar for dismissing it outright). 3. The $1.9B all-cash ACV acquisition is: (a) subject to HSR antitrust clearance in a space where Copart is already the dominant salvage-auction player, so clearance is not guaranteed on current terms; (b) management's own guidance is EPS-neutral in year one, i.e. no near-term financial benefit is being offered to offset the integration and execution risk; and (c) it follows, rather than precedes, a quarter of margin and cash-flow deterioration — a moment of demonstrated operating softness is an unusual time to deploy the balance sheet's full net-cash cushion.

9. Key risks & kill criteria (measurable)

  1. Gross margin below 43% (i.e., not recovering meaningfully from the reported 44.6% FY26 full-year level) for two consecutive quarters.
  2. Operating cash flow (trailing nine/twelve months) below the prior-year comparable period for a third consecutive reporting period.
  3. HSR review of the ACV acquisition extended past a second request, or the deal terminated/repriced.
  4. Any securities-class-action complaint actually filed (as opposed to a law-firm "investigation" solicitation) naming Copart or its officers.
  5. Diluted EPS down year-over-year for two consecutive quarters.

10. Catalysts & calendar

  • Next earnings: Q1 FY2027 (quarter ending 31-Oct-2026), expected early December 2026 (estimated from Copart's historical reporting cadence; not yet confirmed by the company at time of writing).
  • ACV Auctions tender offer/HSR process: deal announced 10-Sep-2026, expected to close by year-end 2026.
  • Antitrust settlement with Auto Auction Services Corp already resolved (Copart obtained a data-access licence) — a closed item, not an open risk.

11. Red-flag scan

  • Leadership: CEO Jeffrey Liaw stepping down effective 31-Jul-2026 (announced 29-Jun-2026); founder/Executive Chairman A. Jayson Adair resumed the CEO role. Stock fell 8.0% (to $28.10) on the announcement day. No company-stated reason for the change was identified in this pass beyond "CEO transition." Liaw sold 27,745 shares on 28-Jul-2026 under a pre-existing Rule 10b5-1 plan (adopted earlier — not opportunistic on its face, but noted).
  • Litigation/investigations: Multiple plaintiff law firms (Pomerantz, Kessler Topaz Meltzer & Check, Bragar Eagel & Squire) issued "investigation" solicitations in Jun–Jul 2026 following the CEO transition and stock decline; no complaint or SEC enforcement action was identified in this pass, so this is disclosed as a monitoring item, not a confirmed adverse finding. A California PAGA wage-and-hour class/representative action (Mejia v. Copart, C.D. Cal.) is pending — a routine-scale employment-law risk for a large hourly workforce, not obviously outsized.
  • Insider selling: director Daniel J. Englander sold 80,000 shares 13-Jul-2026 ($27.50–27.66); routine option exercises by other officers/directors also on file. No pattern of unusual pre-earnings selling identified in this time-boxed pass.
  • No auditor changes, restatements, or going-concern language identified.

Camden Property Trust (CPT) - Fundamental Diligence Dossier (F147, standard depth)

Verdict: WATCH - 12-36 month horizon. A well-run Sunbelt apartment REIT that is selling expensive California assets ($1.625B) to buy Sunbelt homes and shares at lower values, but same-property NOI is still shrinking (Q2'26 -1.4%), leverage peaked at 5.3x net debt to EBITDAre, and my base case returns about 6.8% a year against an 8.5% equity hurdle. Condition that changes it: a price near $83-89 (implied AFFO growth of 0-1%), or two quarters of positive blended lease-rate growth with post-sale leverage back under 4.5x.

Triage reconciliation (Q14 said not advanced): Q14 called the 69x P/E "optically inflated" and saw no catalyst until oversupply clears in 12-18 months. Adopted: the GAAP P/E is meaningless for a REIT (Yahoo forward EPS $1.09; the 2026 GAAP EPS guide of $9.76-$10.10 includes the California gain). Changed: there is a real capital-allocation catalyst (California sale, buybacks at about $104, acquisitions at about $310k per home) that triage missed; it is not enough to reach INCLUDE.

1. Business in plain English

Camden owns and operates about 176 multifamily communities (59,676 apartment homes at 30 Jun 2026 before the sale) in Sunbelt and other growth markets, plus a development pipeline. It earns rent; the public multiple is judged on Core FFO (funds from operations excluding one-offs) and AFFO (after maintenance capex). Competitive position: scale in Texas, Florida, Georgia, Carolinas, Arizona and Nashville, in-house development and operations, investment-grade balance sheet. The 2023-26 supply wave has pushed new-lease rates negative.

Bull: (1) selling California at about $449k per home while buying Sunbelt at about $310k and repurchasing at about $104 creates NAV and deleverages; (2) same-property revenue is still +0.2% YTD and renewals +2.8%, so rent growth reaccelerates when deliveries fall; (3) 4.3% dividend covered 1.4x by AFFO with investment-grade funding. 1. Verdict

INCLUDE — thesis horizon 24–36 months. The largest US-focused building-materials/aggregates group trades at a statistically cheap multiple (~8.6x current EV/adjusted EBITDA, ~13–14x P/E) against a genuinely improving margin trend (12 consecutive years of margin expansion, per management), a clean litigation record, and moderate leverage — against a real, disclosed catalyst risk (the pending $8.5bn all-cash Arcosa acquisition, financed with committed bridge debt) that raises leverage but is explicitly sized to preserve investment-grade credit. [Corrected 2026-10-06: verdict cut to INCLUDE-SMALL. The cheapness case rested on EV/EBITDA, which ignores capex of $2.7-2.9bn a year (about a third of EBITDA); on free cash flow after all capex and SBC the stock yields about 4.2% of EV, and the implied 10-year growth (6.6%) is in line with, not below, the base case (about 6%). See the Re-assessment (RA7, 2026-10-06) section.]

2. Business in plain English

CRH is the largest vertically integrated building-materials company focused on the US market: it owns the quarries, cement/aggregates plants and asphalt/ready-mix operations (Americas Materials Solutions), value-added building products (Americas Building Solutions) and an International Solutions segment (Europe/other), selling to public infrastructure (roads, bridges), non-residential and residential construction customers. It makes money by vertically integrating from raw-material extraction (aggregates, cement) through to finished products and paving/ construction services, capturing margin at each step, and by consistently acquiring smaller regional players ("bolt-ons") to densify its footprint. Its moat is irreplaceable, permitted quarry/reserve locations near population centers (aggregates are heavy/low-value-per-ton, so transport cost creates local pricing power) plus scale in procurement and logistics.

3. Why the model likes it — durable or artefact?

b1_live_scores: composite 0.603448 (decile 7, quintile 4, live_rank 198/~2,300 — a solid but not top-decile score, consistent with quality being real rather than extreme). Durability judgement: the value/cheapness signal is durable and primary-source-verified (guidance reaffirmed twice in 2026, no fundamental deterioration found); the momentum weakness looks more like sector/rate sentiment and rising-leverage concern (§6) than a company-specific problem.
