Bear: (1) leverage is rising on two fronts simultaneously (organic M&A pace + the debt-financed Arcosa deal, pro forma FY2026E net debt/adjusted EBITDA guided to 2.4x by the company itself) — a US non-residential/ infrastructure demand slowdown (e.g., federal IIJA funding lapse) would hit EBITDA and leverage at the same time; (2) Arcosa closing is not guaranteed — subject to Arcosa stockholder approval and regulatory (antitrust) clearance, expected to close only in Q1 2027, leaving a multi-quarter integration/execution risk window; [Corrected 2026-10-06: Arcosa stockholders approved the merger on 4 Sep 2026 (39,595,867 for, 66,113 against; Arcosa 8-K 0001140361-26-035795), so the vote risk is gone. 2. Business in plain English

Salesforce sells cloud software that companies use to manage sales, customer service, marketing and commerce ("Customer 360"), plus Slack (workplace messaging), Tableau (analytics), MuleSoft (integration), and — since November 2025 — Informatica (data management/integration), on top of a fast-growing Data Cloud/Agentforce AI layer. Customers pay recurring subscription fees (over 90% of billings are subscription, invoiced annually in advance), which funds a high-margin, high-switching-cost business once embedded in a customer's workflows. Competitive position: category leader in CRM against Microsoft, Oracle, SAP, ServiceNow and HubSpot, now pivoting the growth narrative to "agentic AI" (Agentforce) monetization.

Cisco Systems, Inc. (CSCO) — Diligence Dossier

Agent: F64 | As of: 2026-09-25 close ($106.70, d4_live_snapshot.parquet) | Depth: Standard

1. Verdict

WATCH (would revisit on a pullback or after 1–2 more quarters confirming durability), 12–24 month horizon. Cisco is executing an unambiguous, primary-source-confirmed "beat and raise" across FY2026 (every quarterly guidance range beaten, full-year guidance raised twice), and FY2027 guidance implies a further large acceleration (revenue +14–16%) on the back of AI-networking hyperscaler orders and Splunk-driven security cross-sell. But this dossier's own reverse DCF shows the current price already requires ~10 more years of ~12%/yr FCF growth — well above both Cisco's mature-networking history and this analyst's own base case, which assumes the current AI-infrastructure order cycle (large, lumpy hyperscaler contracts) normalizes within a few years. A genuinely good business, priced for more than the evidence supports over a full cycle.

2. Business in plain English

Cisco sells the networking, security and collaboration hardware/software that connects and protects enterprise, service-provider and hyperscaler data centers and campuses (switches, routers, Wi-Fi, security appliances, and — since the 2024 Splunk acquisition — observability/security software). Revenue is a mix of product sales (largely one-time, though increasingly subscription-attached) and services. It is now explicitly positioning itself as critical infrastructure for AI data-center buildouts (high-speed Ethernet switching for GPU clusters) sold to hyperscalers and enterprises, on top of its long-standing core networking incumbency and huge installed base.

1. Verdict

2. Business in plain English

CoStar Group sells subscription data, analytics and marketing services to the commercial real-estate industry (CoStar, LoopNet, Apartments.com, Ten-X, STR, Matterport 3D-capture, and others) — a business with a genuine, decades-old data moat (CoStar's owned research/photography/leasing-comp database is very hard to replicate) and ~47% margins in its core segments per the triage note. Since 2021 it has plowed several billion dollars into building "Homes.com," a residential listing portal, to compete with Zillow — a large, still-loss-making bet that has drawn activist pressure (Third Point) to cut spending.

3. Why the model likes it — durable or artefact?

The core CRE-data moat (durable) is being partly offset in the reported numbers by the Homes.com investment phase (a real, disclosed, temporary drag, not an accounting artefact) — durability judgment: durable moat, temporarily depressed consolidated profitability, and the Q2 2026 print is the first primary-source evidence the drag is easing.

8. Bull case / bear case

Bull: (1) Core CRE-data business is a genuine, multi-decade moat with ~47%-margin economics (per triage) that keeps compounding regardless of the Homes.com outcome; (2) Q2 2026 was the first quarter the Residential segment (including Homes.com) was Adjusted-EBITDA-positive, a real, primary-source-verified inflection, with EBITDA guidance raised in the same release; (3) net cash balance sheet gives real optionality (buyback authorization, further bolt-ons) without leverage risk. Bear: (1) GAAP profitability is essentially zero (FY2025 net income $7m on $4.3bn+ of revenue [Corrected 2026-10-06: FY2025 revenue was $3,247.0M]) and has been declining for three straight years as Homes.com spend ramped — the "inflection" is one quarter of data; (2) full-year revenue guidance was cut in the same release that raised EBITDA guidance, a genuinely mixed signal that the market (correctly, per stock-price reaction) treated as a caution flag, not an unambiguous positive; (3) management's capital-allocation credibility is still being actively rebuilt under Third Point activist pressure — the $300m 2026 spending cut was a response to investor pressure, not a self-initiated pivot, and the company does not reach sustained positive Homes.com profitability until 2029–2030 on its own guidance.

9. Key risks & kill criteria (measurable)

  1. Full-year revenue guidance is cut again at the next quarterly release (already cut once, Jan→Jul 2026).
  2. Residential-segment Adjusted EBITDA reverts to negative for two consecutive quarters after the Q2 2026 inflection.
  3. Cash and equivalents fall below $750m (from $1.27bn at Q2 2026) [Corrected 2026-10-06: pro forma cash after the $800M Zonda closing is about $0.47bn] without a corresponding new debt raise, signalling liquidity stress from the M&A + buyback + Homes.com combination.
  4. GAAP net income is negative for the full FY2026 (it was only marginally positive, $7m, in FY2025).
  5. Homes.com net 2026 investment reduction (guided at "more than $300m" cut vs. 2025's $850m) is not delivered by year-end 2026 (i.e., actual 2026 Homes.com net spend comes in above the ~$550m implied level).

10. Catalysts & calendar

  • Next earnings: Q3 2026, estimated late October 2026 (pattern: 2025-10-29, 2024-10-23; not yet officially confirmed — flagged as an estimate).
  • Continued Third Point/activist engagement — any further public letters or board changes are a near-term catalyst risk in both directions.
  • Homes.com quarterly Adjusted-EBITDA trend (2nd data point due at the next print) is the single most important near-term confirming/disconfirming signal for this thesis.

11. Red-flag scan

  • No auditor change, material weakness, restatement or going-concern language identified in this pass; no short-seller report found in searches conducted 2026-09-26 (absence of evidence, not proof of absence, at standard-depth time-box).
  • Activist involvement: Third Point (and reportedly D.E. Shaw) pushed for Homes.com spending discipline; the board/management publicly responded (Jan 2026 8-K) — a governance-attention flag, not a fraud flag.
  • Data conflict vs. triage: the triage note characterised the stock as "at a 7-year low pricing in the burn without much credit for the inflection," implying clearly cheap. Our own (admittedly judgement-heavy) reverse-DCF cross-check lands closer to fair value, not a clear bargain — flagged as a data conflict between the quick-triage read and this deeper pass.
  • Insider Form-4 pattern not separately checked this cycle (time-boxed) — a limitation, not a confirmed finding either way.

CSX — CSX Corporation

Agent: F125 (wave 8 standard diligence). Price basis: 2026-09-25 close $46.78 (d4 snapshot, Yahoo; mkt cap ~$86.7bn on 1,852.5m shares).

1. Verdict

WATCH — a franchise with real operating momentum (Q2 2026 GAAP operating margin 38.3%), but the 25 Sep close already implies ~9.5% 10-year FCF growth against an evidence-based base case of ~7% [Corrected 2026-10-06: at a consistent 10.17% cost of equity the implied growth is about 13.4%]; the quick triage ("excessive", merger-speculation momentum) is broadly confirmed on price, overturned on quality. Horizon 12–36 months. Changes to INCLUDE-SMALL if the price falls to roughly $38–40 (implied growth <= base) [Corrected 2026-10-06: on the corrected 10.17% cost of equity that price is about $29] or FCF (OCF less property additions) TTM exceeds ~$3.4bn.

2. Business in plain English

CSX runs a ~20,000-employee Class I freight railroad covering the eastern US (merchandise ~62% of Q2 revenue, intermodal ~16%, coal ~13%, trucking and other the rest). It earns money by hauling carloads and containers at a price per unit plus fuel surcharges; moat is the fixed rail network and limited duplication east of the Mississippi. Competitor Norfolk Southern is, per the 10-K, party to a pending merger with Union Pacific needing Surface Transportation Board (STB) approval, which is the main strategic overhang.

3. Why the model likes it, and is it durable

b1/V1 shortlisted it on quality and momentum; triage called momentum "merger-speculation driven". Filings show part of the 2026 improvement is real (volume +6%, headcount -1,392 YoY, non-fuel expense -$39m) and part is optical: Q2 revenue +10% includes fuel surcharge revenue of $410m vs $222m, offset by fuel expense +$177m (locomotive fuel price +74%), so margin percentage is flattered while dollars are neutral. Cost savings and 2025 comps (Helene rebuild, network disruption) are partly one-time.

Price $46.78; TTM GAAP EPS $1.73 (0.37+0.39+0.43+0.54); 2026E ~$2.00 (Yahoo consensus cross-check) -> ~23x current-year, ~20.6x forward. V1 (systematic) row: verdict "excessive", NTM P/E 21.2 (76th percentile of own history), implied growth 13.9% vs 5.2% delivered 5y and ~5.0% consensus, base 3y annualised -8.2% (bear -28.1%, bull +15.0%). Basis: starting EPS $2.00 (2026E), growth 0/7/12%, exit P/E 15/20/24x, dividend $0.56/share per year not reinvested. implied_vs_base = above.

8. Bull / bear

Bull: (1) intermodal +9% volume and +26% revenue in Q2 on domestic wins and a tight truck market; (2) headcount -6% YoY with op margin 38.3% shows the cost reset is structural; (3) any STB-driven industry consolidation could reprice eastern rail scarcity. Bear: (1) price already embeds ~9.5% growth vs 5.2% delivered; (2) Q2 fuel lag was -$54m and the surcharge windfall reverses if diesel falls; (3) merger path is unresolved: Q2 MD&A cites "advisory expenses related to potential industry consolidation" and the UNP/NS outcome could strand CSX's positioning.

9. Kill criteria

  1. GAAP operating margin below 34.0% for two consecutive quarters (Q2'26 38.3%, H1'26 37.2%; FY25 32.1%).
  2. Consolidated net debt (current maturities + long-term debt less cash and short-term investments) / TTM (operating income + D&A) above 3.2x (now ~2.6x).
  3. Total carload volume down year over year for two consecutive quarters (Q2'26 +6%, H1'26 +4%).
  4. TTM operating cash flow less property additions below $2.0bn (now ~$2.8bn) or 2026 capex guidance raised above $2.6bn.
  5. CSX signs a definitive agreement to acquire or merge with another Class I railroad at consideration above $10bn, or an STB decision materially adverse to CSX's interchange position.

10. Catalysts and calendar

Q3 2026 earnings 2026-10-21 (Yahoo; not company-confirmed in a filing I opened); STB proceedings on UNP/NS; Q4 capex and 2027 plan (Jan 2027); fuel surcharge appeal oral argument (date unset).

No material weakness noted in the 10-K (one critical audit matter, not a restatement). Litigation per Q2 10-Q Note 5: fuel surcharge antitrust (summary judgment for railroads 24 Jun 2025; appeal briefing complete, argument unscheduled); Lower Passaic/Occidental environmental indemnity; casualty reserves. 8-K 2026-05-14 (acc. 0000950103-26-007181, Item 5.02): CTO Stephen Fortune separated effective immediately. Insider ownership ~0.2%. No going-concern language; I did not review Form 4s line by line.

Verdict: WATCH, 12-36 month horizon. Reason: one of the best-run compounders in the index (organic growth 8.2-8.9% for five quarters [Corrected 2026-10-06: Q1 FY26 organic growth was 7.8%, so the 8.2-8.9% range covers four quarters], record margins, raised guidance every quarter), but at $199.91 the price implies about 12% annual FCF growth for ten years against an evidence-based base case near 9.5%, and there is an unpriced-by-the-triage event: the pending UniFirst acquisition (about $5.5B) is under an FTC second request. Cintas rents and launders uniforms, mats and restroom supplies to over one million businesses, sells first aid and safety products and services, and inspects fire extinguishers and sprinklers. 1. Verdict

INCLUDE-SMALL (half weight) — thesis horizon 24–36 months.

CVS is a genuine, multi-quarter operational turnaround (Aetna medical costs improving, Medicare Advantage star ratings recovered sharply, guidance raised in three of the last four releases) trading at a statistically cheap multiple (10.6x NTM P/E, 8.8th percentile of its own 14-year history). The reservation: ~3.7x net debt/EBITDA, $85.5bn of goodwill (≈75% of market cap), a still-negative-outlook credit profile at two of three rating agencies, and an unresolved post-2028 PBM cost-plus mandate mean the full re-rating to a ~17x historical-average multiple that the V1 model's base case assumes is not assured on this timeline. Size accordingly.

2. Business in plain English

CVS Health is a diversified health-care conglomerate with three engines: Aetna (health insurance, including a large Medicare Advantage book), Health Services (CVS Caremark, the pharmacy-benefit manager that negotiates drug prices and rebates for employers/insurers, plus Oak Street Health primary-care clinics and Signify Health home assessments), and Pharmacy & Consumer Wellness (roughly 9,000 retail pharmacies). It makes money on insurance premiums net of medical claims, PBM spread/rebate economics and dispensing fees, and retail pharmacy margins. Its competitive position is scale: it is one of only three vertically integrated payer-PBM-pharmacy platforms in the US (with UnitedHealth/Optum and Cigna/Express Scripts), which matters because federal PBM reform is now reshaping how all three get paid.

3. Why the model likes it

B1 quant data (v4/data/b1_live_scores.csv, live_rank 25) and V1 valuation both flag CVS as statistically cheap on NTM P/E versus its own history. This is not primarily a momentum or quality signal — the 12-month price move (+28.5% per the underlying momentum factor) is a recovery off a depressed 2024–2025 base, and the "cheapness" is a scar from two years of Medicare Advantage cost misses, guidance cuts and a leadership change, not a hidden gem the market missed. The durability question is whether the 2026 operational improvement (below) is real and sustained, or a cyclical bounce that fades once easy comparisons roll off. The evidence in hard numbers (section 5) leans toward real, but recent.

DAL — Delta Air Lines, Inc. — Diligence Dossier (Agent F41, Wave 2, Standard depth)

1. Verdict

INCLUDE-SMALL — the strongest US airline franchise (SkyMiles/Amex co-brand economics differentiate it from commodity airline economics), fairly priced with no real margin of safety; named reservation: a large mid-2026 jet-fuel spike and a December-2026 pilot-contract re-opener are two concrete, near-term tests the thesis has not yet passed. Thesis horizon: 12–36 months.

2. Business in plain English

Delta is a full-service US "Big 3" airline operating a global hub network (Atlanta, Detroit, Minneapolis, Salt Lake City, New York, LA) plus premium international joint ventures (Air France-KLM, Virgin Atlantic, LATAM, Aeromexico, Korean Air). Roughly half of its earnings power comes from non-ticket sources that are less commoditized than a seat: the SkyMiles/American Express co-brand card program (loyalty cash flow sold to Amex), Delta Premium Select/first-class upsell, cargo, and Delta TechOps/MRO (aircraft maintenance for other airlines) — the reason the triage note calls its "loyalty economics" a differentiator from a pure commodity-seat business.

3. Why the model likes it — durable or artefact?

Triage: quality 4/5, growth 4/5, price_vs_growth 4/5, no red flags; "18.7% revenue growth, 20% ROE at just 10.7x NTM P/E; cheap for the quality." b1 factor read: composite driven mainly by Momentum (12-1m return ~39%, 78th pct) and Earnings-momentum (SUE), with Quality percentiles decent but not exceptional (ROE 44.9th pct is unremarkable for the family average once leverage is included). This is a mostly durable read — the loyalty/co-brand and MRO revenue streams are structurally differentiated and have grown for years — but part of the recent momentum score is a fuel-driven margin swing artefact: the 2026 fare/margin story is entangled with a large jet-fuel cost spike (see §6), which cuts both ways in the numbers below and needs to be read net of fuel, not gross.

5. Guidance track record (last 2 releases)

  • Q1 2026 release (Apr 2026): full-year 2026 adjusted EPS guide $6.50–7.50; free cash flow $3–4bn; gross leverage target ≈2x. Q2 2026 guide given: low-teens revenue growth.

6. Earnings quality & balance sheet

  • Fuel shock: per-gallon jet-fuel cost rose from a $2.30–2.60 range in 2025 to $3.93 in the June-2026 quarter — a large, disclosed, exogenous cost shock (context: a war-driven oil-price spike also flagged elsewhere in this program's diligence, e.g. the EOG dossier). This is the primary driver of the Q1 2026 GAAP net loss (−$289m) and the Q2 2026 adjusted-operating-margin decline (−24% YoY) — not an execution failure; per the sector playbook, airline OPM is "mostly not a skill signal" when the dominant cost line is exogenous fuel.
  • FCF (FY, OCF−capex, $m): FY2022 6,363−6,366=−3 (breakeven); FY2023 6,464−5,323=1,141; FY2024 8,025−5,140=2,885; FY2025 8,342−4,499=3,843.   • Leverage: company-stated gross leverage target ≈2x (guided, presumably lease-adjusted/EBITDAR-based — not independently rebuilt from raw XBRL at this depth, a limitation per the sector playbook's EBITDAR methodology).   • Cash: $3.1–5.1bn range over the last 8 quarters, no liquidity stress signal; diluted share count essentially flat (642m → 658m, +2.5% over 2 years — modest dilution, not buyback-driven reduction).
  • Pilot-contract re-opener: current agreement amendable 31 December 2026; a flight-attendant unionization drive is also underway (per search results) — both are real, disclosed labor-cost risks not yet reflected in the FY2026 guide's assumptions in detail.

7. Valuation snapshot and reverse DCF

V1 systematic valuation exists for DAL (v1_valuation_table.csv): NTM P/E 10.72x, 63.9th percentile of DAL's own 10-year history, peer median 9.90x, "within Street 12m target range," verdict "fair" (verdict_score −0.084), bear/base/bull 3-yr annualized returns −39.6% / −2.8% / +37.2%. - Price (25-Sep-2026 close) $84.94; market cap ≈$55.86bn. - Reverse DCF (own model, 10-yr explicit + Gordon terminal, r=10.0%, terminal g=2.5%) using FY2025 actual FCF ($3,843m, consistent with the company's own FY2026 guide): implies the market is pricing in ≈3.4%/yr 10-year FCF growth. Using the guide's midpoint ($3.5bn) as a slightly more conservative base: ≈4.6%/yr. - Analyst view: fair (in_line). A plausible base case (mid-single-digit FCF growth, ~4.5%/yr, reflecting continued loyalty/MRO/premium-mix growth moderating from today's mid-teens revenue growth as capacity growth normalizes) is very close to both implied-growth readings → implied_vs_base = "in_line." - Reconciliation with V1: V1's own base case (−2.8%/yr) and ours (+2.8%/yr using a symmetric FCF-growth framing) differ in sign but both cluster near zero — i.e., both approaches independently conclude the stock is roughly fairly priced with limited base-case upside, not "cheap." The sign difference likely reflects V1 pricing in more of the fuel-shock margin risk into its base case than our FCF-guide-anchored approach does. Consistent: true (both call it "fair," near-zero excess-return base case).

8. Bull case / bear case

Bull: (1) SkyMiles/Amex co-brand and premium/MRO diversification give Delta a structurally better revenue mix than commodity-seat peers, and it is trading at a discount to its own 10-year P/E history (63.9th percentile is mid-range, not stretched) [Corrected 2026-10-06: a 63.9th percentile means the multiple is above its own median, i.e. a premium to history, not a discount] despite the best fundamentals in the group; (2) FCF has grown for three straight years to a guided $3–4bn in FY2026, funding continued deleveraging (debt down from $18.1bn to $12.9bn since Q1 2024); (3) full-year guidance was reaffirmed despite a real fuel shock, evidence of pricing power/cost-recapture discipline. Bear: (1) Jet fuel per gallon nearly doubled intra-year (2025's $2.30–2.60 range to $3.93 in Q2 2026) and already drove a Q1 2026 GAAP net loss and a 24% YoY adjusted-operating-income decline in Q2 2026 — if oil stays elevated, FY2026 guidance is at risk despite today's reaffirmation; (2) the pilot-contract re-opener (amendable 31 Dec 2026) and a flight-attendant unionization drive are two concrete, dated labor-cost catalysts not yet priced into the guide in detail; (3) V1's own base-case 3-yr return is slightly negative — this is a "fair," not "cheap," entry point in a historically boom-bust, high-fixed-cost industry with no valuation cushion if either fuel or labor costs surprise to the upside.

9. Key risks & kill criteria (measurable)

  1. Company-guided FY2026 free cash flow ($3–4bn) is cut or actual FY2026 FCF comes in below $2.5bn.
  2. Full-year adjusted EPS guidance ($6.50–7.50) is cut at any remaining 2026 release.
  3. Company-stated gross leverage rises above 3.0x (guided ≈2x).
  4. Jet-fuel cost per gallon sustains above $3.50 for two consecutive quarters without offsetting fare/capacity action (already at $3.93 in Q2 2026 — a live trigger to monitor, not yet tripped on guidance terms).
  5. The pilot-contract re-opener (amendable 31-Dec-2026) concludes with a ratified agreement carrying double-digit annual unit-cost escalation beyond current assumptions, or results in a work action/strike.

(3) International expansion via Deliveroo materially increases the addressable market without DASH having to build local density from scratch.

Bear (3): (1) Active Dasher-misclassification litigation and regulatory inquiries in multiple states (California EDD audit/assessment, per the Q2-2026 10-Q's own legal-proceedings note) plus a reported (secondary-source) ~$131.5M multi-state worker-payment settlement create both a cash-cost and business-model risk (reclassification to employees would materially raise costs). DELL — Dell Technologies Inc. — Diligence Dossier (Agent F60, Wave 3)

1. Verdict

INCLUDE-SMALL (12–36 month horizon), with a named reservation: DELL is now, in effect, an AI-server-cycle stock (revenue and backlog concentrated in Nvidia-platform rack integration for a handful of hyperscale/AI customers) wrapped around a legacy, low-margin PC/traditional-server business and a still-large (if improving) legacy-LBO debt load. No V1 systematic valuation row exists for DELL (v1_verdict = null); this verdict rests on my own primary-source work below.

2. Business in plain English

Dell designs, builds and sells servers, storage, PCs and related services to enterprises, governments and consumers, largely through its own direct sales/channel model. Its fastest-growing segment (Infrastructure Solutions Group, ISG) integrates and ships AI-optimized server racks (built around Nvidia GPUs) to hyperscalers and large enterprises; its larger but slower-growing Client Solutions Group (CSG) sells PCs/laptops. It also runs Dell Financial Services (DFS), a captive leasing/financing arm that funds equipment purchases for customers.

3. Why the model likes it — durable or artefact?

b1 factor scores show strong quality (asset growth 88th pct — balance sheet expanding to fund the AI buildout — and strong earnings momentum, SUE 85th pct), with ROE not computed (negative/undefined equity base, a legacy artefact of the 2016 EMC-merger LBO capital structure, not a current red flag by itself). The growth is real and accelerating, not an artefact: revenue, operating income and — critically — the AI-server order backlog have all inflected together across three consecutive quarters of results and two consecutive guidance raises (§5), each corroborated by a specific, disclosed backlog dollar figure rather than vague commentary.

Bull (3): (1) $95B AI-server backlog (disclosed at the Q2 FY2027 earnings call, 2026-09-01) provides multi-quarter revenue visibility well beyond the current guide period. (3) The GAAP-vs-non-GAAP EPS gap is comparatively narrow for a large-cap tech name, meaning the market isn't being asked to look past heavy stock-comp adjustments to believe the growth story.

Bear (3): (1) DELL's AI-server business is a rack-integration/assembly margin on top of Nvidia's GPUs for a concentrated set of hyperscale/AI customers — a single large customer loss, a shift to buying direct, or an Nvidia platform-availability shock would hit disproportionately. (2) $9.6B of the $34.5B total debt is DFS financing debt tied to customer leases — if AI-server demand reverses, DFS receivable credit quality (customer concentration again) becomes a live balance-sheet risk, not just a revenue one. dossiers.DG:
DG — Dollar General Corporation

1. Verdict

INCLUDE-SMALL (half weight) — thesis horizon 12–36 months. Statistically rare valuation (NTM P/E at the 7th percentile of its own 175-month trading history) combined with a primary-source-verified, broad-based operating recovery (four consecutive quarterly guidance raises, six consecutive quarters of positive comps in all four merchandise categories) justifies a position, but a recurring workplace-safety compliance problem, unresolved shareholder securities litigation, and a guidance raise that is partly non-repeating (tariff refunds, a lower tax-rate assumption) are specific, named reservations against taking a full-weight position today.

2. Business in plain English

Dollar General is the largest small-box discount retailer in the US: 21,148 stores (Dollar General, DG Market, DGX, pOpshelf, plus a small Mexico pilot) as of July 31, 2026, mostly in rural and small-town America, selling consumables (food, health/beauty, cleaning — ~82% of sales), seasonal goods, home products and apparel at everyday low prices within a few minutes' drive of its customers. It makes money on thin per-unit margins (gross margin ~30–33%) applied to very high inventory turns and a low-cost, no-frills real-estate/labor model; its moat is store density and proximity in markets too small for Walmart or Target to bother with. It competes on convenience and price against Dollar Tree/Family Dollar, Walmart, and increasingly grocery and drug chains.

3. Why the model likes it — and is it durable?

B1 composite score is in the top decile (live_rank 18/~2,300; composite percentile 96.5; gates: the composite itself carries no disqualifying-red-flag gate — the red-flag/legal check is done separately in §11 below, not netted into this score). Family drivers: Value (fam_V ≈0.88, very high) — cheap on earnings yield, FCF yield, EBIT/EV and book/price; Quality (fam_Q ≈0.63) — solid gross-profit/assets and low accruals; Earnings momentum (fam_S ≈0.84) — SUE has been strongly positive as EPS beat-and-raise repeated; Momentum (fam_M ≈0.70) — the stock has rallied off a 2024 low as the recovery took hold.

Durability check: the Value signal is real and verifiable — DG trades at 15.2x NTM EPS against a 175-month own history whose 7th percentile this is, i.e., DG has traded above today's multiple in ~93% of the months since 2012. The earnings-momentum signal is partly an artefact: of the ~$0.60 increase in the FY2026 diluted-EPS guidance midpoint between the Q1 (Jun-2026) and Q2 (Aug-2026) releases, management explicitly attributes ~$0.25 (≈40%) to a one-time tariff-refund benefit it says will not recur in H2, and part of the earlier Q4→Q1 raise was a lower effective-tax-rate assumption (25.0%→24.5%) rather than operating improvement. The comp/traffic recovery itself (6 straight quarters of positive comps in every category, 5 straight quarters of positive traffic) is corroborated by the primary-source press releases and is the more durable part of the story.

It is not conservative]

Quarterly variance analysis (Q2 FY26 vs Q2 FY25 vs Q1 FY26): Revenue +5.2% YoY / +4.7% QoQ (in line, driven by same-store sales +3.5% — traffic +2.0pp, ticket +1.5pp — plus new-store contribution, partly offset by closures). Gross margin +126bps YoY (just under the 200bp materiality bar): company attributes it to tariff refunds (~+81bps), a lower LIFO provision and lower distribution costs, partly offset by higher markdowns and transportation cost. SG&A ratio flat YoY (25.79% both periods) — no SG&A leverage story here, the margin gain is 100% gross-margin-driven. Operating margin +126bps YoY, +89bps QoQ. Net interest expense −25.7% YoY ($57.7m→$42.9m) on debt paydown. Net income +33.8% YoY, diluted EPS +33.3% YoY (includes ~$0.25 tariff-refund benefit per management's own disclosure).

H1 FY26 cash flow — a >10% material variance, decomposed: operating cash flow fell 17.5% YoY ($1,814.9m→$1,496.7m) and free cash flow fell 34.1% ($1,121.0m→$738.3m) despite net income rising. Source: the primary cash-flow statement. Driver: working capital moved against the company — merchandise inventories used $249.0m of cash in H1 FY26 vs. providing $44.7m in H1 FY25 (a $293.7m swing, inventory levels are up on new-store growth and category mix), and income-tax timing used $140.9m of cash vs. providing $46.6m a year ago (a $187.5m swing). This is a genuine, primary-source-verified earnings-quality flag: the P&L recovery has not yet shown up in operating cash flow.

6. Earnings quality & balance sheet

  • FCF conversion: H1 FY26 FCF/NI = $738.3m / $994.4m = 0.74x, down from 1.40x in H1 FY25 — driven by the working-capital swing in §4, not by a change in underlying profitability.
  • SBC: immaterial, 0.10%–0.34% of quarterly net sales across the last 8 quarters — not a distorting factor for this name.
  • GAAP vs adjusted: DG reports clean GAAP with limited non-GAAP adjustment; the main "quality" question is the tariff-refund/tax-rate composition of the EPS raise (see §3/§5), which management itself discloses and quantifies — a genuine positive for transparency.
  • Balance sheet (2026-07-31 vs 2025-08-01, from the 10-Q balance sheet): cash $1,589.6m (was $1,284.6m, +23.7%); merchandise inventory $6,552.8m (was $6,609.7m, −0.9% gross, "−2.7% per store" per the release — real inventory discipline against store-count growth); total debt (LT obligations + current portion) $4,570.8m, down 20.4% YoY from $5,745.1m — meaningful deleveraging, which is the direct cause of the 25.7% YoY drop in net interest expense; shareholders' equity $9,288.6m (+15.9% YoY). Operating lease liabilities (current + long-term) ≈$11.2bn — large but flat YoY and, being US GAAP (ASC 842), already sit as a P&L opex line rather than mechanically inflating EBITDA the way IFRS 16 lessees' would (per the sector playbook's US/IFRS distinction) — DG's margins are not artificially flattered by lease accounting the way a European retail peer's might be.
  • Net debt/EBITDA: using V1's inputs (net debt $2,981m, TTM EBIT $2,440m + TTM D&A $1,085m ≈ TTM EBITDA $3,525m) ≈ 0.85x — very low, leaving real balance-sheet capacity.
  • Share count: diluted shares essentially flat (~220–222m) over the period; buybacks only resumed in FY2026 so have not yet meaningfully reduced the count.
  • M&A: none pending or recent.

7. Valuation snapshot — reconciliation with V1

V1 verdict: attractive (score 0.80/1.0). NTM P/E 15.2x vs DG's own 175-month history — 7th percentile (DG has traded richer than this in ~93% of months since 2012) — and vs peer median 16.1x (COST/DLTR/TGT/WMT). Reverse-DCF implied 10-year growth is −2.9% (the market is pricing gradual decline), against consensus FY1 growth of +4.0% and delivered 5-year/10-year CAGRs of +5.3%/+7.6% — i.e., the price already assumes something worse than the depressed recent past, not a return to form. V1 base case: revenue growth 7.6%/yr (in line with the 10-year delivered rate — not aggressive), margin reaching only 5.8% by year 3 (below the FY22 peak of 8.79% and roughly in line with what FY2026 guidance already implies for the current year — not aggressive), exit multiple 19.0x (below DG's own historical norm, which a 7th-percentile ranking implies was routinely higher) → base annualised 3-yr return +34.7%; [Corrected 2026-10-06: V1's bear case is also +19.7% a year (net margin 5.2%, exit 16.7x, EPS $12.42), which is not a bear case; the garbled bear/bull wording in this paragraph is superseded by the re-assessment below] bear −19.7%/bull +50.9%×wait, bear scenario is stated as an annualised return of +19.7% (V1's "bear" scenario is still a positive return here, reflecting how depressed the starting multiple already is) and bull +50.9%. Street 12-month target range $90–$176 (mean $140.76); V1's base 3-year value of ~$305/share exceeds the Street's 12-month high, which V1 itself flags as a sanity-check flag (street_flag) — a reasonable flag given the difference in horizon (3-year vs 12-month), not evidence the model is broken.

My view: consistent = true, dossier_view = cheap. I agree the stock is statistically cheap on both an absolute (own-history) and relative (implied-vs-delivered-growth) basis, and the base case's margin/multiple assumptions are, if anything, conservative relative to what has already been guided and delivered. [Corrected 2026-10-06: wrong, see the correction in section 4: the base case needs EPS to roughly double ($7.90 FY26 guide to $15.67), not a margin 'in line with guidance'] My reservation is not with the valuation math but with two things V1's arithmetic cannot see: (i) the durability of the recovery is not yet proven across a full year without one-off tailwinds (tariff refunds explicitly flagged by management as non-repeating), and (ii) the legal/compliance overhang in §9 is a real tail risk to the "clean execution" assumption embedded in continuing to re-rate toward 19x.

8. Bull case / bear case

Bull (3): 1. Six consecutive quarters of positive comps across all four merchandise categories, with positive traffic for five straight quarters — a broad, primary-source-verified demand recovery, not a one-category fluke. 2. Deleveraging is real and already showing up (net interest expense −25.7% YoY) with net debt/EBITDA ≈0.85x, giving room to keep resuming buybacks (guided up to $700m in FY26, versus none in FY25) while continuing store growth (~460 new stores planned FY26). 3. Valuation sits at the 7th percentile of its own 13+ year history — a rare entry point if the recovery merely continues rather than accelerates.

Bear (3): 1. Roughly 40% of the most recent guidance raise is a one-time tariff-refund benefit management itself says will not repeat in H2 FY2026 — strip it out and the "beat" is smaller than headline. 2. H1 FY2026 operating cash flow fell 17.5% YoY and free cash flow fell 34.1% YoY even as net income rose — a genuine, unexplained-by-one-offs working-capital drag that bears watching for a second consecutive half. 3. A corporate-wide OSHA safety settlement ($12m, July 2024, on top of >$15m in cumulative penalties since 2017) and an unresolved shareholder securities class action (dismissed without prejudice June 2025; plaintiffs seeking leave to amend as of Aug 2025) both point to unresolved execution/governance friction in a 21,000-plus-store, high-labor-turnover business.

9. Key risks & kill criteria (measurable)

  1. Same-store sales growth turns negative for two consecutive quarters (from +3.5% currently).
  2. Full-year diluted-EPS guidance is cut versus the prior quarter's range (four straight raises to date; a cut would break the trend).
  3. Net debt / TTM EBITDA rises above 2.5x (currently ≈0.85x).
  4. The Board suspends or fails to execute materially against the "up to $700 million" FY2026 buyback authorization.
  5. A new OSHA penalty or DOJ/regulatory safety action exceeding $5 million, or the securities class action is reinstated with an expanded class/damages theory.

10. Catalysts & calendar

  • Next earnings: Q3 FY2026, estimated early December 2026 (historical pattern: first Thursday of December in 2022–2025; not yet confirmed by the company — treat as an estimate).
  • H2 FY2026 will show whether the tariff-refund/margin gain holds without the one-off (management's own stated test).
  • Continued Project Renovate/Project Elevate remodel cadence (2,000/2,250 stores planned FY2026) and ~460 new store openings.
  • Any ruling on the pending motion for leave to amend the consolidated shareholder securities complaint.

11. Red-flag scan

  • OSHA settlement (July 2024): $12m corporate-wide penalty resolving allegations of blocked emergency exits, blocked electrical panels/fire extinguishers and unsafe storage across (ex-pOpshelf) stores; DG has paid >$15m in cumulative OSHA penalties since 2017 — a recurring, structural safety-compliance issue, not a one-off (source: US DOL/OSHA press release, 2024-07-11; Grocery Dive, CBS News).
  • Shareholder securities class action: Washtenaw County Employees' Retirement System v. Dollar General Corp. (M.D. Tenn., No. 3:23-cv-01250), alleging DG and officers misrepresented the impact of store labor, inventory and pricing practices on results (putative class period May 2020–Aug 2024). Court granted defendants' motion to dismiss the second consolidated amended complaint without prejudice on 2026-06-23; lead plaintiffs filed a motion for leave to amend on 2025-08-25. Status as of this dossier: dismissed but not fully resolved — monitor.
  • Store-portfolio charge: FY2024 (ended Jan-2025) results included a ~$0.81/share negative impact "related to the store portfolio"; separately, ~45 pOpshelf stores were closed and 6 converted to Dollar General banners with associated impairment in the same window.
  • Executive change: EVP & General Counsel Rhonda Taylor announced retirement 2026-08-25 (Item 5.02 8-K); internal successor (Kelly Collier) named, long transition through April 2027 — routine succession, not a red flag on its own.
  • No auditor change, no restatement, no going-concern language identified in the filings reviewed.

D.R. Horton, Inc. (DHI) — Diligence Dossier

Agent: F113 | Depth: Standard | As of: 2026-09-25 close ($141.51) | CIK 0000882184

1. Verdict

INCLUDE-SMALL (half weight). Reason: the market is pricing DHI for roughly flat-to-low-single-digit long-run FCF growth, close to what a cyclically depressed but structurally durable #1 US homebuilder can plausibly deliver — but fiscal-2026 guidance has been cut twice in a row and margins are still compressing, so conviction is capped. Horizon: 24–36 months (through a housing-cycle trough and recovery).

2. Business in plain English

D.R. Horton is the largest homebuilder in the US by volume, building and selling single-family homes (and increasingly rental homes and multi-family) across ~120 markets in 36 states, plus a captive mortgage-origination arm (DHI Mortgage) and a majority-owned land developer (Forestar). It makes money by buying/developing lots, building homes at scale with a "just-in-time," asset-light-relative-to-peers model, and selling to first-time and move-up buyers; competitive position rests on national scale, broad price-point coverage and a large controlled lot pipeline that lets it flex volume with demand.

3. Why the model likes it / is it durable

b1_live_scores (2026-09-26 snapshot): composite 0.309 (decile 4, live_rank 343/503) — mixed. Quality (fam_Q 0.273) middling: ROE 12.8%, OCF/assets 9.2%, but net share issuance is negative (buybacks, pct_net_issuance percentile not in top tier) and asset growth is low (0.3%), consistent with a company deliberately slowing land spend into a softer market. Momentum (fam_M 0.382) and earnings momentum (fam_S 0.174, SUE −0.42) are weak — EPS has been declining YoY for several quarters. This is a value/quality-lite signal, not a growth or momentum one; the "cheapness" is largely an artefact of the market correctly discounting a cyclical earnings peak (FY2023–24), not a mispricing. 1. Verdict

WATCH, horizon 12–36 months. Excellent franchise, but $224.49 implies ~9.3% 10-year free-cash-flow growth against my base of ~7%: a great business priced for more than it can deliver. The triage verdict (advance=false) stands, but its stated reasons rested on general knowledge; the filings add three new facts that raise the bar: Danaher swapped $9.8bn of cash for Masimo in June 2026 (consolidated net debt about $22bn, ~2.9x EBITDA), it cut the top half of its 2026 core-growth range (3–6% to 3–4%) in July, and the CEO hands over on 1 Oct 2026. 2. Business in plain English

Danaher sells the tools and consumables of biotech and diagnostics: bioprocessing (Cytiva/Pall filters, bioreactors, resins for making biologic drugs), life-science instruments (SCIEX, Leica, Beckman's research lines), and diagnostics (Cepheid molecular tests, Beckman Coulter lab analyzers, Radiometer, and now Masimo patient monitoring). Revenue is mostly recurring consumables on an installed base; the Danaher Business System (continuous improvement) is its edge, and ~60,000 associates. FY25 sales were $24.6bn.

All figures below are on a consolidated basis (Digital Realty Trust, Inc., the parent REIT, plus its operating partnership and subsidiaries); no standalone-only figures are used. This is a genuine, broad-based guidance raise across revenue, FFO and leasing-economics metrics — not merely a beat-and-hold.

6. Earnings quality & balance sheet (REIT metric set — see sector playbook)

  • Leverage: net debt / adjusted EBITDA 4.7x (flat Q1→Q2 2026; down from 5.1x a year ago); debt-plus-preferred / enterprise value 22.3% (down from 22.7% Q1 2026); fixed-charge coverage 5.2x; Q2 interest expense $113.9m. New long-term debt issuance guided at 4.5–5.5% pricing (raised from 4.0–4.5% — a real, disclosed increase in marginal borrowing cost).
  • Development capex and dilution: FY26 development capex guidance raised to $4.25–4.75bn (net of partner contributions) to hit targeted 10%+ stabilised yields on new capacity. YTD through Q2 2026 the company sold 13.5 million shares at an average $184.94 via its ATM programme, raising $2.5bn — real, ongoing dilution funding the growth, which is the standard trade-off for this business model (see REIT sector playbook: never judge FCF/dividend coverage without checking the funding source of growth capex).

7. Valuation snapshot and reverse-multiple check (REIT framework, not FCFF DCF)

No V1 systematic-valuation row exists for DLR (outside V1's original 69-name universe) — v1_verdict = null. Per the finance-skills REIT playbook, P/E and generic reverse-FCF-DCF are the wrong tool here (REIT depreciation and gain/loss accounting break both); the correct anchor is P/Core FFO and the implied cap rate.

  • P/Core FFO: $178.61 ÷ ~$8.175 (FY26 guide midpoint, ex-net-promote) ≈ 21.9x — a premium to the developed-market office-REIT range (12–18x) that the sector playbook flags as normal for a contracted, hyperscale-demand growth REIT rather than a stabilised income REIT; comparable data-center peers command similar-to-higher multiples in the current AI-capex cycle (not independently peer-benchmarked this pass — flagged as a limitation).
  • Reverse dividend-discount sanity check: trailing dividend yield ≈2.7% (Yahoo/d4 snapshot); at an estimated ~8% cost of equity for a REIT running 4.7x leverage, the yield alone implies the market requires only ≈5.3%/yr perpetual distribution growth — well below the double-digit Core FFO/share growth management is currently guiding to for 2026 (and says the backlog supports "through 2027 and 2028"). This is the basis for calling the valuation "in_line" rather than "expensive": the price does not appear to demand the company sustain today's growth rate indefinitely, only that it decelerate toward high-single-digit/low-double-digit — a lower bar than current guidance implies.

[Corrected 2026-10-06: restated 2026-10-06 to above (narrowly): the 8% cost of equity and perpetual-growth test understate the hurdle against a 5.17% 10-year Treasury; at 5.17% + 4.5% ERP = 9.67% the price needs about 10.4%/yr Core FFO/share growth for 3 years (exit 20x) vs the 9% base case; see Correction section DV13]

Scenario framework (analyst estimate; Core FFO/share compounding + multiple + dividend yield, 3-year horizon): - Bear (30%): hyperscale capex pause, dilution/leverage force multiple compression — Core FFO/share ~3%/yr to $8.93, exit 16x → ~$143 (≈ −4.3%/yr, 3y annualised incl. dividend). - Base (45%): backlog converts as guided, ~9%/yr Core FFO/share growth to $10.59, exit ~20x (slight de-rate from 21.9x) → ~$212 (≈ +8.6%/yr). - Bull (25%): hyperscale demand stays structurally undersupplied, ~13%/yr growth to $11.80, exit 23x → ~$271 (≈ +17.8%/yr).

8. Bull case / bear case

Bull: (1) A record $1.9bn signed-not-commenced backlog (~30% of in-place revenue) gives multi-year visibility that few REITs can match. (2) Leasing economics are accelerating, not decelerating — renewal spreads jumped to 25%+ and 0–1MW-plus-interconnection bookings hit a third consecutive quarterly record. (3) Leverage (4.7x) is stable-to-improving even through the heaviest development phase, evidence of disciplined balance-sheet management alongside the growth.

Bear: (1) Growth is being funded by continuous ATM equity issuance ($2.5bn YTD) — existing holders are diluted every quarter this cycle continues, and per-share metrics (not aggregate FFO) are what matter. (2) An open SEC investigation into the adequacy of DLR's cybersecurity-risk disclosures and disclosure controls is unresolved; the company calls it immaterial but cannot yet prove that. (3) The business is now more exposed to a small number of hyperscale/JV counterparties (the new $3.5bn Northern Virginia stake) — a concentrated bet on AI-capex durability that would re-rate sharply lower if hyperscaler capex plans slow.

Recency: latest reported period incorporated: Q2 FY2026 (13 weeks ended 2026-08-01), published 2026-08-27 (8-K Ex-99.1 and 10-Q); events checked to the 2026-09-25 close, including the 2026-09-24 by-law 8-K. 1. Verdict

INCLUDE-SMALL (half weight). Horizon 12–36 months. The Dollar Tree banner itself is sound and fairly priced: comps were positive in all 8 quarters, FCF is solid, lease-adjusted leverage is moderate, and normalized NTM P/E is about 15.7x. But the model's near-top Quality score is largely an accounting artefact. Family Dollar impairments and buybacks shrank the equity base. The latest quarter is also about half one-off (a tariff refund). So the factor composite overstates the case, and the position should be sized below the model's weight.

2. Business in plain English

Dollar Tree runs 9,436 small-box variety stores in the U.S. and Canada (at 2026-08-01, 84.0M selling sq ft). They sell consumables, seasonal goods, party supplies, crafts and household basics to value-seeking shoppers. It is a 1P principal: it buys, owns and marks up its inventory, and occupies leased stores. Its historic edge was a single fixed price point ($1.00, then $1.25). The current strategy is a "multi-price" (Dollar Tree 3.0) assortment. About 6,600 stores had it by Q2 FY2026, and the CEO said in December 2025 that 85% of the assortment is priced at $2 or less. Competitors are Dollar General, Five Below, Walmart and online retail. Family Dollar was sold on 2025-07-05. Before that, the combined company had 16,500 stores (at 2025-02-01).

3. Why the model likes it, and whether that is durable

The pre-registered QVM percentiles are Q 0.962, V 0.917, M 0.836, composite 0.905. The Quality score is largely an artefact. - ROE of about 47% (d4) comes mostly from the equity denominator. ratios.py gives 45.1% on average equity, using actual TTM NI of $1,618.6M. Equity fell from $8,751.5M (FYE Jan-2023) to $3,425.3M (2026-08-01). The bridge, in round numbers: - +$4.4bn of continuing-ops earnings - −$6.3bn of after-tax Family Dollar discontinued-ops losses, most of them impairments: Q4 FY2023 −$2,242.2M and Q4 FY2024 −$4,096.1M - −$3.6bn of buybacks - Continuing-ops ROE on average equity went from ~16% (FY2023) to ~18% (FY2024), ~32% (FY2025) and ~45% (TTM). Over the same run, continuing-ops NI went $1,265.8M → $1,042.5M → $1,225.3M → $1,618.6M. TTM NI is about $1.37bn excluding the after-tax tariff refund. - At the FY2023 average equity level, TTM ROE would be about 20% (17% ex-refund). Roughly 25 of the ~29 points of ROE expansion are denominator. - ratios.py's DuPont credits asset turnover (0.94x → 1.46x). But fixed-asset turnover is flat (3.90x → 3.99x). The turnover gain is the balance sheet shrinking after Family Dollar left, not more productive stores. ROIC excluding goodwill (17.5% TTM, 12.8% FY2025) is the better gauge: good, not elite. - GP/assets of 0.503 uses d4's gross profit of $7,050.7M. That is the FY2025 fiscal-year figure, not TTM (see data conflicts). The asset denominator fell 25% when Family Dollar was deconsolidated. - The Value inputs are flattered too. d4's FCF yield of 10.27% rests on understated capex. The company's own tables give a TTM FCF yield of 9.2% reported and ~7.5% ex-refund. The earnings yield of 7.53% includes a $1.31/share one-off; ex-refund it is about 6.1%. - Momentum (+34.1% 12-1) is real but fading. The stock is $114.07 against a 52-week high of $142.40. It was about $131 on 2026-09-04 (the Form 4 price). - What is durable: comp growth, a modest organic margin gain (TTM EBIT margin about 9.4% ex-refund vs 8.3% in FY2024), cash conversion, and buybacks.

Agent: F74 (wave 4) | As of: 2026-09-25 close (px $20.31, mktcap $14.00bn per b1_live_scores.csv 2026-09-25)

1. Verdict

INCLUDE-SMALL (half weight). Thesis horizon 24–36 months. Named reservation: the Lab (life-science) segment — 34% of same-store NOI — is in a sector-wide oversupply downturn (-3.2% same-store NOI in Q2 2026) with no confirmed bottom, and Healthpeak's economic exposure to its fastest-growing segment (senior housing) is being diluted by the 2026 partial IPO of that business as a separate public company (Janus Living, Inc., NYSE: JAN). The offsetting case for including at half weight: management raised full-year FFO guidance on a beat, insiders bought back stock at $16.81/share (23% below the current price), leverage is conservative (4.7x net debt/EBITDAre), and there is no material litigation. GAAP EPS/P-E for this name is meaningless (see §3/§7) — everything below is built on FFO/AFFO.

2. Business in plain English

Healthpeak is a diversified healthcare real estate investment trust: it owns outpatient medical office buildings (56% of same-store NOI, leased mostly to hospital systems and physician groups), life-science lab buildings (34%, leased to biotech/pharma tenants), and — until a 2026 restructuring — senior housing communities. In March 2026 it spun its senior-housing portfolio into a newly IPO'd, separately-traded REIT, Janus Living, Inc. (NYSE: JAN), in which Healthpeak retains a 73.6% economic stake (down from 81.6% at the March IPO) that is still consolidated into Healthpeak's financial statements (source: Q2 2026 earnings release, 8-K Ex.99.1, filed 2026-08-04; and Janus Living Form 424B4, sec.gov, March 2026).

3. Why the model likes it / is this durable

b1_live_scores.csv (as_of 2026-09-25): composite decile 4, quintile 2, live_rank 338/500 — not a top-tier quant score; triage (Q13) advanced it mainly on price-vs-growth (4/5) after correcting for the GAAP distortion below. GAAP P/E of ~160x (flagged by triage as misleading) is a real accounting artefact, not a data error: REIT straight-line depreciation on appreciating buildings depresses GAAP net income structurally (stock-analysis skill, references/sectors/realestate-reit.md, "REIT depreciation" distortion). The correct earnings measure is Nareit FFO / FFO as Adjusted, used throughout this dossier. Durability of the "why it's cheap" story is mixed: the outpatient-medical base is durable (hospital-system tenants, long leases); the lab weakness reflects a genuine, sector-wide supply glut (triage-flagged, confirmed below) that could persist multiple years; the senior-housing growth is real and accelerating but Healthpeak's own claim on it is shrinking as Janus Living issues more equity.

1. Verdict

INCLUDE (12–36 month horizon). A genuine, broadening AI-data-center growth driver (thermal/liquid-cooling and cryogenic connectors) layered on a diversified, low-leverage industrial base, trading at a valuation that a reverse DCF shows is pricing in materially less growth than the company is currently delivering or guiding to. [Corrected 2026-10-06: verdict cut to INCLUDE-SMALL. The reverse DCF used an 8.5% WACC and 4.0% terminal growth, inconsistent with a 5.17% 10-year Treasury, and compared the result with a mis-stated 13-15% EPS growth. On a 9.8% WACC the price implies about 8.1%/yr, in line with the base case. See the Re-assessment (RA7, 2026-10-06) section.] Reservation acknowledged: a real Q2 2026 execution miss in the Climate & Sustainability (refrigeration) segment is a legitimate quality concern, not yet a thesis-breaker.

Thesis (plain English): Dover is a diversified industrial-products company (pumps, thermal/CO2 systems, marking equipment, fueling systems, biopharma components) that is quietly becoming a picks-and-shovels supplier to the AI data-center build-out through its heat-exchanger and cryogenic-connector businesses, and it is available at a below-market multiple with a debt-light balance sheet.

2. Business in plain English

Dover makes and sells industrial equipment and components across five segments: Engineered Products (waste handling, aerospace/defense, environmental), Clean Energy & Fueling (retail fueling systems, cryogenic/hydrogen equipment), Imaging & Identification (marking/coding, digital textile printing), Pumps & Process Solutions (precision pumps, biopharma single-use components, polymer processing), and Climate & Sustainability Technologies (commercial refrigeration, heat exchangers, including SWEP data-center liquid-cooling heat exchangers). It sells mostly to industrial and commercial end-customers (food retail, data centers, biopharma manufacturers, fueling-station operators) and earns money on equipment sales plus a growing aftermarket/service tail. Its competitive position is built on engineered, application-specific products with real switching costs (biopharma single-use systems, precision pumps) rather than commodity manufacturing, though a meaningful minority of revenue (e.g. refrigeration, polymer processing) is more cyclical and execution-sensitive.

3. Why the model likes it — durable or artefact?

Triage (Q10, quality 4/5, growth 4/5, price_vs_growth 4/5, no red flags) cited accelerating revenue growth (6.9%) on data-center thermal-connector demand at only 16.9x NTM P/E with low leverage (0.8x). The v4 quant composite (b1_live_scores.csv) is unusually aligned with this pick: composite 0.466 (decile 5, quintile 3 — mid-pack, not a top-decile quant favourite, but far better than DIS/DLR in this batch), with the strongest score in Value (fam_V 0.694) and reasonable Momentum (0.618); Quality (0.373) and Earnings-momentum/SUE (0.296) are middling — no material conflict between the quant read and the fundamentals. The durable part of the thesis is the data-center liquid-cooling/cryogenic-connector exposure (management is actively doubling SWEP heat-exchanger capacity over 12 months to meet demand it cannot currently fill) and a genuinely broad-based order recovery (bookings +16% YoY, book-to-bill 1.06 across all five segments in Q2 2026 — a "rare breadth event" per management). DPZ — Domino's Pizza, Inc.

1. Verdict: INCLUDE-SMALL (half weight). Thesis horizon 24–36 months. High-quality, asset-light franchisor trading near the low end of its own valuation history, but FY2026 guidance was already cut once this year, U.S. same-store sales are barely positive, and the buyback-funded, negative-equity capital structure leaves less room for error than the "cheap franchise" framing suggests.

2. Business in plain English. Domino's is the world's largest pizza company by sales, operating almost entirely through franchisees (only ~2% of the U.S. system is company-owned). It earns royalties on franchisee retail sales (~5.5–7% of sales) plus supply-chain margin from selling food, boxes and equipment to its own U.S. franchisees, and collects a smaller royalty from ~100 international master franchisees who run the stores abroad. Competitive position: #1 or #2 pizza QSR share in most markets it operates in, built on delivery speed/technology (10–30 minute promise, app/AI ordering) and the lowest menu prices in category.

3. dossiers.DRI:
DRI — Darden Restaurants, Inc.

1. Verdict

INCLUDE (full weight) [Corrected 2026-10-06: verdict changed to INCLUDE-SMALL (half weight) on re-assessment; the valuation gap that carried full weight is gone, see the section below] — thesis horizon 12–36 months. The cleanest evidence base of the three names reviewed in this batch: a modest but genuine valuation discount to own history and peers, a reverse-DCF that prices growth well below what the company has actually delivered, four consecutive quarters of guidance that was met or modestly raised (never cut), broad-based positive same-restaurant sales across every segment, and no unresolved securities litigation or regulatory-fine overhang. The one adverse fact that must be surfaced prominently: the most recently reported quarter (Q1 FY2027, filed one day before this dossier's cutoff) showed operating margin compress ~116bps year-over-year even as sales grew — a real, primary-source-verified data point that tempers, without breaking, the thesis.

2. Business in plain English

Darden owns and operates full-service ("sit-down") restaurants under nine brands — Olive Garden and LongHorn Steakhouse are by far the largest, alongside Cheddar's Scratch Kitchen, Yard House, Ruth's Chris Steak House, The Capital Grille, Chuy's (acquired 2024), Seasons 52 and Eddie V's — comprising 2,218 company-owned restaurants as of August 2026. It makes money on food/beverage sold to diners less the cost of ingredients, labour, restaurant occupancy and marketing; unlike many restaurant peers it owns and operates almost all of its restaurants directly (limited franchising), so it captures the full economics (and the full capital intensity) of the dining-room model rather than a royalty stream. Its moat is brand recognition, purchasing/supply-chain scale across ~2,200 units, and site selection built over decades.

3. Why the model likes it — and is it durable?

B1 composite is top decile (live_rank 46/~2,300; composite percentile ~91%; gates: no disqualifying-red-flag gate is netted into this score — see §11 for the separate red-flag check). Family drivers: Earnings momentum (fam_S ≈0.93, very high) — SUE has been consistently positive; Momentum (fam_M ≈0.72); Quality (fam_Q ≈0.65); Value (fam_V ≈0.47, mid-pack) — DRI is not a deep-value name, it is a modest discount to peers/history.

Durability check: the earnings-momentum signal is corroborated by four straight quarters of guidance that management met or narrowed upward (§5), and same-restaurant sales that were positive in every segment in the two most recently reported quarters (Q4 FY26: Olive Garden +2.4%, LongHorn +9.5%, Fine Dining +1.9%, Other +4.6%; Q1 FY27: Olive Garden +1.0%, LongHorn +6.8%, Fine Dining +1.0%, Other +4.5%, comparable-calendar basis) — a genuinely broad-based result, not one brand carrying the average. The counter-evidence, which I surface rather than average away: LongHorn's segment margin fell ~71bps YoY in FY2026 even as its sales grew +13.1% (fastest-growing brand, but its incremental sales are not flowing through at the historical rate), and Fine Dining's segment margin fell ~92bps. Consolidated operating margin in the single most recent quarter (Q1 FY27) was down ~116bps YoY. The SUE/momentum signal is real, but the margin-durability question is more open than the sales-growth headline suggests.

4. Last two years of results (SEC 10-Q/10-K, GAAP)

Quarterly variance analysis (Q1 FY27 vs Q1 FY26 — the two most comparable periods available): sales +5.1% (comparable-calendar same-restaurant sales +3.2%, all four segments positive); operating income fell 5.9% ($339.2m→$319.3m) despite the sales increase — a >200bps margin variance, the single most important adverse fact in this dossier, driven per the income statement by higher restaurant labour (+4.1%), higher restaurant expenses (+5.2%) and higher D&A (+6.7%) outrunning the sales gain; net earnings from continuing operations −9.2% reported ($257.9m→$234.3m) but this reported decline is entirely explained by last year's one-off Olive-Garden-Canada gain (§ above) — on the adjusted basis both companies and I use, EPS grew +4.1%. Operating cash flow fell 18.5% YoY ($342.5m→$279.0m) and free cash flow fell 39.3% ($162.9m→$98.9m) — a material (>10%) variance, decomposed from the cash-flow statement: "change in current assets and liabilities, net" swung to a $122.2m use of cash from a $33.5m use a year ago (a $88.7m unfavourable working-capital swing). In the same quarter the company still paid $184.2m of dividends and repurchased $220.8m of stock (total capital return $405.0m vs. FCF of only $98.9m), funded by a $285.9m net draw on short-term debt — a real, quantifiable, primary-source-verified capital-allocation fact (see §6), not a one-off DG-style tax-timing item.

5. Guidance track record (verbatim, last four releases)

This is a track record of accuracy and reliability rather than dramatic beats: guided ranges were narrowed toward, and actual results landed inside, the guided range in three of the last three cases checked; no guidance cut was found in any of the four releases reviewed. FY2027 initial guidance also included: new restaurant openings 75–80, total capex ~$875m, inflation ~3.0%, effective tax rate ~13.5%, EBITDA $2.26–2.29bn, ~114m weighted-average diluted shares. Per CFO Raj Vennam (Q4/FY26 release): "Since 2019, we have delivered 9% annualized adjusted EBITDA growth."

6. Earnings quality & balance sheet

  • FCF conversion: volatile quarter to quarter (FCF/NI ranged 0.50x–1.47x over the last 8 quarters) but the two most recent quarters (Q4 FY26 0.94x, Q1 FY27 0.42x) show a downward trend, driven by working-capital timing (§4) and rising capex, not by a change in reported profitability.
  • SBC: modest, 0.34%–1.26% of quarterly sales (Q1 FY25's 1.26% was an outlier, likely annual-grant timing); not a material distortion.
  • GAAP vs adjusted: DRI discloses clean, itemised reconciliations every quarter (Chuy's integration costs, restaurant-closure/impairment charges, the Olive Garden Canada sale gain, tax items) — a transparency positive; I have used both reported and adjusted figures throughout and labelled which is which.
  • Balance sheet — a real, quantified deterioration worth watching: short-term debt + current portion of long-term debt jumped from $693.6m (2026-05-31, fiscal year-end) to $979.7m (2026-08-30), a $286.1m increase in one quarter, funding the capital-return gap noted in §4. Long-term debt $1,636.1m (roughly flat). Total gross debt ≈$2,615.8m, up from ≈$2,331.3m at fiscal year-end — a ~12% quarter-over-quarter increase. Cash is small and stable (~$220m). Retained earnings are negative: $(259.5)m as of 2026-08-30 (worsened from $(108.4)m at FYE), i.e. cumulative dividends + buybacks now exceed cumulative historical net income — common for a mature, buyback-heavy restaurant compounder, and the mechanical reason DRI's ROE (54.7% per the B1 dataset) looks extremely high: it is flattered by a shrunk equity base, not by extraordinary returns on capital, and should be read alongside segment-level margins (§4) rather than at face value, per the stock-analysis playbook's own warning about ROE manufactured by buybacks.
  • Net debt/EBITDA: using FY2027 guided EBITDA ($2.26–2.29bn) against ≈$2.6bn gross debt less ~$220m cash ≈ $2.4bn net debt → ≈1.0–1.1x — still low in absolute terms, but the trend (rising within a single quarter, debt-funded buybacks exceeding FCF) is the item to monitor, not the level. [Corrected 2026-10-06: net debt was on the wrong basis. Darden carries $1,760.3M of finance lease liabilities (current $21.6M, non-current $1,738.7M, 10-Q acc. 0000940944-26-000042) that the $2.4bn figure leaves out. Net debt including finance leases is $4,156M, i.e. about 1.8x FY2027 guided EBITDA and about 1.95x TTM EBITDA (TTM EBIT $1,562.9M + D&A $570.2M), not 1.0-1.1x]
  • M&A: Chuy's Holdings acquired for ~$605m enterprise value / $649.1m total consideration, $37.50/share all-cash, announced 2024-07-17, closed 2024-10-11 — now 112 locations (from 108 a year ago), fully integrated into the "Other Business" segment and no longer flagged as a same-restaurant-sales exclusion after Q4 FY2026 (its 16-month anniversary). Bahama Breeze wind-down: the brand (28 units mid-2025) is being fully exited — ~14 locations closed around 2026-04-05, the remaining ~14 being converted to other Darden brands through Q4 FY2027; only 10 Bahama Breeze units remained at 2026-08-30. This is a small, well-telegraphed, already-substantially-executed restructuring, not a fresh risk.

7. Valuation snapshot — reconciliation with V1

V1 verdict: attractive (score 0.35/1.0). NTM P/E 17.2x vs. DRI's own 165-month history — 27th percentile, a modest but real discount — and vs. peer median 18.9x (CMG/DPZ/MCD/SBUX). As with ABNB, I flag this peer set as heterogeneous: CMG is a much higher-growth, higher-multiple pure-play with a different unit-economics model (no full bar/table service), MCD and SBUX are global, franchise/royalty-heavy models with far less capital intensity than DRI's mostly-company-owned estate, and DPZ is franchise-heavy pizza delivery — DRI is the only "true" full-service, company-owned comparable in its own peer list. The resulting ~9% discount to that blended median is directionally fine to use but should not be read as a precise like-for-like gap.

Reverse-DCF implied 10-year growth is +2.7%, against consensus FY1 growth of +6.1% and delivered 5-year/10-year CAGRs of +12.9%/+6.7% — the market is pricing DRI for growth well below both what it has delivered and what the Street expects next year, which is the core of the "attractive" case and one I can corroborate: FY2027 guided total-sales growth (3.0–4.1% ex-53rd-week effects) and same-restaurant-sales growth (2.5–3.5%) are themselves modest, in-line-to-slightly-above the reverse-DCF-implied rate, not requiring any acceleration. [Corrected 2026-10-06: the 2.7% rests on V1's FCFF at WACC 8.28% with net debt of $1.42bn, which omits finance leases and uses FCF before SBC and before the FY2027 capex step-up to about $875M; recomputed at equity level (FCF after SBC about $0.99bn, price $199.75) the implied growth is 5.2% at Ke 8.39% and 6.7% at 9.0%, in line with or above a 5% base]

A genuine data conflict I flag rather than pass over silently: V1's own scenario margin_assumed values are bear 5.2% / base 7.8% / bull 9.2% — all three below the TTM operating margin V1 itself uses elsewhere in the same record (ebit_margin_used = 11.98%, which I independently confirm from D3/GAAP: $1,582.8m TTM EBIT ÷ $13,210.9m TTM revenue = 11.98%). I cannot fully resolve from the data available whether this is (a) an intentional, conservative fade toward a longer-run/mid-cycle margin (in which case the "attractive" verdict is, if anything, understated — even V1's bull case doesn't require margin expansion above what's already been delivered), or (b) a scenario-construction basis mismatch (e.g., a segment-profit-style margin excluding D&A/real-estate items being compared against a different EBIT base). Given the bear/base/bull returns V1 reports (−17.6%/+7.4%/+22.5% annualised) are still directionally sensible and roughly consistent with the multiple/growth inputs, I treat this as a modelling note for the lead/V1 agent to confirm rather than a reason to override the verdict, and record it in data_conflicts. [Corrected 2026-10-06: resolved: V1's scenario 'margin_assumed' (bear 5.2%, base 7.8%, bull 9.2%) is a NET margin (EPS = revenue x margin / shares; base: $16.02bn x 7.84% / 110.3M shares = $11.39). FY2026 net margin was 9.1% ($1,206.7M / $13,210.9M; TTM 8.8%), so the base case is a fade, not a basis mismatch; but V1's base EPS ($11.39) is below the FY2027 guide, and its 7.4% base return is below the 8.4% cost of equity, which does not support 'attractive' or full weight]

My view: consistent = true, dossier_view = cheap (modest). Base case assumes revenue growth 6.6%/yr (below the 5-year delivered 12.9%, in line with the 10-year delivered 6.7% — not aggressive) and an exit multiple of 20.1x (close to today's 17.2x and below the peer median 18.9x — a small, not heroic, re-rating). Combined with the guidance-accuracy track record in §5 and the broad-based same-restaurant-sales strength in §3, I agree with V1's "attractive" call and do not see a basis to downgrade it to "fair" — the main things working against the thesis (margin compression in the two most recent segment/consolidated readings, and the debt-funded capital return in Q1 FY27) are real but, on the evidence available, second-order relative to the valuation discount and demonstrated sales/guidance durability. [Corrected 2026-10-06: V1's own base return is 7.4% a year, below Ke 8.4%, and the corrected implied growth is no longer below the base; 'cheap (modest)' is replaced by 'fair']

8. Bull case / bear case

Bull (3): 1. Every reportable segment posted positive same-restaurant sales in each of the last two quarters — a broad, not single-brand-dependent, recovery, and guidance has been met or modestly raised for four straight releases with no cut. 2. Valuation is a genuine, if modest, discount to both own history (27th percentile) and the reverse-DCF-implied growth rate is well below what the company has actually delivered over 5 and 10 years. 3. Disciplined, well-disclosed capital allocation: dividend raised 8% (to $1.62/quarter) in June 2026, a new $1.5bn buyback authorization, and a small, already-largely-executed brand rationalisation (Bahama Breeze exit) rather than a large, uncertain restructuring.

Bear (3): 1. Consolidated operating margin fell ~116bps YoY in the single most recently reported quarter (Q1 FY27), and LongHorn's and Fine Dining's full-year segment margins each fell 71–92bps in FY2026 despite strong sales growth — cost inflation (labour, restaurant expense, D&A) is outrunning sales growth in the two brands driving most of the comp strength. 2. Q1 FY27 free cash flow fell 39% YoY, and the company funded capital returns (dividends + buybacks, $405m) well in excess of free cash flow ($98.9m) with a $286m single-quarter increase in short-term debt — a real, quantifiable, and newly-emerging capital-discipline question, not yet a crisis (net debt/EBITDA still ~1x) but worth a full-year read before dismissing. 3. Ordinary industry-standard tip-credit/wage litigation (One Fair Wage-affiliated FLSA claims over the $2.13/hour tipped minimum wage) is an ongoing, if not unusual-for-the-industry, legal cost and headline-risk item.

9. Key risks & kill criteria (measurable)

  1. Consolidated same-restaurant sales growth turns negative for two consecutive quarters (currently +3.1–4.6% depending on calendar basis).
  2. Olive Garden (the largest segment, ~42% of FY26 sales) same-restaurant sales turn negative for two consecutive quarters — it is already the slowest-growing segment (+1.0–2.4%).
  3. Full-year diluted-EPS guidance is cut versus the prior quarter's range (no cut found in the four releases reviewed).
  4. Net debt / TTM EBITDA rises above 2.0x (currently ≈1.0–1.1x, but rising within the most recent quarter). [Corrected 2026-10-06: on the corrected basis including finance leases the ratio is about 1.8x (guided EBITDA) to 1.95x (TTM), within 0.05-0.2x of this line; on the dossier's original basis it is about 1.1x. Not fired, amber]
  5. Cumulative incremental Chuy's-integration or Bahama-Breeze-wind-down charges exceed $50 million beyond what is already disclosed in the FY2026 10-K/8-Ks (scope-creep signal on the two known restructuring items).

10. Catalysts & calendar

  • Next earnings: Q2 FY2027, estimated mid-to-late December 2026 (historical pattern: Dec 15–19 in prior years; not yet confirmed by the company).
  • Full closure/conversion of the remaining ~10 Bahama Breeze locations, expected to complete by Q4 FY2027 (May 2027).
  • Chuy's now past its 16-month "same-restaurant-sales inclusion" anniversary (Q4 FY2026) — FY2027 comps will, for the first time, include Chuy's on a like-for-like basis.
  • Annual shareholder meeting was held 2026-09-23 (Item 5.07 8-K filed 2026-09-24) — voting results not reviewed in this dossier; no indication of a contested vote in the filing index.

11. Red-flag scan

  • Wage/labour litigation: One Fair Wage (a restaurant-workers advocacy group) sued Darden alleging FLSA and state wage-and-hour violations tied to the tipped-minimum-wage model ($2.13/hour federal tip credit); an associated race-discrimination claim was dropped, wage claims reportedly remain. This is a real, ongoing legal item but structurally common across the full-service restaurant industry (tip-credit litigation is not unique to Darden) rather than a company-specific governance failure.
  • Debt-funded capital return in the most recent quarter: see §6/§8 — a real, quantified, newly-emerging item to track for a second consecutive quarter before treating it as a trend.
  • 53rd-week / fiscal-calendar effects: real and disclosed by the company itself; already addressed via the "comparable calendar" same-restaurant-sales metric — a modelling nuance, not a governance or accounting-quality concern.

INCLUDE-SMALL (half weight). Thesis horizon 24–36 months. Named reservation: consolidated leverage is meaningfully higher than the regulated-utility parts of the business alone would justify, and the core regulated electric segment has twice in a row recovered materially less than it asked for from its regulator — real execution risk sits underneath the headline growth story. DTE Energy is a Michigan-based utility holding company: DTE Electric (regulated, ~2.3 million customers, Southeast Michigan) and DTE Gas (regulated, ~1.4 million customers) earn a regulator-set return on their asset base; DTE Vantage (non-utility gas storage, pipelines, renewable natural gas, industrial energy) and Energy Trading are unregulated, market-exposed businesses layered on top (source: Q2 2026 earnings release, 8-K Ex.99.1, filed 2026-07-28, "About DTE Energy"). 1. Verdict

INCLUDE-SMALL (half weight) — thesis horizon 24–36 months.

DaVita is statistically cheap (10.8x NTM P/E, 9.6th percentile of its own 177-month history) and its earnings-per-share growth has genuinely compounded. But that growth is majority financially engineered (debt-funded buybacks against a negative-equity balance sheet), not organic — normalized non-acquired treatment growth was −0.6% in FY2025 and only +0.1–0.3% in H1 2026. Named reservation: leverage (3.37x company-defined ratio, rising) on a negative-equity balance sheet, concentrated in a single ~45%-owner (Berkshire Hathaway) that has been trimming even as its percentage stake mechanically rises, at 44% one-year volatility — the highest of any name in this batch and near the mandate's 45% ceiling.

2. Business in plain English

DaVita operates ~2,700 outpatient dialysis centers in the US (plus a smaller international business), providing life-sustaining hemodialysis and peritoneal dialysis to patients with end-stage kidney disease (ESKD). About two-thirds of US patients are reimbursed at government (Medicare/Medicaid) rates; the remaining roughly one-third of revenue comes from commercial insurers, who pay materially higher rates per treatment — this small commercial cohort disproportionately drives profitability (source 8). Competitive position: a near-duopoly with Fresenius Medical Care in US dialysis, with high switching costs (dialysis is a recurring, life-critical service tied to a physical location) and real regulatory/reimbursement dependence.

B1/live-rank 14 (the highest-ranked of this batch's three names) reflects strong per-share earnings growth and a very low valuation multiple. 1. Verdict

INCLUDE-SMALL (half weight; thesis horizon 12-36 months). Triage said "no, solid but unremarkable" and described a pre-merger Devon. On 7 May 2026 Devon closed its all-stock merger with Coterra, which changed the company: about 1.66-1.69 million Boe/d guided for Q3, at least $1.0B of targeted annual synergies, an $8.0B buyback, debt of $11.4B. At $47.05 the price implies roughly flat free cash flow on a $68 oil deck (implied 10-year growth 0.0% vs my base 2.0%), so it passes the INCLUDE-SMALL test. The named reservation: current earnings sit on a spike in oil (Q2 WTI $92.47 vs $64.87 for all of 2025), and the integration and the portfolio review are unproven. If WTI reverts to $55 my bear case returns about -12%/yr.

2. Business in plain English

Devon finds and pumps oil, natural gas and natural-gas liquids from US shale, mostly the Delaware Basin (Permian), plus the Anadarko, Eagle Ford, Rockies and, since the merger, Coterra's Marcellus gas. It earns money at the well-head price of oil (guided at 98%-100% of WTI for the full year: "Oil - % of WTI ... 98 % ... 100 %", 8-K acc. 0001193125-26-332824 Ex.99.2), and returns cash through a fixed dividend ($0.32 a quarter), buybacks and debt repayment. It is one of the largest US shale operators after the merger; its edge is acreage quality and scale, not a moat: it is a price-taker.

eBay runs an online marketplace connecting buyers and sellers, monetised through final-value/listing fees (take rate on Gross Merchandise Volume) plus a fast-growing first-party advertising business sold to its own sellers.
