dossiers.LVS:
LVS — Las Vegas Sands Corp. — F20 diligence dossier

1. Verdict

INCLUDE — thesis horizon 12–36 months. This is the cheapest name in the F20 batch by a wide margin on a systematic reverse-DCF basis (the price implies FCF shrinking more than 11%/yr for a decade against a 5-year delivered CAGR of +27%), the business is genuinely improving (Macau mass-market share gains, a monopoly Singapore asset, an investment-grade upgrade), and management is returning capital aggressively and consistently. Named risks below (Macau concession renewal in 2032, a doubled Singapore expansion budget, family control) are real but are dated, sized and monitorable — none of them breaks the thesis today. [Corrected 5 Oct 2026: verdict restated INCLUDE-SMALL; the '11%/yr' decline implied by V1 could not be reproduced and the price implies about -4% a year (range -6% to 0%) on consistent bases; Macau market GGR turned negative in Q3 (about -3.8% YoY). See the Correction section below]

2. Business in plain English

Las Vegas Sands owns and operates large integrated resorts (casino, hotel, retail, convention/MICE space) — today essentially Macau (through ~70%-owned Sands China: The Venetian Macao, Londoner, Parisian, Plaza) and Singapore (Marina Bay Sands, 100%-owned). It sold its US Las Vegas properties in 2022 and is no longer a US casino operator in the traditional sense; earnings come almost entirely from Asian gaming and premium-mass tourism. It makes money on gaming win (mass-market table games and slots, plus VIP/junket-driven rolling chip volume), room/retail/MICE revenue, and — for Macau specifically — is subject to a government concession that sets the terms under which it may operate.

3. Why the model likes it — durable or artefact?

b1_live_scores.csv ranks LVS moderately (composite percentile 56th, decile 6/quintile 3, live_rank 219 — not a top-70 name; it reached full diligence via the triage/quality-growth route after Q02 flagged it). The valuation gap the model is really responding to is in V1's own systematic reverse-DCF (see §7), not the factor composite. The underlying growth is durable, not a sugar-high: Sands China mass GGR +8% YoY in Q2-26 (vs the overall Macau market's +4%, i.e. genuine share gain, not just market recovery), and Marina Bay Sands mass gaming revenue +5% YoY in a quarter where overall visitation was depressed by the football World Cup — both are volume/share stories, not one-off VIP-hold luck.

5. Guidance track record

Las Vegas Sands, like most casino operators, does not issue formal quantitative revenue/EPS guidance. The closest analogue is management's informally stated Macau EBITDA aspiration of ~$700m/quarter, which the company missed in Q2-2026 ($430m actual, ~$517m hold-normalised) — disclosed above as a genuine, measurable shortfall against management's own stated bar, not glossed over. No formal guidance-track-record table applies; this absence itself is stated rather than treated as a pass (per the addendum's "missing evidence is not a pass" instruction).

6. Earnings quality & balance sheet

  • OCF (TTM through Q2-26, sum of last 4 quarters): 567+... — quarterly OCF only reliably available at Q1-tagged (~90-day) contexts in this dataset for several years plus the two most recent 10-Qs; FY2025 OCF was strong and full-year metrics (below) are the more reliable read.
  • FY2025: net revenue $13.02bn, operating income $2.82bn (21.7% margin), net income (consolidated) $1.63bn, diluted EPS $2.35, adjusted property EBITDA $5.23bn (vs $4.38bn FY2024, +19.4%).
  • Net debt (30-Jun-2026): long-term debt & capital leases $13,694m + current portion $1,568m − cash $3,376m = $11,886m (matches V1's independently sourced figure to the dollar). Against TTM EBITDA of roughly $4.4–4.9bn, net debt/EBITDA is approximately 2.4–2.7x — S&P's own stated expectation is leverage sustained "around 2.5x" through the Singapore expansion, with a 3.0x downgrade threshold; S&P upgraded LVS/Sands China from BBB- to BBB in 2026 on disciplined financial policy, and LVS raised $1bn of bonds at the improved rating. This is a genuinely improving credit story, not a deteriorating one.
  • Capital return is aggressive and shrinking the equity base: $740m of buybacks in Q1-2026 and $787m in Q2-2026 (H1-2026 total $1,542m) plus $400m of dividends YTD; diluted share count fell from 675m (Q4-25) to 648m (Q2-26), a ~4% reduction in two quarters. Stockholders' equity attributable to LVS fell from $1,198m (Q1-26) to $581m (Q2-26) — this looks alarming in isolation but is mechanically explained by buybacks retiring equity faster than retained earnings accrete it, not by asset impairment or losses; still worth monitoring since it leaves a thin common-equity cushion on a historical-cost balance sheet that materially understates the properties' market value.
  • SBC is small (~$13–24m/quarter, under 1% of revenue) — not a distortive factor here.
  • Governance/control: the Adelson family (Dr. Miriam Adelson, Irwin Chafetz and related trusts) beneficially owns/controls ~59.7% of voting power — LVS is a controlled company. This concentrates capital-allocation authority in one family (a genuine governance risk for minority holders) but that family has run the business consistently and, on the evidence above, is currently allocating capital toward buybacks at a statistically cheap multiple — a reasonable use of control, not an obvious expropriation risk, but disclosed as a structural fact.

My view: cheap, and I agree with V1, with two named caveats V1's own price-only model cannot see: (1) the Macau concession expires 31-Dec-2032 — six years inside V1's 10-year DCF horizon — carrying real (if currently low-probability, given the 2023 industry-wide 10-year renewal cycle just completed) renewal-terms risk that a naive perpetuity-style reverse DCF does not explicitly price; (2) the Singapore Marina Bay Sands expansion cost has already doubled to ~$8bn, a real execution/cost-overrun risk on top of the ~2.5x leverage plan. Neither changes the direction of the call — an implied decade of shrinking cash flow is not a plausible base case even after discounting for concession-renewal uncertainty and a capex overrun — but both are why this dossier flags them as explicit, named risks rather than accepting V1's "attractive" score uncritically. implied_vs_base = below.

8. Bull case

  1. Genuine, share-gaining mass-market recovery in both Macau (Sands China mass GGR +8% vs market +4%) and Singapore (MBS mass +5% in a soft-visitation quarter) — the durable part of the business is accelerating, while the volatile part (VIP hold) is what is currently depressing headline EBITDA.
  2. Credit quality is improving, not deteriorating: S&P upgrade to BBB, leverage target ~2.5x, and a successful $1bn bond raise at the better rating — the balance-sheet risk the market may be pricing (via the thin post-buyback common-equity base) is not corroborated by the rating agencies actually holding the debt.
  3. Marina Bay Sands is a structurally scarce, effectively monopoly asset (Singapore issues a small, fixed number of casino licences) now being expanded at scale ($8bn), and the concession renewal cycle for Macau just completed in 2023 with a full 10-year grant, i.e. the closest major renewal risk (2032) is still six years away.

9. Bear case

  1. The 2032 Macau concession renewal sits inside any decade-long valuation horizon and is a real, if not immediate, source of uncertainty on operating terms, tax/gaming-levy rates, and required non-gaming capex commitments (VML has already committed ≥35.84bn patacas / ~$4.47bn under the current concession).
  2. Singapore capex has already doubled from original estimates to ~$8bn — a live execution-risk pattern (cost overruns on large gaming-resort construction projects are common in the industry) that could pressure free cash flow and the capital-return program if it recurs.
  3. VIP-hold volatility (the Q2-2026 Macau EBITDA miss) demonstrates that quarterly headline numbers can swing by ~20% on pure statistical variance in a business line management does not fully control — a reminder that near-term print risk is real even if the multi-quarter trend (mass-market share gains) is sound; combined with majority family control (59.7% voting power), minority shareholders have limited recourse if capital-allocation priorities were ever to shift away from buybacks.

10. Key risks & kill criteria (measurable)

  1. Sands China mass-market GGR growth falls below the overall Macau market's growth rate for two consecutive quarters (loses the share-gain thesis).
  2. Consolidated net debt/EBITDA rises above 3.0x (S&P's own stated downgrade threshold) for two consecutive quarters.
  3. Marina Bay Sands expansion capex guidance is revised upward again beyond the current ~$8bn, or the 2031 opening date slips by more than two quarters.
  4. Any formal notice or public commentary from the Macau government casting doubt on standard renewal terms ahead of the December-2032 concession expiry.
  5. Quarterly dividend or buyback pace is cut (a reversal of the current aggressive capital-return program) absent a stated, value-accretive reinvestment alternative.

8. Bull case / Bear case

Bear: (1) the April-2026 U.S. merchant class action seeking to void the scope of the 2023 Damages Class Settlement release could reopen interchange-fee claims dating to January 2019 at much larger scale than the $296M currently reserved (see §11); (2) rebates/incentives to customers grew faster than gross payment- network revenue in 2Q26 (+22% vs +10%), a mix shift that could compress net take-rate if it continues; (3) regulatory interchange caps (EU, and periodic U.S. state/federal proposals) remain a standing structural risk to the core payment-network economics that no dossier section can fully price.

dossiers.MAS:
MAS — Masco Corporation — Fundamental Diligence Dossier

1. Verdict

WATCH — 12–24 month horizon. Reasonable, business-appropriate balance sheet and a valuation sitting at the cheap end of both its own history and the Street's own 12-month target range, but two straight years of declining operating cash flow and a Q2 2026 guidance raise that is substantially a one-off tariff-refund story, not a volume recovery. Condition to upgrade to INCLUDE-SMALL: two consecutive quarters of organic (ex-tariff, ex-FX) revenue growth, or TTM operating cash flow inflecting positive year-over-year.

2. Business in plain English

Masco makes and sells branded home-improvement products — faucets and fixtures (Delta, Hansgrohe), paints and coatings (Behr), and cabinetry/other decorative building products — sold mainly through home-improvement retailers (Home Depot, Lowe's) and wholesale plumbing distributors to contractors and remodelers. It makes money on unit volume and price/mix across two reporting segments, Plumbing Products (~67% of Q2 2026 revenue) and Decorative Architectural (~33%). Its competitive position is strong (leading share in faucets and paint in North America, high brand recognition), but demand is tied to discretionary U.S. home-repair-and-remodel spending, which is cyclical and currently soft.

3. Why the model likes it — durable or artefact?

B1 ranks MAS #52 (composite percentile ~89.6th) driven almost entirely by Value (earnings yield, FCF yield, EBIT/EV and book/price all in the 79th–87th percentile) and Quality (gross-profit/assets 90.6th percentile, OCF/assets 72.0th percentile), with weak Momentum (38.2nd percentile — the stock has lagged over the trailing 12-1 month window) and middling Earnings-momentum/SUE (70.1st percentile). This is partly an artefact: the "cheap and high quality" read is flattered by a shrinking denominator — MAS has been shrinking its own balance sheet and share count via buybacks (share count down from 233M in mid-2022 to 201.7M at Q1 2026, ‑13.4%) while GAAP net income has fallen in each of the last two fiscal years (FY2023 $908M → FY2024 $822M → FY2025 $810M, source: DEF 14A summary compensation table figures, filed 2026-04-21). Gross-profit/assets and OCF/assets ratios can stay statistically "high quality" even as the underlying earnings power softens, if assets shrink in step. The valuation is fair given the trend, not a mispricing being handed to us for free.

7. Valuation snapshot — reconciliation with V1

V1 (systematic reverse-DCF, v4/outputs/v1_valuation.json / v1_valuation_table.csv) verdict: fair (score −0.003, near-neutral). NTM P/E 14.9x — 25.2nd percentile of its own ~13-year history (cheap vs. own history) and slightly below the peer median of 16.2x (peers AOS, ALLE, CARR, JCI, LII). WACC 8.22%. Implied 10-year growth from the current price is just +0.44%/yr, versus consensus FY1 growth of +2.7% and a delivered 5-year CAGR of −0.8%. Bear/base/bull 3-year annualised returns: −29.3% / +2.4% / +29.8%. Current price ($68.85) sits at the low end of the Street's own 12-month target range ($68–$96, mean $80.33). I agree with V1's "fair" call. The market is pricing in continued stagnation, which is roughly consistent with what has actually been delivered (declining OCF, declining GAAP net income, tariff-refund-flattered guidance raise). This is not a name priced for a turnaround that isn't happening — it is fairly priced for the malaise that is happening. I would not call it cheap on a forward-looking basis until organic volumes show two consecutive quarters of improvement; I would not call it overvalued either. dossier_view: fair; consistent with V1: yes.

8. Bull case / Bear case

Bull: 1. Repair-and-remodel is needs-based, not discretionary new-construction demand; management cites >$20bn of pent-up demand, and Q2 2026 adjusted margin expanded to 24.2% (+410bps YoY) even as revenue fell, showing real cost/price discipline. [Corrected 2026-10-08: the ~$95M tariff refund (about 4.8 points of margin) accounts for all of it; ex-refund the adjusted margin was about 19.4% vs 20.1%; see Correction DV27] 2. Buybacks at a below-average multiple (13.4% share-count reduction since mid-2022) compound per-share value even in a flat-volume world. 3. Valuation is already at the low end of Street targets and cheap vs. its own history; further de-rating (V1's −29%/yr bear case) looks like it would require a genuinely severe demand shock, not merely "more of the same."

Bear: 1. FY2025 revenue −3%, operating profit −8%, OCF down for a third straight year (cumulative −27.7% since 2023); Q2 2026's guidance raise is substantially a one-off ($95M tariff refund), and 2026 sales guidance is still only "low single digits" — no recovery is embedded even in management's own numbers. 2. Negative equity (−$242M) and a flat $2,945M of long-term debt for years mean the balance sheet has already been leaned on; if OCF keeps falling, buybacks would need to be trimmed or debt-funded. 3. Direct tariff exposure is real and outside management's control: ~$450M of China-sourced goods, with a scenario management itself has cited implying up to ~$625M of annualised incremental exposure in a worst case, plus ~$50M more from steel/aluminum/reciprocal tariffs — the Q2 refund is one-time, not a standing offset.

9. Key risks & measurable kill criteria

  1. Organic net sales growth negative year-over-year for three consecutive quarters (already 2 of the last 3: Q4'25 −2%, Q2'26 −2.9%).
  2. TTM operating cash flow declines for a fourth consecutive fiscal year (would mean FY2026 OCF below ~$1,000M).
  3. Net debt/EBITDA rises above 2.5x (currently ≈1.79x).
  4. FY2026 adjusted EPS guidance is cut from the current $4.40–$4.60.
  5. Incremental China-tariff exposure escalates materially above the ~$625–675M scenario management has already flagged.

10. Catalysts & calendar

Next earnings: ~late October 2026 (estimated from historical cadence — 2025-10-29, 2024-10-29, 2023-10-26; not yet officially confirmed). No investor day identified in this pass.

11. Red-flag scan

No 8-K Item 4.01 (auditor change) or 4.02 (non-reliance/restatement) filings found in the submissions history reviewed (SEC EDGAR, CIK 0000062996, filings 2022–2026). No going-concern language encountered. MCD (McDonald's Corporation) — Diligence Dossier

Agent: F36 · Standard depth · Prepared 2026-09-26 · Prices/market data as of 2026-09-25 close ($236.50; mkt cap ≈$167.4B)

1. Verdict

INCLUDE-SMALL — 24–36 month horizon; named reservation: US comparable-sales/traffic momentum has decelerated for three straight quarters and the balance sheet carries high, buyback-driven leverage (negative book equity), so this is a lower-conviction "half-weight" holding rather than a full-conviction one despite a clearly favourable reverse-DCF read. No V1 systematic valuation row exists for MCD; v1_verdict = null.

2. Business in plain English

McDonald's is the world's largest quick-service-restaurant franchisor by system sales: ~95% of its ~43,000+ restaurants are owned and run by independent franchisees who pay McDonald's rent (McDonald's owns or leases much of the underlying real estate) plus a royalty on sales. McDonald's own P&L is therefore mostly a real-estate/ royalty annuity on other operators' sales, not a direct food-service P&L — which is why its operating margins (mid-to-high 40s%) look nothing like a typical restaurant operator's. It competes on value, speed and brand ubiquity, currently leaning on "McValue" promotions to defend US traffic.

8. Bull case / bear case

Bull (3): 1. Systemwide sales (+5%, +4% cc) and loyalty engagement (+13% 90-day actives to ~220M) are still compounding even while US in-restaurant traffic is soft — the platform is bigger than the comp-sales headline. 2. Operating margin has already recovered from a Q1 2026 trough (45.3%) back to 47.0% in Q2 2026, suggesting the value-menu-driven margin pressure is moderating, not structural. 3. At ~2.8%/yr implied growth, the reverse DCF gives a wide margin of safety versus a business with a multi-decade record of mid-single-digit systemwide growth even through prior soft-traffic cycles.

Bear (3): 1. US comparable sales have now decelerated for three consecutive quarters (to +0.8% in Q2 2026), and management's own explanation ("inconsistent restaurant execution," "lower consumer awareness" of value offerings) describes an execution problem the company itself has not yet fixed — this could persist. 2. Net debt/EBITDA ≈2.8x on a negative-equity balance sheet leaves little room for a real downturn in systemwide sales without credit-metric pressure; MCD's capital-return policy has structurally prioritised buybacks/dividends over deleveraging. 3. Franchise-system litigation (Section 11) — while mostly narrowed in McDonald's favour — signals ongoing friction in the franchisee relationship that is a second-order but real operating risk for a business entirely dependent on franchisee execution and goodwill.

  4. A credit-rating downgrade by S&P/Moody's/Fitch below the current investment-grade tier.
  5. Systemwide sales growth (constant currency) below 3% for two consecutive quarters.

1. Verdict

WATCH (would revisit if the price falls or the deleveraging catches up to the recovery) — overturning the triage's ADVANCE lean. Microchip is genuinely in a real, primary-source-confirmed cyclical recovery from a severe 2023–25 inventory correction (revenue +38% YoY last quarter, guided to keep accelerating), but my own reverse DCF shows the current price already requires ~12.5%/yr EPS growth for ten years — above even my bull case for a mature, still-more-levered-than-peers analog/MCU semiconductor company. Per the wave-4 instruction, a great recovery story priced for more than it can plausibly deliver over a full decade is a WATCH, not an INCLUDE. No V1 systematic valuation row exists for MCHP (not run by V1 at this ticker) — v1_verdict = null.

2. Business in plain English

Microchip Technology designs and sells analog and mixed-signal semiconductors, microcontrollers (MCUs) and field-programmable gate arrays (FPGAs) used to control and connect electronic systems — in industrial equipment, automotive electronics, data centers/AI infrastructure, aerospace/defense and consumer devices. It sells through direct sales and a large distributor network, and makes money on unit volumes times price across a very broad, diversified product catalog (tens of thousands of parts), rather than a few blockbuster chips.

3. Why the model likes it — durable or artefact?

The growth recovery itself is durable — it is a real, dated, filing-confirmed sequential improvement (net sales $1,026M trough quarter, Dec 2024, to $1,485M, Jun 2026, +45% off the trough) — but the price already reflects a very optimistic continuation of it, which is the basis for the WATCH verdict.

McKesson Corporation (MCK) — Diligence Dossier

Agent: F103 | As of: 2026-09-25 close ($866.64, NYSE) | Wave: 6

1. Verdict

INCLUDE. Thesis horizon: 12–36 months. One-sentence reason: the largest US drug distributor, now compounding faster via its oncology/specialty platform, trades at a reverse-DCF-implied growth rate well below both its own guided growth and its recent delivery, even after pricing in a major pending business separation and a real (already-reserved) opioid liability. [Corrected 5 Oct 2026: verdict is now INCLUDE-SMALL. The dossier missed the 25 Aug 2026 cybersecurity incident (8-K Item 7.01 filed 28 Aug) and used a free-cash-flow base that does not match company-defined FCF; on a corrected base the price implies about +2% a year, not -2.9%.]

2. Business in plain English

McKesson buys pharmaceuticals in bulk from manufacturers and distributes them to pharmacies, hospitals and physician practices across the US — a low-margin, high-volume logistics business (North American Pharmaceutical, ~82% of revenue). Layered on top is a faster-growing, higher-margin Oncology & Multispecialty segment (specialty drug distribution plus the US Oncology Network of community cancer clinics) and a smaller Prescription Technology Solutions (data/analytics) business. It is in the process of separating its lowest-growth segment, Medical-Surgical Solutions (branded "Wellverse"), into a standalone company.

3. Why the model likes it — durable or artefact?

b1 composite 0.180 (decile 2 — not a top-decile quant score), driven mainly by a high free-cash-flow yield (6.3% FCFP) and momentum (mom_12_1 +14.9%); quality/ROE percentile is unavailable in the snapshot (ROE field blank, likely because reported stockholders' equity is negative, making a standard ROE ratio uninformative rather than a true quality signal — see §6). The earnings-momentum factor (SUE) is actually negative (−0.348), i.e., the model's own short-window EPS-surprise measure does not currently favor MCK; the case here rests on valuation and segment mix, not on the composite score, which is itself a useful adversarial check: this is not a top-quant-decile name, and the thesis needs to justify itself on fundamentals, which the sections below attempt.

5. Guidance track record

  • FY2027 adjusted EPS guidance raised twice within the last two releases: FY2026 10-K (2026-05-08) initial FY2027 guide, then raised at Q1 FY2027 (2026-08-05) to $44.20–$45.00 from $43.80–$44.60 — implying 13–15% YoY adjusted EPS growth. No guidance cuts identified in the last 4 releases (FY2025 Q4/FY2026 guide, FY2026 Q1/Q2/Q3, FY2026 10-K, FY2027 Q1 — all raised or maintained the trend).
  • Board also raised the quarterly dividend 15% to $0.94/share (tenth consecutive annual increase) alongside the Q1 FY2027 release — a tangible, cash-backed confirmation of management's confidence, separate from the adjusted-EPS narrative.

6. Earnings quality & balance sheet — entity scope stated explicitly

  • Consolidated operating cash flow, FY2026 (year to 2026-03-31, 10-K): $6.155B; but Q1 FY2027 (Apr–Jun 2026) alone was negative $220M (seasonal working-capital swing typical for this business, consistent with Q1 FY2026 also being negative $918M) — not a new problem, but a structural feature that makes single-quarter FCF unreliable as a valuation input (see §7 caveat).
  • Consolidated balance sheet, as of 2026-06-30 (10-Q filed 2026-08-05): cash & equivalents $5.164B (up sharply from $3.975B at FY2026-end, 2026-03-31); long-term debt + capital leases (consolidated) $8.432B (up from $5.259B at FY2026-end) — this jump is explained by a new $2.25B secured Term Loan B raised 2026-06-09 specifically to support the Medical-Surgical Solutions separation, not by organic releveraging. Stockholders' equity (consolidated) is negative: −$4.240B as of 2026-06-30 (was −$2.172B at FY2026-end) — this is a known, longstanding feature of McKesson's capital structure (decades of buybacks against a low-margin, asset-light distribution balance sheet) and is not itself a solvency red flag given the cash-generative operating model, but it does make equity-based ratios (ROE, book value) meaningless here; leverage should be assessed on debt/EBITDA instead. EBITDA (TTM, d4 cross-check) ≈ $7.071B; gross debt $9.729B (LongTermDebt tag, 2026-06-30) → gross debt/EBITDA ≈ 1.4x, cash-adjusted ≈ 0.65x — manageable, not a red flag on its own.
  • Opioid litigation liability (consolidated, from the FY2026 10-K, period 2026-03-31): accrued liability $5.692B total ($601M current + $5.091B long-term), already on the balance sheet (this is why equity is so negative) — this is a known, sized, multi-year cash-payment schedule, not an open-ended tail risk, and materially different in character from JNJ's unresolved talc exposure (§9 of the JNJ dossier).

This is the direct cause of most of the FY2027 GAAP/adjusted EPS gap and the debt/cash swings noted above — flagging this clearly is the main correction this dossier makes to the underlying quant data, which does not price in transaction complexity.
  • Share count: 116.6M shares outstanding, down from prior periods — McKesson has been an aggressive net repurchaser (consistent with the negative-equity capital structure).

No V1 row exists for MCK yet — v1_verdict = null. - NTM P/E (d4): 18.2x; FCF yield (TTM, d4): 6.3% — cheap for a business guiding 13–15% adjusted EPS growth. - Reverse DCF (own calc), using TTM FCF/share $58.33 (FCF $6.801B ÷ 116.6M shares — caveat: this quarter's FCF is depressed by the working-capital swing and Term Loan proceeds noted above, so treat as a rough, possibly conservative base): solving for the constant 10-year FCF/share growth that justifies $866.64 at an 8% WACC (higher than JNJ's, reflecting thinner margins/more capital-structure complexity) and 4% terminal growth gives ≈ −2.9%/yr — i.e., the market is pricing in FCF decline, which is far below both the company's own 13–15% adjusted EPS guidance and this dossier's realistic base case (high-single-digit consolidated revenue growth plus continued Oncology mix-shift, call it 8–10%/yr FCF/share growth once the separation is complete). Verdict: priced "below" my base case — genuinely cheap on this lens, even after discounting adjusted-EPS inflation from one-off transaction costs. [Corrected 5 Oct 2026: the -2.9%/yr figure rested on $58.33/share, which does not reconcile to company-defined free cash flow (TTM $6.145bn = $52.70/share; FY27 guide $4.5-4.9bn = about $40/share). On those bases the implied FCF/share growth is -1.6% to +1.7% at the 25 Sep price ($866.64) and -0.9% to +2.4% at the 5 Oct close ($917.21), at an 8% WACC and 4% terminal growth. Normalised company-defined FCF (FY26 $5.41bn; FY27 guide $4.5-4.9bn) is lower than the $6.801bn used, which raises the implied growth rate, i.e. makes the stock less cheap, not more.]

8. Bull case / Bear case

Bull: 1. Oncology & Multispecialty segment growing 33% YoY, higher-margin, structurally shifting the mix away from thin-margin pure distribution. 2. FY2027 adjusted EPS guided +13–15%, raised twice this year, with a tangible 15% dividend hike backing management's confidence. 3. Wellverse separation should crystallize value for a slower-growing, lower-multiple segment and let the remaining pharma-distribution + oncology business re-rate on its own higher growth profile.

Bear: 1. GAAP EPS fell 17.6% YoY this quarter — the "20% adjusted growth" headline hides real cash cost from the separation and NCI remeasurements; if transaction costs run longer/higher than guided, adjusted-EPS credibility erodes. 2. Negative consolidated equity and a newly-added $2.25B Term Loan B mean the balance sheet is more levered through the separation window than the pre-separation numbers suggest; execution risk on the Wellverse IPO/spin (timing, market conditions, retained stake value) is real and unhedged in the current price. 3. $5.7B of opioid liability remains on the balance sheet with multi-year cash outflows still due; a new opioid-related claim wave (e.g., from PBM or hospital classes not yet settled) would add to this.

Moody's Corporation (MCO) — Diligence Dossier

Agent: F54 | As of: 2026-09-25 close ($468.70) | Depth: Standard

Note on naming: Moody's Corporation (ticker MCO) has two operating segments that it labels "MIS" (Moody's Investors Service — credit ratings) and "MA" (Moody's Analytics — data/research/software). This dossier always writes "MA segment" for Moody's Analytics to avoid confusion with Mastercard's ticker MA, which is a separate company covered in a separate dossier.

1. Verdict

INCLUDE-SMALL (24–36 month horizon), reservation: the price already assumes MCO keeps delivering mid-teens adjusted EPS growth and margin expansion every quarter — my reverse DCF implied growth (≈12%/yr) is essentially in line with, not below, a realistic base case, so there is limited valuation cushion if rated-debt issuance (structurally procyclical) turns down. Near-duopoly ratings franchise (with S&P Global) plus a fast-growing analytics/software arm, with an excellent and improving guidance track record, but a thin (and recently shrinking) equity base funded mostly by debt against a buyback program.

2. Business in plain English

Moody's has two businesses under one roof: MIS, which rates bonds and loans for issuers (governments, corporates, structured finance) and earns a fee — largely a toll on global debt-capital-markets issuance volume, in a global duopoly with S&P Global; and the MA segment, which sells data, analytics, research, risk-management software and now AI-enabled decision tools to banks, insurers and corporates on a subscription/ARR basis. MIS is highly cyclical with issuance volumes but very high-margin; the MA segment is recurring-revenue and growing faster, diversifying MCO away from bond-market cyclicality over time.

3. Why the model likes it — durable or artefact?

Triage (Q05) called out 76.9% ROE and a "near-regulatory moat," with the 25.5x multiple looking fair for 20% EPS growth. Confirmed and refined: b1_live_scores.csv (2026-09-25) shows gross-profit/assets in the 99th percentile and OCF/assets in the 99th percentile — genuinely best-in-class capital efficiency, not an accounting artefact, because MIS requires almost no incremental capital to rate an additional bond. The "76.9% ROE" figure is itself partly an artefact of a small, buyback-shrunk equity base (Total Moody's shareholders' equity fell from $4.054bn to $3.025bn in just six months — see §6) rather than pure operating economics; this dossier relies on operating cash flow, adjusted operating margin and the guidance track record (§5) rather than ROE as the primary quality evidence.

Own reverse DCF (two-stage FCF/share basis, $14.89 TTM FCF/share from d4 FCF $2.579bn ÷ ~173.2M shares; cost of equity 11.1% from CAPM, beta 1.334 — MCO's beta is meaningfully above MA's or MRSH's, reflecting its issuance-volume cyclicality; 10-year explicit growth then a 20x terminal FCF multiple) implies the market is pricing in ≈11.7%/yr [Corrected 2026-10-08: the 20x terminal FCF multiple embeds about 5.8% perpetual growth and SBC was added back; with 3% terminal growth at 10.2% the price implies about 14-15%, above base; verdict changed to WATCH; see Correction DV27] FCF-per-share growth for 10 years. That is close to, i.e. roughly in line with, the company's own guided/realized trajectory (FY2026 adjusted EPS guidance implies ~13% growth off FY2025's $14.94 at the midpoint; medium-term algorithm is high-single-digit revenue plus buyback-assisted double-digit EPS growth). This is priced in line with, not below, the base case — a fine business, but not one offering a demonstrable margin of safety at the current price.

8. Bull case / Bear case

Bull: (1) the MA segment (Moody's Analytics) grew ARR +9% YoY in 1Q26 and margins expanded 250bps, diversifying MCO's earnings away from bond-issuance cyclicality over time; (2) MIS delivered record quarterly revenue ($1.26bn, 2Q26, +25% YoY) on record global rated issuance, showing the ratings franchise still has significant operating leverage in a strong issuance environment; (3) four consecutive guidance raises/narrowings-upward (§5) show real forecasting discipline and execution, not promotional guidance. Bear: (1) MIS revenue is a leveraged bet on global debt-issuance volumes, which are macro- and rate-cycle dependent — a credit-market slowdown (the historical pattern in every prior MCO down-cycle) would hit transactional MIS revenue (34% YoY growth in 2Q26, meaning a high base to lap) hard and fast, with limited warning; (2) the equity base is thin and shrinking ($3.0bn against $6.9bn of debt) — MCO relies on continued market access to refinance debt as it comes due, a real (if currently low-probability) risk if credit markets seize up precisely when MIS revenue would also be falling; (3) the reverse DCF shows little valuation cushion — a growth disappointment would likely be met with a multiple de-rating, not just slower growth.

9. Key risks & kill criteria (measurable)

  1. FY2026 adjusted diluted EPS guidance is cut below the $16.50–$17.00 range reaffirmed/narrowed as of the 2026-07-22 release.
  2. Consolidated revenue growth falls below the guided high-single-digit range (i.e. below 7% YoY) for two consecutive quarters.
  3. MIS transactional revenue declines YoY for two consecutive quarters (a leading indicator of an issuance-volume downturn).
  4. Consolidated net debt/TTM EBITDA exceeds 3.0x (from ≈1.35x currently).
  5. Total Moody's shareholders' equity turns negative on the consolidated balance sheet (from $3,025M currently), which would signal buybacks have outpaced retained earnings by a materially wider margin than today.

Next earnings: 2026-10-21 (Q3 2026, per d4_live_snapshot.parquet). No investor day date found in the documents reviewed.

  • No material weakness, going-concern language, restatement, SEC/DOJ investigation, or auditor-change language found in the Q2 2026 10-Q or the earnings releases reviewed.
  • GAAP vs adjusted EPS gap in 2Q26 ($5.03 GAAP vs $4.68 adjusted) is wider than usual and favors GAAP, driven by the $181M divestiture gain (§6) — flagged so the strong GAAP EPS headline ("+57% YoY") is not mistaken for underlying run-rate growth; adjusted EPS growth (+31% YoY) is the more representative figure.
  • Thin/shrinking consolidated equity base (§6) is a longstanding, disclosed structural feature of MCO's balance sheet, not a new deterioration, but is flagged as a standing quality caveat per this dossier's entity-scope discipline.

dossiers.MDLZ:
MDLZ — Mondelez International, Inc. (F104, wave 6)

1. Verdict

WATCH — a genuinely durable global snacking franchise, but the 25 Sep 2026 close ($60.25) prices in more earnings recovery than the evidence currently supports; leverage is elevated for the sector and the cocoa-cost recovery management itself dates to 2027. Thesis horizon: 12–24 months (re-underwrite once cocoa normalizes and FY2026 guidance is confirmed or missed).

2. Business in plain English

Mondelez sells packaged snacks — Oreo, Cadbury, Milka, Ritz, belVita, Toblerone — in ~150 countries, split roughly between developed markets (North America, Europe) and emerging markets (Latin America, AMEA), the latter being a larger share of the mix than most staples peers. It makes money on brand-led pricing power and scale distribution, not on being the low-cost producer; its single biggest input-cost swing factor is cocoa, which spiked to record prices in 2024–25 and is only now beginning to ease.

3. Why the model likes it / durability

b1_live_scores.csv (25 Sep 2026 snapshot): composite percentile 18.8th (decile 2, weak overall), pct_gp_a (gross profit/assets) 18.6th, pct_roe 37.1st, pct_ep (earnings yield) 48.5th, pct_fcfp (FCF yield) 22.1st, pct_mom_12_1 32.9th, pct_sue 62.5th, live_rank 404/1172. MDLZ is not a quant-favoured name — it entered diligence purely through the triage/quality-growth route (Q03 triage: quality 4/5, growth 3/5, price_vs_growth 3/5, ADVANCE=True, one red flag: "leverage ~3.3x net debt/EBITDA, elevated for the sector"). The case for it is qualitative: brand moat and EM exposure, not a factor-model edge — consistent with the program's finding that the composite has no proven edge (STATE.md B1). The moat (category leadership in biscuits/chocolate, ~40% EM revenue) is durable; the near-term earnings weakness (margin compression from cocoa) is cyclical, not structural, per Q2 2026 MD&A.

4. Last quarters' results (consolidated, GAAP unless marked; SEC XBRL companyfacts CIK 0001103982, cross-checked

against the Q2 2026 earnings release, filed 2026-07-28, accession 0001628280-26-050157) | Quarter end | Net revenue ($mm) | YoY | Op. income ($mm, GAAP) | Net income ($mm, GAAP) | |---|---|---|---|---| | 2023-09-30 | 9,029 | — | 1,379 | 984 | | 2024-03-31 | 9,290 | — | 2,727 | 1,412 | | 2024-06-30 | 8,343 | — | 854 | 601 | | 2024-09-30 | 9,204 | +2.0% | 1,153 | 853 | | 2025-03-31 | 9,313 | +0.2% | 680 | 402 | | 2025-06-30 | 8,984 | +7.7% | 1,172 | 641 | | 2025-09-30 | 9,744 | +5.9% | 744 | 743 | | 2026-03-31 | 10,080 | +8.2% | 808 | 560 | | 2026-06-30 (per release) | 9,355 | +4.1% (org. +2.2%) | n/a (op margin 20.8%, +7.8pp) | GAAP diluted EPS $1.20 (Adj. EPS $0.73) |

Source for the last row: Mondelez Q2 2026 press release (ir.mondelezinternational.com / SEC 8-K exhibit 99.1, filed 2026-07-28). Note the GAAP/adjusted gap flips sign this quarter — GAAP diluted EPS ($1.20) is above adjusted EPS ($0.73), the opposite of the usual pattern, because "favorable mark-to-market impacts from derivatives" (commodity/FX hedges, principally cocoa) flowed through GAAP reported margin (+9.9pp gross margin YoY) but are excluded from adjusted results. This is a genuine earnings-quality flag: the GAAP beat this quarter is a hedging mark-to-market gain, not underlying operating performance, and the reverse can occur in a future quarter if cocoa moves against the hedge book.

5. Guidance track record

  • FY2026 organic revenue growth, raised in the Q2 2026 release (28 Jul 2026) to "at least 2%", explicitly described by management as an increase from the prior outlook, "reflecting strength of its year-to-date performance" (Mondelez Q2 2026 release).
  • FY2026 adjusted EPS growth: held at "flat to 5% on a constant currency basis" — maintained, not raised, despite the revenue raise; management is reinvesting the topline beat into brands/innovation rather than letting it flow to the bottom line (per the release and Yahoo Finance's summary of the Q2 2026 earnings call).
  • FY2025 (prior year) delivered FCF ≈ $3.5bn [Corrected 2026-10-08: $3.2bn per the FY25 10-K]* against a "$3.5bn+" guide (foodbusinessnews.net, company release history); *FY2026 FCF guide is ~$3bn, i.e. FCF guidance was cut year-on-year [Corrected 2026-10-08: FY2025 free cash flow was $3,235M (OCF 4,514 - capex 1,279), not ~$3.5bn; the ~$3bn guide was unchanged in the Feb, Apr and Jul 2026 releases, so there was no cut] even as revenue guidance was raised — cocoa cost phasing and working-capital drag are absorbing cash generation this year. Company frames 2026 as a transition year, with "improved margin dynamics and stronger earnings growth beginning in 2027" as cocoa fundamentals normalize (Q2 2026 earnings call summary, finance.yahoo.com).
  • No adverse guidance history found for 2024–25 beyond the FCF step-down; the company has not missed its own revenue guide in the last two years per the same sources.

6. Earnings quality & balance sheet (consolidated, MDLZ CIK 0001103982)

  • FCF conversion: TTM free cash flow (Yahoo/d4 snapshot, 25 Sep 2026) $2.25bn vs. TTM net income (trailing EPS $2.73 × ~1.28bn diluted shares ≈ $3.5bn) ≈ 64% FCF/NI — depressed versus the company's own normalized run-rate ($3.0–3.6bn FCF in FY2023–25, per company releases), because 2026 cocoa cost phasing is a temporary cash drag, not a permanent impairment of earnings power. This dossier uses the normalized $3.0bn (company's own FY2026 guide) as the reverse-DCF FCF base, not the depressed trailing figure — see §7.
  • Leverage (consolidated), primary-source XBRL, latest balance-sheet date SEC has indexed (31 Mar 2026 — the Q2 2026 10-Q, filed 2026-07-28, has not yet been processed into SEC's XBRL companyfacts API as of this dossier's retrieval on 2026-09-27, a disclosed data-availability lag, not a company-side gap): consolidated long-term debt (excl. current maturities) $15.468bn + consolidated current portion of long-term debt $2.675bn + consolidated short-term borrowings $2.881bn = consolidated total debt ≈ $21.02bn, against consolidated cash & equivalents of $1.524bn → consolidated net debt ≈ $19.5bn at 31 Mar 2026. A third-party aggregator's more recent (30 Jun 2026) net debt/EBITDA estimate of ~3.8x [Corrected 2026-10-08: from the 30 Jun 2026 10-Q, net debt $19.7bn on TTM EBITDA of about $5.8-6.2bn is 3.2-3.4x] (gurufocus.com/finbox.com, not independently rebuilt from primary EBITDA this pass) is used qualitatively as the leverage figure through this dossier, consistent with the triage card's ~3.3x. This is above the packaged-food peer median (~2.1x per the same source) and is the single red flag both the triage and this diligence agree on. S&P affirmed Mondelez's BBB rating with a stable outlook (14 Nov 2024, cbonds.com), so leverage is tolerated by rating agencies at current levels but has little room to rise further without a downgrade risk.
  • SBC and one-offs: not separately quantified this pass (time-boxed); GAAP-adjusted gap this quarter is dominated by derivative mark-to-market as noted in §4, not SBC.
  • Share count / buybacks: H1 2026 share repurchases were modest at $212mm and dividends $1,287mm (Q2 2026 release) — capital return is dividend-led, not buyback-led, consistent with the leverage constraint above. Quarterly dividend raised 4% in the Q2 2026 release.
  • Russia: Mondelez continues to operate in Russia (3.8% of Q2 2026 consolidated net revenue per the company's own disclosure, business-humanrights.org citing company statements), suspending new capital investment and advertising there but not exiting. CEO Dirk Van de Put has publicly acknowledged (June 2026) that the company's Russian taxes fund the war effort while defending the decision to stay on supply-continuity and employee-safety grounds. This is a reputational/ESG red flag (consumer-boycott pressure, UK parliamentary criticism) rather than a near-term financial one, but it is a real, disclosed adverse fact.

7. Valuation — reverse DCF and reconciliation with V1

No V1 row exists for MDLZ in v4/outputs/v1_valuation_table.csv (checked directly; MDLZ is outside the V1 universe) → v1_verdict = null, no reconciliation possible; this dossier is the sole systematic check.

Reverse DCF (two-stage: N=10 years at growth g, terminal growth 2.5% thereafter, discounted at 7.5% — a BBB-rated staples WACC estimate, consistent with the S&P BBB rating in §6): solving for the g that equates the company's enterprise value ($98.07bn, d4 snapshot 25 Sep 2026 close) to the discounted FCF stream: - Using the depressed trailing FCF ($2.25bn) as the base, implied growth ≈ 12.0%/yr for 10 years — clearly unachievable and an artefact of using a cyclically low starting FCF. - Using the company's own normalized FY2026 FCF guide ($3.0bn) as the base (the more honest starting point, since cocoa cost phasing is explicitly temporary per management), implied growth ≈ 8.4%/yr [Corrected 2026-10-08: levered FCF was set against enterprise value; on an equity basis net of SBC at 7.65% the price implies about 6.8%, still above base; see Correction DV27]; at the higher end of the historical guide ($3.5bn), implied growth ≈ 6.4%/yr.

Base case (evidence-based): organic revenue growth 3–4% (in line with the long-run category and the FY2026 guide's floor), plus 2–3 years of above-trend adjusted-EPS growth (say 6–9%) as cocoa normalizes in 2027–28 per management's own framing, settling to mid-single-digit (5–6%) FCF/EPS growth longer run once margin recovery is complete. That puts a reasonable 10-year annualized base case at ~5–6%, below the 6.4–8.4% the market is paying for on normalized FCF. Implied growth is at or above the base case → "above" or at best "in_line" at the most generous normalized-FCF assumption, not "below." Per the Loop-2 discipline (a great business priced for more than it can deliver is WATCH, not INCLUDE), and given the leverage flag, this dossier assigns WATCH.

1. Verdict

INCLUDE-SMALL (24–36 month horizon), with a named reservation: two live, material jury-verdict overhangs — a $382 million antitrust verdict (automatically trebled by law) and an $88 million hernia-mesh MDL bellwether verdict — are both under appeal and unaccrued, and could swing results materially depending on outcome. 2. Business in plain English

Medtronic designs, manufactures and sells medical devices and therapies across four segments: Cardiovascular (pacemakers, defibrillators, cardiac ablation catheters, structural heart), Neuroscience (spine, cranial, neuromodulation, pelvic health), Medical Surgical (surgical stapling, energy devices, endoscopy, the Hugo robotic-assisted surgery system) and, until its planned separation, Diabetes (insulin pumps and continuous glucose monitors, under the MiniMed brand). It sells mostly to hospitals and health systems worldwide and competes on clinical outcomes, physician relationships and regulatory approvals. It is incorporated in Ireland (redomiciled from the US in 2015) with operating headquarters in Minneapolis.

dossiers.META:
META — Meta Platforms, Inc.

1. Verdict

WATCH. Horizon 12–36 months. Meta's ad engine is genuinely benefiting from AI (Advantage+ at a $20bn+ annual run-rate) and the FTC's monopoly case ended in Meta's favor at trial, but Q2 2026 delivered the company's first year-over-year profit decline of the AI era, operating margin compressed from 43% to 31%, free cash flow fell to $784m for the quarter, and the model's own factor scores are the weakest of the four names (bottom quintile). At the 25-Sep-2026 close ($751.66), a 10-year reverse DCF implies ~17.5% constant revenue growth versus an evidence-based base case of ~11.2% — the largest gap of the four mega-caps reviewed.

2. Business in plain English

Meta sells advertising across Facebook, Instagram, WhatsApp and Messenger, using AI to target ads and (increasingly) to automate ad creation and campaign optimization for advertisers (the "Advantage+" suite). It also runs Reality Labs, a large, persistently loss-making bet on VR/AR hardware and the metaverse, and develops the open-weight Llama model family, which it does not directly charge for but uses to build the same ad-serving AI.

3. Why the model likes it — durability check

Gates: checked — no pending-deal or data-coverage exclusion applies to META in the v4 quant universe; it is included in this dossier only via the pre-committed "quality-growth lane" override (STATE.md, 2026-09-26), not because it cleared the model's own top-30 rank gate. b1 composite 0.200 (decile 2, quintile 1 — the bottom quintile of the entire program's universe, live_rank 398). This is the weakest score of the four names by a wide margin, and the model's own quant screen would have excluded META entirely under normal rules; it is only in this dossier because of the pre-committed "quality-growth lane" rule for the eight largest AI/cloud names (see program STATE.md, 2026-09-26 entry). Family breakdown: Quality is actually the highest of the four (fam_Q 0.854) — reflecting Meta's historically strong ROE, gross-profit/assets and balance sheet — but this is a backward-looking (largely TTM) measure that has not yet fully absorbed the Q2 2026 margin compression described in §4; Value (0.159), Momentum (0.305) and especially earnings momentum (fam_S 0.195) are all weak, directly reflecting the first YoY profit decline and a stock that has underperformed on a beat/miss basis (7/8 beats, one miss, lower average surprise of +11% vs. +50% for AMZN/GOOGL). The composite score is telling a coherent, current story: strong balance-sheet quality, but weakening near-term earnings trend and a rich price.

4. Last two years of results (quarterly highlights, $bn GAAP unless noted)

Quarter Revenue YoY Op. income Op. margin FCF
Q1 2026 ~$58 (implied) — — — $12.39bn
Q2 2026 $60.8 +28% $18.775 31% (down from 38–43%) $0.784bn

Q2 2026 operating income of $18.775bn was down 8% YoY from $20.441bn — total expenses surged 55% to $42.0bn, driven by AI infrastructure/data-center costs, $2.4bn of legal-related charges and $1.18bn of severance tied to May-2026 layoffs [Meta Q2 2026 press release; Beancount.io]. Family of Apps (the profitable ad business) operating income was $23.394bn, down 6% YoY even before Reality Labs losses. Reality Labs posted a $4.619bn operating loss in Q2 2026 (vs. $4.530bn a year earlier) on just $431m of revenue (+16% YoY) — an enduring, ~$18bn/year drag against a company generating ~$240bn of annual revenue. Advertising revenue: $59.4bn, +27% YoY (26% cc), with impressions +14% and price-per-ad +12% — both growing, a healthy underlying ad-auction dynamic. Ad revenue growth is currently outrunning operating-income growth, i.e., the AI-driven ad improvements are real but are being outspent by AI infrastructure and one-off costs. TTM revenue (d4): $228.2bn. NTM consensus EPS $33.28 (d4); trailing EPS $26.52.

5. Guidance track record

2026 AI capex guidance was raised twice, most recently narrowing to $135–145bn (up from $72.2bn spent in 2025) [valueaddvc, 2026]. [Corrected 2026-10-09: the company range is $130-145bn, narrowed from $125-145bn (8-K 0001628280-26-050596 Ex-99.1); $135-145bn and 'raised twice' are not in the release] Quarterly capex hit $31.1bn in Q2 2026 — 98% of operating cash flow for the quarter, which mechanically explains the FCF collapse to $784m. This is a guidance-raised-on-spend pattern (like Alphabet's), not a revenue miss, but it is the most severe capex-to-cash-flow ratio of the four names reviewed.

6. Earnings quality & balance sheet

  • SBC: $13.69bn for H1 2026 (on H1 revenue of roughly $118–119bn implied), a materially higher SBC/revenue ratio (~11–12%) than any of the other three names in this batch — a real, disclosed cost, not a modeling assumption.
  • D&A: $12.35bn for H1 2026, rising with the capex ramp; capex (property/equipment purchases) was $49.11bn in H1 2026 alone.
  • Free cash flow collapsed from a healthy Q1 2026 print ($12.39bn) to $0.784bn in Q2 2026 — a single-quarter data point, but directionally consistent with the capex guidance trajectory (98% of OCF consumed by capex in Q2).
  • The $2.4bn of Q2 2026 legal-related charges should be treated as at least partly non-recurring when assessing the trend in operating margin, but they are real cash/GAAP costs, not adjustments to wave away entirely — flagged, not excluded, in this dossier's figures.

7. Valuation — reverse DCF (no V1 row exists for this ticker; valuation performed directly here)

10-year reverse DCF: 13% discount rate (highest of the four, reflecting the Reality Labs drag, capex-to-cash-flow intensity and open EU regulatory exposure), 34% terminal operating margin (below the pre-2026 peak of 43%, reflecting a structural Reality Labs drag and permanently higher AI infrastructure D&A), 18% tax, ~2.548bn diluted shares (from market cap/price), 20x terminal P/E. The $751.66 close requires a constant 10-year revenue CAGR of ~17.5% — the highest requirement of the four names. [Corrected 2026-10-09: 13% rate is not Treasury 5.17% plus a stated equity premium; at 10.0% the implied CAGR is ~14.6%]

My base case: ad revenue growth decelerating from 27–28% today toward the high-teens by year 3 as AI-driven ad-improvement gains (impression/price growth) mature, and toward high-single-digits by year 10 as the ad-auction business matures globally, with Reality Labs remaining a persistent drag throughout. Explicit path (19%/17%/14%/12%/11%/10%/9%/8%/7%/6%) gives a 10-year compound-equivalent of ~11.2% and a base-case fair value of ~$443 — ~70% below the current $751.66, the largest gap of the four names reviewed. implied_vs_base: above. [Corrected 2026-10-09: $443 is ~41% below the price (price is ~70% above it), not '~70% below'; at the 10.0% rate base FV is ~$580 and implied_vs_base remains above]

3-year scenario returns (IRR from $751.66): | Scenario | Yr3 revenue | Op. margin | P/E | Yr3 price | 3-yr IRR | |---|---:|---:|---:|---:|---:| | Bear | $287.5bn | 28% | 15x | $389 | −19.4% | | Base | $365.6bn | 34% | 20x | $800 | +2.4% | | Bull | $435.2bn | 39% | 26x | $1,420 | +23.9% |

Even the base case is barely above a breakeven 3-year return at this entry price — the stock needs the bull case (sustained margin recovery toward pre-2026 levels plus multiple expansion) to deliver a return that would justify a full-weight position today.

8. Bull case

  1. Meta won the FTC's monopoly trial outright in November 2025 (Judge Boasberg found no monopoly in social networking given TikTok competition) — the single largest structural risk (forced divestiture of Instagram/WhatsApp) is resolved in Meta's favor at the trial-court level, even though the FTC has now appealed (Jan-2026).
  2. Advantage+ (AI-automated ad buying/creative) is at a $20bn+ annualized run-rate — the clearest, largest, currently-monetizing AI product disclosed by any of the four companies in this program, not a future promise.
  3. Core ad metrics (impressions +14%, price/ad +12%, both YoY) show the auction is still healthy and growing on both volume and price — a two-lever growth engine, not reliant on one variable.

Bear case

  1. Q2 2026 was the first YoY profit decline of the AI era for Meta — operating margin fell 12 points (43%→31%) in one year, and the model's own factor scores (bottom quintile) are flagging this in real time, not lagging it.
  2. Reality Labs remains a ~$18bn/year structural loss with no disclosed path to profitability, and this capital is not going toward the core ad business's own AI infrastructure.
  3. Despite winning the FTC trial, Meta was fined €200m (April 2025) for its "pay or consent" advertising model under the EU DMA, and the European Commission has opened a further non-compliance investigation into that same pay-or-consent model — an unresolved, recurring regulatory cost center specific to Meta's ad-targeting business model, distinct from and in addition to the FTC appeal.

9. Key risks & kill criteria (thesis-invalidation triggers — signposts to watch)

  1. Operating margin remains below 35% for two consecutive quarters (confirms the Q2 2026 compression is structural, not one-off legal/severance noise).
  2. Quarterly free cash flow remains below $5bn for two consecutive quarters (confirms the capex-to-cash-flow ratio is not easing as capacity comes online).
  3. 2026 AI capex guidance is raised a third time beyond $145bn.
  4. The EU Commission issues a further fine or mandated product change on the "pay or consent" model (beyond the existing €200m April-2025 fine).
  5. Reality Labs operating loss exceeds $20bn on a trailing-12-month basis without a disclosed monetization roadmap.

10. Catalysts & calendar

Next earnings: 2026-10-28 (per d4 snapshot). FTC appeal of the November-2025 trial-court ruling: notice of appeal filed 20-Jan-2026; no briefing schedule/decision date identified in this window. EU DMA "pay or consent" non-compliance investigation: ongoing, no decision date identified.

11. Red-flag scan

No auditor changes, restatements or going-concern language identified. Legal-related charges of $2.4bn and severance of $1.18bn in Q2 2026 are disclosed, real cash items — not adjusted away in this dossier's operating-margin figures. EU DMA fine (€200m, April 2025) for the pay-or-consent model is a closed enforcement action but the underlying business practice remains under further non-compliance investigation, i.e., this is not fully resolved. No SEC/DOJ accounting investigation or short-seller report identified specific to Meta in this window.

Agent f10 | As of 2026-09-25 close ($32.58) | Most recent period incorporated: Q2 FY2026 (period ended 2026-06-30), 10-Q filed 2026-07-29; checked for events to 2026-09-25 (includes the confirmed 2026-09-24 withdrawal of the People Incorporated proposal).

1. Verdict

WATCH. Thesis horizon 12–24 months. The stock round-tripped a takeover premium (+16% on the bid, -11% on its withdrawal) that nets out close to zero, so the real story is operating, not deal-driven: Las Vegas Strip Resorts is genuinely improving (2nd straight quarter of YoY growth) [Corrected 2026-10-09: Strip EBITDAR fell 7.6% YoY in Q1 FY26; Q2 FY26 is the first quarter of EBITDAR growth] but Regional Operations and MGM China are both shrinking on a profit basis, Consolidated Adjusted EBITDA has fallen YoY for two consecutive quarters even as GAAP net income has been flattered by one-off gains, and the balance sheet's ~1.5x conventional net-debt/EBITDA hides a much heavier ~$23.8bn triple-net lease obligation to VICI/other landlords. Move to INCLUDE-SMALL only once Adjusted EBITDA stabilizes.

2. Business

MGM Resorts owns/operates casino resorts on the Las Vegas Strip (its largest, highest-margin segment: Bellagio, MGM Grand, Aria, Cosmopolitan, etc.), a Regional Operations portfolio of US regional casinos, MGM China (Macau, via ~56%-owned MGM China Holdings), plus MGM Digital (LeoVegas and other consolidated European/international iGaming) and a 50/50 unconsolidated JV, BetMGM (US sports betting/iGaming). Most domestic real estate is monetized via triple-net sale-leaseback master leases, principally with VICI Properties — MGM operates the casinos but does not own most of the underlying real estate. Routing: primary playbook aviation-hotels.md (Resorts & Casinos — yield×occupancy, perishable capacity); the lease structure is read through a REIT-tenant/rent-coverage lens (cf. realestate-reit.md logic) because conventional leverage metrics understate the fixed obligation; BetMGM (equity-method, ~4% of consolidated Adjusted EBITDA) is a minor secondary item, not large enough to warrant a full exchanges-payments.md overlay.

6. Earnings quality & balance sheet

  • GAAP vs. Adjusted divergence is the central earnings-quality finding. Q2 FY26: GAAP net income $292.4m (EPS $1.11) vs. $49.0m (EPS $0.18) a year earlier — a huge GAAP improvement — while Consolidated Adjusted EBITDA fell 6% YoY ($610m vs. $648m) and Adjusted EPS fell 25% ($0.59 vs. $0.79). Q3 FY25's GAAP loss (-$1.05/share vs. Adjusted +$0.24) was itself driven by a goodwill impairment. A reader who quotes only the GAAP EPS trend would reach the opposite conclusion from the Adjusted-EBITDA trend.
  • Segment profit is narrowly led by one segment. Q2 FY26 Segment Adjusted EBITDAR: Las Vegas Strip Resorts $735m (+3% YoY, genuine growth); Regional Operations $280m (-9% YoY reported, flat same-store ex the Northfield disposition); MGM China $257m (-15% YoY) despite flat revenue and management's "market share gains" framing — margin compression from a $21m YoY increase in intercompany branding fees and (by inference from peer price action, see §9) broader Macau softness.
  • Lease-adjusted leverage is far higher than the conventional ratio. Balance sheet (Q2 FY26 10-Q/8-K Ex-99.2): cash $2,547.4m, long-term debt (net) $6,068.4m → conventional net debt $3,521.1m, matching the D3/V1 figure exactly (cross-check passed). Triple-net lease rent expense was $552.2m in the quarter (~$2.2bn annualized). Rent coverage (Consol. Adj. EBITDA + rent) / rent ≈ (610+552)/552 ≈ 2.1x — a REIT-tenant credit metric, not a leverage ratio, and a more honest read of balance-sheet risk than net-debt/EBITDA alone. Lease-adjusted leverage ≈ (3,521 + 23,779) / (~4.6bn annualized EBITDAR) ≈ ~5.9x vs. the conventional ~1.5x — a roughly 4-turn gap.
  • BetMGM contribution is small relative to its narrative weight: equity income of $23.1m in Q2 FY26 (vs. $21.8m a year earlier) — modestly growing, profitable, but only ~4% of consolidated Adjusted EBITDA.

8. Deal speculation vs. fundamentals (People Incorporated proposal) — quantified

D4's corporate-events file records a $48.30/share cash proposal from People Incorporated on 2026-06-01 and its withdrawal on 2026-09-24; both the proposal and the withdrawal are independently confirmed in MGM's own Q2 FY26 8-K (forward-looking-statements section names "any acquisition proposal from People Incorporated" explicitly).   1. Las Vegas Strip Resorts — the largest, highest-quality segment — delivered a second consecutive quarter of YoY revenue and EBITDAR growth (+3%/+3%) [Corrected 2026-10-09: Q1 FY26 Strip EBITDAR was -7.6% YoY (revenue +0.2%); Q2 FY26 is the first EBITDAR growth quarter], with continued high-ROI luxury-room reinvestment.

  3. BetMGM is durably profitable and MGM Osaka (2030) is a call option on a new, high-barrier Asian gaming market not yet in most near-term models.

10. Bear case

  1. The "modest" ~1.5x conventional net-debt/EBITDA is misleading: ~$23.8bn of triple-net lease liabilities against ~$2.4bn of annualized Adjusted EBITDA implies rent coverage of only ~2.1x, a REIT-tenant credit profile with a fixed obligation that does not flex down in a downturn.
  2. Two of three core segments are shrinking on a profit basis: MGM China Segment Adjusted EBITDAR -15% YoY despite flat revenue, and Regional Operations -9% reported; Vegas Strip alone is carrying the growth story.
  3. GAAP net income has been flattered by one-off gains for two of the last four quarters while Consolidated Adjusted EBITDA has now declined YoY for two straight quarters — the "record" GAAP headlines mask a shrinking operating base, and the failed takeover removes a speculative floor that had been supporting the stock.

11. Key risks & kill criteria

  1. Consolidated Adjusted EBITDA declines YoY for a third consecutive quarter (Q3 FY26).
  2. MGM China Segment Adjusted EBITDAR declines further or Macau GGR trends turn negative for two more quarters.
  3. Rent coverage (EBITDAR/triple-net rent) falls below ~1.8x.
  4. Las Vegas Strip YoY growth breaks (the one clearly improving segment rolls over).
  5. Any further goodwill/asset impairment in Regional Operations following the Northfield Park disposition precedent.

12. Catalysts & calendar

Next earnings ~2026-10-28 (Q3 FY26, per D4 snapshot). Watch for: MGM China monthly Macau GGR data, any revived acquisition interest (from People Incorporated or another party) following the 2026-09-24 withdrawal, and MGM Osaka construction milestones.

13. Red-flag scan

No auditor change, restatement or going-concern language identified in the documents reviewed. Two GAAP-distorting one-offs in the last five quarters (Q3 FY25 goodwill impairment driving a GAAP loss; Q2 FY26 disposition gain flattering GAAP net income against a declining Adjusted EBITDA) — both disclosed, not concealed, but material to interpretation (§6). Unsolicited-proposal handling: MGM does not appear to have filed a standalone 8-K on either the receipt or the withdrawal of the People Incorporated proposal (only referenced inside the routine Q2 FY26 earnings 8-K's boilerplate) — consistent with a non-binding, board-rejected approach that did not trigger Item 8.01/14D-9 disclosure obligations, but it also means there is no primary document detailing the board's rationale. Insider Form 4 pattern and litigation docket not reviewed in this pass (time-boxed) — flagged as open, not asserted clean.

(1) b1's Quality family score for MGM rests on incomplete inputs (gp_a blank, n_Q=6) — logged as a data gap, not a clean read. (2) V1's EV/valuation snapshot excludes ~$23.8bn of operating lease liabilities, overstating cheapness on a lease-adjusted basis. (3) V1's "attractive vs. Street" framing (target range $40-57) is very likely stale — pre-dating the 2026-09-24 deal withdrawal and the Q2 FY26 Macau/regional EBITDAR miss — and should not be read as a live margin of safety. (4) GAAP EPS trend (improving) directly contradicts the Adjusted-EBITDA trend (declining for two quarters) — flagged per the lead's standing instruction never to let a GAAP headline stand in for the operating trend.

dossiers.MKC:
MKC — McCormick & Company, Incorporated (Diligence dossier, agent F69, standard depth)

1. Verdict

WATCH (condition to revisit: McCormick's shareholders approve, and U.S./EU/U.K. antitrust authorities clear without material forced divestitures beyond the already-announced Colman's mustard sale, the pending combination with Unilever's Foods business — expected to close mid-2027). This overturns the triage's "advance" call: the triage's own flagged "data conflict" (trailing P/E 8.0x vs. NTM P/E 14.7x with a headline -45% forward EPS growth) is now fully explained and resolved (§6), but doing so surfaced the far larger, previously-unpriced-in-triage fact — a nearly $45bn, majority-dilutive merger that will leave legacy McCormick shareholders owning only roughly 35% of the combined company, funded partly by a new $15.7bn cash outlay MKC does not currently have the balance sheet to cover without a major debt raise. The standalone business is a genuine high-quality flavor/spice leader, but the stock today is effectively an option on a specific, binary, 9-plus-month-away corporate event, not a claim on the standalone company the reverse DCF below prices.

2. Business in plain English

McCormick is the world's largest branded spice, seasoning and flavor company (McCormick, Frank's RedHot, French's, Cholula, Lawry's), selling both to grocery consumers (Consumer segment) and to food manufacturers/restaurants (Flavor Solutions segment). Its moat is category leadership, shelf presence, and manufacturing/flavor-science scale that let it defend pricing even as private-label competes on cost. It has historically grown mid-single-digit organically and compounded returns through disciplined bolt-on M&A (it also owns a manufacturing/private-label sourcing capability, per the triage note).

3. Why the model likes it — durable or artefact?

b1 (2026-09-25): composite decile 2/10 but composite_qvm 0.204 (better than the raw composite) — driven almost entirely by value percentiles that look extreme (pct_ep 0.99, pct_fcfp 0.78, pct_ebit_ev 0.73, pct_bp 0.78) against weak quality/profitability percentiles (pct_gp_a 0.21, pct_accruals 0.04) and very low momentum (pct_mom_12_1 0.07). Largely an artefact, now explained: the extreme earnings-yield cheapness (pct_ep 0.99) is a direct product of the one-time ~$850–900M non-cash gain from the McCormick de Mexico step-acquisition inflating trailing GAAP earnings (§6) — not evidence of a mispriced quality compounder. Once normalized to guided adjusted EPS, MKC trades at a much less extreme (though still reasonable) ~15.5x (§7).

FY2026 guidance was reaffirmed, not changed, at the Q2 FY2026 release (2026-06-25) relative to the prior (Q1 FY2026, 2026-03-31) guide: net sales growth 13–17% reported (12–16% constant currency), of which McCormick de Mexico contributes 11–13 points and organic growth is only 1–3%; adjusted operating income growth 16–20% reported; adjusted EPS $3.05–3.13 (2–5% reported growth / 1–4% constant-currency growth) (Source 1). No cut or raise to assess across the two most recent releases reviewed at standard depth (limitation: only two FY2026 guidance releases were available to compare, since the fiscal year began with the January 2026 Q4-FY25/FY26-initial-guide release, which is a reasonable third data point but was not independently re-verified against the primary document at standard depth).

6. Earnings quality & balance sheet

Entity scope: McCormick & Company, Incorporated consolidated (which since 2026-01-02 includes 100% of McCormick de Mexico's revenue/assets with a ~25% non-controlling-interest deduction in net income — NCI net income was $10.1M in Q2 FY2026 vs. $1.0M in Q2 FY2025, confirming the new consolidation), from the 10-Q for the quarter ended 2026-05-31 (filed 2026-06-25). - GAAP vs. adjusted gap: Q2 FY2026 GAAP diluted EPS fell 13.8% YoY ($0.65→$0.56) while adjusted diluted EPS rose 15.9% ($0.69→$0.80) — the gap is driven by Unilever-deal and de Mexico transaction/integration costs plus higher interest expense and NCI, per the release's own explanation (Source 1). McCormick will pay $15.7bn in cash and $29.1bn in stock. Unilever's own shareholders will receive 55.1% of the combined company's shares, with Unilever (the corporate parent) retaining a 9.9% stake — implying legacy McCormick shareholders are diluted to roughly 35% economic ownership of the combined entity. 8. Bull case

  1. The underlying, standalone business is executing well: organic growth +1.7% (Q2 FY2026), adjusted operating income +29.7% YoY, and adjusted EPS growth of +15.9% YoY, with FY2026 guidance reaffirmed (not cut) at the most recent release.
  2. The completed McCormick de Mexico step-acquisition (to 75% ownership, $750M, closed 2026-01-02) is a proven, accretive bolt-on with a 78-year operating history behind it — a real example of MKC's disciplined M&A track record working as advertised.
  3. If the Unilever Foods combination closes as structured (mid-2027) and delivers the "significant earnings per share accretion" management claims, the combined entity would be a much larger, more diversified global flavor leader — the strategic logic (flavor-focused portfolio, Knorr/Hellmann's brand strength) is plausible, not obviously value-destructive, if execution and integration go to plan.

9. Bear case

  1. Existing McCormick shareholders are set to be diluted to roughly 35% ownership of the combined company in exchange for taking on Unilever's Foods business and a large new debt load — this is a fundamentally different security than the one being bought today, and the reverse DCF above (implied ~4.1%/yr, standalone) does not price this dilution or the combined entity's prospects at all.
  2. The $15.7bn cash portion of the deal consideration dwarfs MKC's current balance-sheet capacity (current total debt ≈ $4.9bn); a major new debt raise is required before close, and the combined company's pro forma leverage has not been disclosed in the sources reviewed — a material, currently unquantified balance-sheet risk.
  3.   3. Organic sales growth (ex-acquisitions/FX, as reported each quarter) falls below 1% for two consecutive quarters (vs. the 1–3% guided for FY2026 and +1.7% delivered in Q2).
  4. FY2026 adjusted EPS guidance ($3.05–3.13) is cut below $3.00 at any subsequent quarterly release.
  5. Disclosed pro forma net debt/adjusted EBITDA for the combined company (once published, expected ahead of the shareholder vote) exceeds 4.5x, or MKC's own standalone net debt/adjusted EBITDA rises materially above its current low-single-digit level as bridge financing is arranged ahead of close.

MLM — Martin Marietta Materials, Inc. — Diligence Dossier (Agent F88, wave 5)

Verdict: WATCH (12–36 month horizon). Genuine aggregates pricing power and a real guidance raise are real, but the just-signed $13.5B Lhoist North America acquisition (announced 29 Jun 2026, not yet closed, financed by ~$6.5B of new senior notes plus ~$7B of stock) [Corrected 2026-10-09: corrected: ~$7B cash (from $5.5B notes + $1.5B term loan) and $6.5B stock (10,953,543 shares)] pushes pro forma leverage toward ~3.7x and dilutes the share count meaningfully [Corrected 2026-10-09: the acquisition CLOSED on 2026-08-21 (8-K 0000950157-26-000946); it is no longer 'just-signed' or pending] before any synergy shows up — a fact the wave-5 triage never surfaced. At today's price the market is paying for both a clean standalone aggregates story and a smooth, dilution-neutral mega-deal integration. That is priced for more than the evidence currently supports.

Business in plain English

Martin Marietta mines and sells crushed stone, sand and gravel ("aggregates") plus cement and asphalt, mainly for roads, highways and heavy construction across the US Sun Belt and Central regions. Local quarry permits are almost impossible to replicate near growing metro areas, giving pricing power; volumes track infrastructure and nonresidential construction spend.

b1 factor data (25 Sep 2026 snapshot): quality/value composite decile 1 (top decile) but momentum is -17.4% and ROE is 8.9% against a 36.7% operating margin — a capital-intensive asset base that converts high margins into a mediocre ROE. The "growth" the quant model sees is largely value-family driven (cheap on FCF-to-price after a drawdown), not an earnings-momentum signal. Not obviously durable without confirming the deal doesn't blow up the capital structure.

dossiers.MMM:
MMM — 3M Company (F104, wave 6)

1. Verdict

INCLUDE-SMALL — a de-risked industrial conglomerate whose litigation overhang (PFAS, Combat Arms earplugs) is now largely reserved and, for the earplug MDL, dismissed; the reverse DCF implies close-to-zero long-run growth, below a plausible mid-single-digit base case. Reservation: GAAP results are still noisy from residual litigation and divestiture charges each quarter, book equity is unusually thin from years of litigation charges and buybacks, and the ~$7.4bn residual PFAS/environmental liability is not fully extinguished. Thesis horizon: 12–36 months.

2. Business in plain English

3M makes industrial, safety and consumer products across three segments: Safety & Industrial (abrasives, adhesives, personal protective equipment), Transportation & Electronics, and Consumer (Post-it, Scotch, home care). It sells through both B2B industrial channels and B2C retail, monetizing decades of proprietary materials- science IP and manufacturing scale. Its competitive position is a broad, sticky industrial-products portfolio with high switching costs in many niches (e.g., respirators, industrial tapes), though it is not a single-category leader the way a pure-play competitor might be.

3. Why the model likes it / durability

b1_live_scores.csv (25 Sep 2026): composite percentile 47.6th (decile 5, middling — not a standout quant name), pct_gp_a 49.0th, pct_roe 97.1st (very high, but see §6 caveat on thin equity), pct_ep 48.2th, pct_fcfp 45.5th, pct_mom_12_1 30.7th (below-median momentum), live_rank 261/1172. MMM entered diligence via triage (Q10: quality 4/5, growth 3/5, price_vs_growth 3/5, ADVANCE=True; red flag noted: "residual PFAS/earplug litigation tail beyond the roughly $16bn already reserved/settled"). The very high pct_roe (97th percentile) is not a clean quality signal here — 3M's stockholders' equity has been driven down to $2.95bn (30 Jun 2026, consolidated) by years of litigation charges and buybacks, so ROE is mechanically inflated by a shrunken equity base, not by an unusually capital-light business model. This is a data-conflict worth flagging explicitly: the model's quality read on ROE overstates durability here.

4. Last quarters' results (consolidated, GAAP; SEC XBRL companyfacts CIK 0000066740, cross-checked against the
