Agent: F14 | As of: 2026-09-25 close (price $33.84) | Classification: Multi-Family Residential REIT

1. Verdict

INCLUDE-SMALL — thesis horizon 12–36 months. UDR is a statistically cheap, well-capitalized apartment REIT buying back its own stock, but this is a valuation-repair/capital-allocation thesis, not a near-term growth story: FFO-as-Adjusted per share has been range-bound ($0.61–$0.65) for eight straight quarters, the company's own FY2026 guidance implies roughly flat per-share cash flow versus FY2025, same-store NOI is outright declining in the Southeast and Southwest, and leverage (5.6x net debt/EBITDAre) is on the high side of the multifamily peer group. Reservation: hold at reduced weight until same-store NOI reaccelerates broadly (not just in the West/Northeast) or leverage comes down.

2. Business in plain English

UDR owns and operates ~60,000 apartment homes (as of Q2 2026) concentrated in coastal gateway markets (Boston–DC corridor, California, Seattle) and Sunbelt growth markets (Florida, Texas, Southeast). It makes money from rent, minus operating costs, property taxes and depreciation; it also runs a "Debt and Preferred Equity" program that lends to other apartment owners/JVs and recycles capital via property sales into new development and buybacks. Competitive position: a top-10 U.S. apartment REIT by scale, S&P 500 member, geographically diversified (no single region is more than a third of same-store NOI), competing with AvalonBay, Equity Residential, Camden, Mid-America and Essex Property Trust for both tenants and capital.

8. Bull case / bear case

Bull: (1) Trades at the bottom decile of its own 15-year P/FFO range with an active, board-expanded buyback shrinking the share count ~4%/yr annualized; (2) same-store fundamentals are healthy in West/Northeast/Mid-Atlantic (+3–4% NOI) as new supply moderates nationally into 2027; (3) monthly dividend and 217 consecutive quarterly-equivalent payouts signal capital-return discipline, covered at ~69% of FFOA.

Bear: (1) FFOA per share has not grown in two years and FY2026 guidance implies another flat year; (2) Southeast (-2.0%) and Southwest (-2.2%) same-store NOI are still contracting on new supply (23% of the same-store book) — the cited "waning supply" thesis is not yet visible in the numbers there; (3) leverage (5.6x net debt/EBITDAre) has crept up, not down, over the last year, reducing balance-sheet flexibility just as buybacks and development ($167M remaining commitment on 2 wholly-owned projects, plus $200M remaining JV commitments) compete for capital.

9. Key risks & measurable kill criteria

The specific, observable, time-bound conditions that would invalidate this thesis:

  1. Same-store NOI growth negative for two consecutive quarters (FY26 guide is barely positive at +0.625% midpoint).
  2. Consolidated Net Debt-to-EBITDAre (adjusted) rises above 6.0x (from 5.6x now).
  3. FFO-as-Adjusted per-share guidance is cut (not just plain FFO) at either of the next two quarterly updates.
  4. Southeast or Southwest same-store NOI decline exceeds -4% YoY in any quarter (supply absorption failing, not just slowing).
  5. Share buyback program paused or reduced to a token level for two consecutive quarters (loss of the primary capital-return signal underpinning the thesis).

2. Business in plain English

UHS operates acute-care hospitals and a large network of behavioral-health facilities (facility counts not verified in this pass). Acute care sells inpatient and outpatient hospital services paid by commercial insurers, Medicare and Medicaid; behavioral health (psychiatric and addiction treatment) is paid mostly by Medicaid, commercial plans and state programs. The moat is regulated local capacity (certificates of need, licensing) and scale in behavioral care where supply is scarce; the economics depend heavily on state Medicaid supplemental payments.

dossiers.ULTA:
ULTA — Ulta Beauty, Inc. (F107, agent F107)

1. Verdict

INCLUDE-SMALL (half weight) — thesis horizon 12–24 months. Reservation: comp-sales growth has structurally decelerated from the ~10%+ era to mid-single digits as Sephora (inside Kohl's, now 1,100+ doors, run-rating >$2bn/yr) takes share in mass-prestige overlap categories; the current re-acceleration (Q1 FY26 comps +5.3%) needs one more quarter to confirm it is durable rather than a promotional/loyalty-relaunch pop.

2. Business in plain English

Ulta Beauty is the largest U.S. specialty beauty retailer (~1,450+ stores plus e-commerce) [Corrected 2026-10-06: the Q2 FY26 10-Q reports 1,622 stores worldwide at 1 Aug 2026: 1,534 Ulta Beauty US stores plus Space NK stores in the UK and Ireland], selling prestige and mass cosmetics, skincare, haircare, fragrance and salon services under one roof, monetizing through merchandise margin, a large loyalty program (Ultamate Rewards) and in-store salon fees. It just closed the Space NK acquisition [Corrected 2026-10-06: the 10-Q places the Space NK acquisition in the second quarter of fiscal 2025, about a year before this period] (UK prestige beauty retailer), its first material international/inorganic move. Competitive position: category leader by store count and loyalty base, but facing a structural challenger in Sephora's expansion inside Kohl's, which gives Sephora suburban/off-mall reach it never had.

3. Why the model likes it / durability

b1_live_scores.csv (as of 2026-08-27 filing lag 55 days): composite percentile decile 9 (top decile), ROE 45.8%, earnings yield 5.2%, FCF yield 4.9%, EBIT/EV 6.9%, book/price 11.3%, momentum 12-1m −1.8% (negative — the market has been lukewarm), SUE 1.42 (strong recent earnings surprise). The pull is Quality (very high ROE, capital-light model) and Value/earnings-yield, not Momentum — consistent with a name whose growth story is questioned even as current-quarter execution beats. Durability judgment: the high ROE is a real structural feature (asset-light specialty retail, high inventory turns, loyalty-driven repeat purchase) not an accounting artefact, but the growth rate that justified past multiples is not durable at the old pace — Sephora share loss is real and ongoing, so the quality score should not be read as guaranteeing double-digit growth resumes.

  • Price used: $545.20 (2026-09-25 close, per b1_live_scores.csv, mktcap $23.31bn).
  • NTM P/E on updated FY26 EPS guide midpoint ($28.85): 18.9x. Triage's 17.6x used a slightly different NTM window; both point to a mid-teens-to-high-teens multiple, not the 25–30x the stock traded at during its double-digit-comp years.
  • FCF yield (FY25 FCF $1,068M / $23.31bn mktcap): ~4.6%. [Corrected 2026-10-06: TTM FCF to 1 Aug 2026 is $1,149.5M, a 4.9% yield (matches the 4.9% in section 3)]
  • V1 systematic valuation: no row exists yet for ULTA in v1_valuation_table.csv / v1_valuation.json (wave 6 names have not been through the V1 valuation agent). v1_verdict = null, per instructions; nothing to reconcile.
  • Reverse-DCF sense (my own, qualitative-quantitative, since V1 has not run): using FCF yield ~4.6%, a retail-sector WACC of ~8.5%, and the simple Gordon relationship (yield ≈ WACC − g), the price implies roughly 4–5% perpetual FCF/EPS growth. That sits below both the company's FY26 guided operating-income growth (8.3–9.3%) and its own historical growth rate, but is roughly in line with or a little above what mid-single-digit comps plus modest buyback accretion can plausibly deliver over 10 years once Sephora/Kohl's share losses are netted out. My base case for 10-year FCF/EPS growth is 5–7% (3–4% comps + 1–2pp margin/mix + buyback accretion), i.e. at or slightly above what the price implies — this is the borderline case the addendum flags: a good business, not egregiously priced for perfection, but not obviously cheap either.   • 3 closest peers for context (not independently re-priced this pass): e.l.f. Beauty, Sally Beauty, and the Sephora business embedded in LVMH — none is a clean apples-to-apples public comp; peer comparison is directional only.

8. Bull case / Bear case

Bull: 1. Q1 FY26 comp reacceleration (+5.3%, ticket and traffic both positive) shows the "Ulta Beauty Unleashed" strategy (loyalty relaunch, brand newness, omnichannel) is working, not just lapping easy compares. 2. Guidance has been raised, not cut, in the two most recent quarters — the opposite of the deceleration story priced in a year ago. 3. Space NK gives a first credible international growth vector and diversifies away from single-market (US) beauty retail concentration.

Bear: 1. Comp growth still decelerated sequentially within FY26 (5.3% → 3.8%), and Sephora's Kohl's footprint (>1,100 doors, run-rating >$2bn) is a structural, not cyclical, share-donor dynamic that management does not control. 2. 12-month price momentum is negative (−1.8% per b1 data) despite the earnings beats — the market is not yet rewarding the re-acceleration, which could mean it sees it as unsustainable (promotional, loyalty-relaunch sugar-high) rather than durable. 3. Buyback-driven EPS growth (13–16%) well above operating-income growth (10–12%) means a meaningful share of the "beat and raise" is capital allocation, not organic execution — if buybacks slow (cash is down to $158.5M and the company is drawing $339.6M of short-term debt to help fund them), EPS growth decelerates further.

9. Key risks & kill criteria (measurable)

  1. Comparable sales growth below 2.0% for two consecutive quarters (below the low end of the raised FY26 guide range).
  2. FY26 diluted EPS guidance cut from the current $28.70–29.00 range at any subsequent quarterly release.
  3. Gross margin below 38.5% for two consecutive quarters (vs. 39.1–40.1% in the last four quarters shown above).
  4. Net new Sephora-at-Kohl's door count growth re-accelerates materially (company/press disclosure) alongside a renewed comp deceleration below 3%, confirming share loss rather than a temporary lapse.
  5. Short-term debt balance grows beyond $500M while cash stays below $200M, signalling buybacks are being [Corrected 2026-10-06: (short-term debt is seasonal: $289M in Aug 2025, $552M with cash of $205M in Nov 2025, $62M in Jan 2026)] funded by leverage rather than FCF.

  • Holiday-quarter comp trends (Q3/Q4 FY26) are the key near-term catalyst given the seasonal weighting of beauty retail.

dossiers.UNH:
UNH — UnitedHealth Group Incorporated

1. Verdict

WATCH — thesis horizon 12–36 months. The franchise is intact and 2026 is a genuine recovery year (guidance raised at every 2026 release), but at $376.59 the stock is priced at 19x 2026 adjusted EPS, a premium to managed-care peers, while the two issues that matter most are unresolved: formal criminal and civil DOJ requests about Medicare Advantage, and IRS transfer-pricing proposals. My base case returns about 6% a year over three years, below a 9% hurdle; it becomes INCLUDE-SMALL at about $350 or lower, or once the DOJ matter is closed without charge and H2 medical cost ratio lands inside guidance. Triage (Q08) also said not to advance, citing the DOJ probe; filings confirm the probe exists, so I agree on direction, but for valuation-plus-tail-risk reasons rather than "value trap".

2. Business in plain English

UnitedHealth is America's largest health insurer (UnitedHealthcare: 48.5m people served at 30 Jun 2026; Medicare Advantage 7.565m, commercial, Medicaid) and the owner of Optum, a services arm (Optum Health clinics and value-based care, Optum Insight data/software, Optum Rx pharmacy benefits). It earns premiums minus medical costs, plus fees. Scale in claims data, networks and pharmacy is the moat; the weakness is that most profit hangs on government-funded Medicare and Medicaid rates and on how coding and medical costs are policed.

3. Why the model likes it — and is it durable?

Prices as of the 25 Sep 2026 close ($273.79). Research only, not personalised investment advice.

1. Verdict

WATCH (horizon 12-36 months). A top-quality franchise with improving operations and a record quarter, but at 21.0x 2026 EPS the price already embeds about 7.7% a year of EPS growth for ten years against my 6.5% base case, and the pending Norfolk Southern (NSC) merger adds a $2.5B break fee exposure, about 225M new shares and about $20B of new cash debt with approval not expected before Q3/Q4 2027. What would change it: a pullback to about $240 (18x), or an STB decision with acceptable conditions.

Triage (Q10) said not to advance on "19.7x NTM multiple already embeds merger synergies". I confirm the verdict but correct the reason: the quoted "29% margin, 40% ROE" are not what the filings show (Q2-26 operating margin 40.3%; return on equity about 35% on a book equity base that is small because of buybacks), and standalone valuation, not merger synergy, is what the price is testing. V1 could not run a reverse DCF (D&A missing) but gave "demanding", base 3y return +2.9%.

2. Business in plain English

UNP runs the western half of the US freight rail network ("Operating in 23 western states", 8-K acc. 0000100885-26-000249). It charges customers to move grain, chemicals, autos, containers and coal. Two railroads per region give it real pricing power: it has raised price above inflation for years ("Pricing dollars in excess of inflation dollars"). Earnings depend on volume, fuel surcharges and the operating ratio (costs as a share of revenue; lower is better). It has agreed to buy Norfolk Southern to create a coast-to-coast railroad.

3. Why the model likes it, and whether that is durable

b1 composite 0.867 (decile 9, live rank 66): momentum is the driver (M 0.70; 12-1 month return +29.9%), S 0.80, V only 0.56, Q 0.54. High ROE (35.5%) is partly a product of leverage and a depleted book equity after buybacks (net issuance 0.2%; buybacks paused since the NSC deal: $26M in H1-26 vs $2,679M in H1-25). Momentum will not persist by itself; the quality part (pricing power, OR near 60%) is durable.

dossiers.UPS:
United Parcel Service (UPS) — Diligence Dossier

Recency gate: Most recent period incorporated: Q2 FY2026 (quarter ended 2026-06-30, 10-Q filed 2026-08-05; earnings released 2026-07-28). Checked for events to 2026-09-25 close, including an August 2026 8-K (leadership, items 5.02/7.01/9.01, filed 2026-08-31) not analyzed in depth here — flagged for follow-up. Data-quality note: SEC EDGAR's Archives server had a maintenance outage for part of this session and UPS's 10-K is heavily inline-XBRL-tagged, which degraded automated text extraction of the narrative sections; segment, headcount and buyback figures below are corroborated by the company's own press releases and prior-year 10-Ks rather than a full read of the FY2025 10-K narrative — flagged wherever this applies. UPS reports both GAAP and non-GAAP "adjusted" figures every quarter with a large and growing gap between them — every number below is explicitly labeled.

1. Verdict

WATCH. Thesis horizon: 12–24 months. UPS is executing a real, now-largely-complete restructuring (the "Amazon glide-down" is done, management says, as of Q2'26) that is genuinely improving the business's unit economics — but the GAAP results are currently ugly (Q2'26 GAAP operating margin 4.1% vs adjusted 9.2%; GAAP EPS $0.71 vs adjusted $1.76), the dividend is frozen and paid out of a thin FCF margin, buybacks have been suspended entirely in 2026, and the company is now in active litigation with the Teamsters over the very buyout program driving the "adjusted" earnings story. This is a legitimate turnaround candidate, not yet a demonstrated one — WATCH until GAAP and adjusted results converge and at least one full guided quarter is delivered cleanly.

2. Business in plain English

UPS moves and delivers packages and freight through three segments: U.S. Domestic Package (ground and air parcel delivery within the US, the largest segment), International Package (parcel delivery outside the US, structurally the highest-margin segment), and Supply Chain Solutions (freight forwarding, contract logistics, and healthcare logistics — including the recently acquired Andlauer Healthcare Group). It earns money on a per-package basis (yield), competing against FedEx, national postal services, regional carriers, and — as both customer and increasingly competitor — Amazon's own logistics network.

3. Why the model likes it

From the preliminary quant screen (lead_prelim_rank.csv, families Q/V/M): UPS ranks #16 of ~500, prelim composite 0.790, with the Value family strongest (0.876) — consistent with a stock trading near multi-year lows on a depressed earnings base — and Quality (0.751) and Momentum (0.742) more middling. This is a coherent, explainable combination: the stock is cheap in absolute terms (trailing P/E 17.5x looks unremarkable, but on adjusted TTM earnings the multiple is materially lower, and NTM P/E is 12.0x per the calendarized d4 snapshot) precisely because GAAP earnings are currently depressed by restructuring charges that management says are largely one-time. Whether the Value signal is durable depends entirely on whether the "adjusted" story becomes the GAAP story within the thesis horizon — this is not yet proven (see §4, §6).

4. Last two years of results (GAAP; adjusted/non-GAAP figures shown alongside and clearly labeled — UPS's own reconciling items are restructuring/"transformation" charges, network-reconfiguration costs, and pension mark-to-market)

6. Earnings quality & balance sheet

FCF conversion: FY2025 FCF/NI (GAAP) ≈ $4.77B/$5.572B = 86%; the GAAP-vs-adjusted gap is the dominant earnings-quality issue this quarter (§4) — treat adjusted EPS as management's estimate of run-rate earning power, not as a substitute for GAAP cash economics. SBC: not independently broken out in this session — flagged as a gap for the quant/valuation team. Leverage: gross debt $24.2B, cash $4.65B, net debt ≈ $19.6–24.2B depending on treatment; net debt/EBITDA ≈ 1.8–2.2x (via ratios.py, FY2025 GAAP EBITDA ~$10.9B) — moderate, not alarming, but up from UPS's historical low-1x range, and ROE of ~37% is substantially leverage-driven (equity multiplier 4.7x per the DuPont decomposition), not purely an operating-quality signal. Interest coverage ~11x on FY2025 GAAP EBIT — adequate. M&A: completed the ~$1.6B (CAD $2.2B) acquisition of Andlauer Healthcare Group on 2025-11-05 (healthcare/cold-chain logistics, adds debt-funded growth capital intensity); separately, UPS sold Coyote Logistics (freight brokerage) to RXO for $1.025B, closed 2024-09-16 — both add real complexity to any YoY comparison of the Supply Chain Solutions segment. Share count / capital return — a genuine adverse fact: UPS repurchased $1.0B of stock in 2025 but has repurchased zero shares in H1 2026 (confirmed via XBRL: PaymentsForRepurchaseOfCommonStock = $0 in both Q1 and Q2 2026 10-Qs), while continuing to pay $5.398B of dividends in FY2025 ($6.56/share annualized, 7.1% trailing yield) — the quarterly dividend has been held flat for seven consecutive quarters and the payout ratio is ~80–90% of GAAP net income, well above UPS's own long-stated 50–60% target [Corrected 2026-10-08: dividends were 97% of FY2025 GAAP net income, 118% over the trailing twelve months, and 156% / 225% in Q1 / Q2 2026]. This is not a dividend cut, but it is real, current strain, not a hypothetical risk, and the buyback suspension is the clearest evidence management is prioritizing balance sheet and the dividend over total shareholder return via repurchases.

7. Valuation snapshot

NTM P/E (calendarized, per d4_live_snapshot.parquet) 12.0x; trailing P/E on GAAP EPS 17.5x (valuation.py EV bridge: EV $99.5B on FY2025 GAAP EBITDA ~$10.9B → EV/EBITDA 9.2x, EV/EBIT 12.6x); FCF yield ~6.0–7.0%. Versus its closest listed peer, FedEx trades at a similar forward P/E (~15–16x both names) but a higher EV/EBITDA (~10.6x FedEx vs ~9.1–9.2x UPS) — i.e. UPS is not obviously cheaper than FedEx once capital structure is normalized, despite the much lower headline P/E some sources quote. [Aggregator cross-check only, not a source of record: stockanalysis.com and GuruFocus, accessed 2026-09-26, source 11 — dated differently than the program's own d4 snapshot; treat this specific peer comparison as directional, not primary-sourced.] Reverse-DCF (WACC 8.0%, terminal growth 2.5%): the current EV implies only ~4% per-year FCF growth for a decade [Corrected 2026-10-08: programme basis (Ke 9.42%, equity, FCF after SBC) gives ~2.1%/yr; implied vs base below, very sensitive to FCF] — a low, easily-clearable bar if the transformation savings ($3B targeted for 2026, $1.2B delivered in H1) show up in free cash flow rather than being reinvested or absorbed by restructuring cash costs. A probability-weighted bear/base/bull scenario (bear $5.50 EPS/12x, base $7.22 adjusted-EPS guide/14x, bull $8.50/17x) centers on ~$101/share, roughly 8% above the current price — i.e., unlike JBHT, this dossier's own scenario math does not find UPS obviously overpriced; the risk here is much more about whether the adjusted-EPS trajectory is real than about paying too much for a proven number.

8. Bull case

  1. The Amazon glide-down is complete, not still unfolding — management says Amazon is now ~9% of UPS's business (down from a much larger, lower-yield share), and US Domestic revenue-per-piece rose 8.3% in FY2025 as low-yield volume was deliberately shed. If the "leaner, more automated, more agile network" the CEO describes is real, incremental volume from here should carry materially better margin.
  2. International segment remains a genuinely high-margin, resilient business (17.5% GAAP / 18.0% adjusted operating margin in FY2025, +2.5% revenue with +7.1% RPP) that is under-appreciated when the narrative is dominated by the US Domestic/Amazon story.
  3. Valuation already reflects a depressed earnings base: at 12x NTM P/E and a reverse-DCF hurdle of only ~4%/year FCF growth, this is priced for a company in distress, not for the "return to consolidated revenue and operating profit growth" management guided to starting Q2'26.

9. Bear case

  1. The GAAP results, not the adjusted ones, are what the balance sheet and dividend actually run on, and Q2'26 GAAP operating margin of 4.1% (vs. 9.2% adjusted) is the worst GAAP print in the two-year window reviewed here. A thesis that requires "trust the adjustments" is exactly the pattern this research program's own prior audit flagged as a repeat mistake — this dossier does not resolve that tension, it surfaces it.
  2. The dividend is under real, current strain: flat for seven quarters, 80–90% GAAP payout ratio vs. a 50–60% target, and buybacks fully suspended in 2026. A dividend cut — while not our base case — is a plausible tail outcome if transformation cash costs run longer than the "largely complete" framing suggests, and would likely trigger a sharp de-rating given the stock is partly held for yield.
  3. Active Teamsters litigation directly tied to the restructuring (the union sued in Q1 2026 alleging that UPS's buyout program breaches the 2023 National Master Agreement, which runs through July 2028 and covers roughly 80% of UPS's US workforce) is a concrete, current legal risk that could constrain management's ability to execute the very cost program the bull case depends on, and is a cost/distraction regardless of outcome.

10. Key risks & kill criteria

These are the specific, observable, time-bound conditions that would invalidate the WATCH-to-INCLUDE upgrade path: - GAAP operating margin fails to close materially toward the adjusted figure by Q4 2026 (i.e., the gap is still >300bps a year from now) — would indicate "one-time" charges are recurring. - The Teamsters litigation results in an injunction or settlement that reverses or materially slows the network-restructuring program. - The board cuts the dividend, or the payout ratio (GAAP basis) exceeds 100% for two consecutive quarters. - Full-year 2026 guidance is cut (not just "raised by less than expected") at the Q3'26 or Q4'26 release. - Buybacks remain at zero through year-end 2026 with no board commentary on resumption — would confirm capital-return capacity is more impaired than management's framing suggests.

11. Catalysts & calendar

Next earnings: 2026-10-27 (Q3 2026; per company snapshot data, confirm closer to date). An 8-K with items 5.02/7.01/9.01 was filed 2026-08-31 (leadership/regulation-FD/exhibits) — not examined in depth in this session; recommend a follow-up read before the position is sized, since 5.02 items indicate an officer or director change. Watch for Q3'26 commentary on whether the GAAP/adjusted gap narrows and any update on buyback resumption.

12. Red-flag scan

Auditor: Deloitte & Touche LLP; no change identified. Litigation — material and current: the Teamsters sued UPS in early 2026 alleging the pending buyout program breaches the September 2023 National Master Agreement (ratified through July 2028); UPS is contesting the suit. This is the single most important red flag in this dossier and is discussed in §9 and §10 — do not treat it as boilerplate litigation. Pension: UPS carries a legacy multiemployer pension withdrawal liability related to the New England Teamsters and Trucking Industry (NETTI) Fund — $813M non-current + $9M current as of the most recent figure located (FY2023 10-K; not re-confirmed for FY2025 in this session, flagged for follow-up) — a real, if legacy and apparently stable, quasi-debt obligation. Union exposure: ~80% of the US workforce (out of ~460,000 employees total) is union-represented, primarily Teamsters plus separate pilot and mechanic unions; the current National Master Agreement runs through July 31, 2028, so there is no near-term full-contract renegotiation risk, but the buyout litigation above shows contract disputes can still arise mid-term. Material weakness/restatement/going concern: none identified in the sources reviewed. Insider ownership: negligible per the quant snapshot (0.02%) — this is a widely-held, dispersed-ownership company; no unusual Form 4 pattern was identified in this session, but a dedicated insider-trade pull was not completed due to a third-party data vendor rate limit during this session and should be done as a follow-up. Short-seller reports: none identified in this session's research.

lead_prelim_rank.csv's rev field for UPS ($75.656B) is wrong — verified FY2025 GAAP revenue (10-K, filed 2026-02-17) is $88,661M, and TTM-through-Q2'26 is ~$89,930M ($13–14B, or ~15–16%, understated). Also separately verified: the Q/V/M/prelim percentile scores do not appear to depend on the broken rev column (they reconcile from ni/ocf/assets/equity/mcap/capex instead).

dossiers.URI:
United Rentals, Inc. (URI) — Diligence Dossier (Agent F93, standard depth)

1. Verdict: INCLUDE-SMALL (half weight), 12–36 month horizon. The largest US equipment-rental company, a real beneficiary of mega-project/data-center/infrastructure capex, with accelerating growth and raised guidance twice in 2026 — but it is a capex-intensive, cyclical industrial already priced at a full multiple, funding buybacks partly with rising net debt. Reservation: construction/capex-cycle sensitivity and the debt-funded capital-return pace.

2. Business in plain English. United Rentals rents construction and industrial equipment (aerial work platforms, earthmoving equipment, generators, specialty tools) to professional contractors, industrial customers, and — an increasingly important growth vector — data-center and mega-infrastructure builders, through the largest branch network in North America. It earns rental income on its fleet, plus equipment/parts sales. Its moat is scale (fleet availability, national-account relationships, used-equipment residual-value management), not IP or switching costs.

The main durability risk is cyclicality — equipment rental is one of the more capex-cycle-sensitive industrial models, and current growth partly reflects an unusually strong non-residential construction cycle that will not run forever.

1. Verdict

INCLUDE — 24–36 month horizon. A diversified super-regional bank (parent of U.S. Bank National Association) with a genuinely strong and improving Q2 2026 quarter — record net revenue, positive operating leverage of 400 bps, rising ROTCE, improving efficiency ratio, improving credit quality, and stable capital — trading at a trailing P/E and P/TBV that price in essentially no further growth. This is the strongest of the three names in this batch: the fundamentals are getting better each quarter, not just cheap on a stale multiple.

2. Business in plain English

U.S. Bancorp is the parent of U.S. Bank, a super-regional commercial and consumer bank (deposits, commercial and consumer lending, wealth management/trust), plus a large payments franchise (Elavon merchant acquiring/processing) and, since 1-Jun-2026, an equity capital-markets and institutional brokerage arm (BTIG, newly acquired). It earns net interest income on the spread between loans/securities and deposits, plus a large and growing stream of fee income from payments, wealth management, capital markets, mortgage banking and other services — a more fee-diversified model than a typical regional bank, which the model's quality score picks up as scale/moat in payments (Elavon).

3. Why the model likes it — durable or artefact?

Triage (Q05) called it "Best ROE (12.6%) among peer regionals, double-digit revenue growth, and cheap at 10.5x forward earnings; payments scale is a real moat" — confirmed and, on ROE, now understated: the 12.6% figure the triage cited matches USB's own Q1 2026 return on average common equity exactly (per the Q2 2026 release's comparative table), and that figure has since improved to 14.0% in Q2 2026. Double-digit revenue growth is also confirmed (net revenue +10.1% YoY in Q2 2026, computed below). dossiers.V:
Visa Inc. (V) — Fundamental Diligence Dossier

Verdict: INCLUDE — 24–48 month thesis horizon. One-sentence reason: the highest-quality payments network in the batch (51% net margin, net-cash-like leverage, mid-teens EPS growth reaffirmed and raised twice this fiscal year) trades at a price that a reverse DCF says requires only ~9% 10-year FCF growth — below this analyst's 13% base case — even after netting out a large, real, recurring interchange-litigation drag.

1. Business in plain English

Visa operates the world's largest card-payment network (VisaNet), connecting banks, merchants and consumers; it does not lend or take credit risk itself (that sits with issuing banks). Revenue is a small, growing take-rate on global consumer/commercial spend (service and data-processing fees) plus incentive-netted assessments, so nominal GDP + card-share-of-spend + cross-border travel/e-commerce are the underlying volume drivers. The moat is network effects (merchants accept Visa because consumers carry it; consumers carry it because merchants accept it) plus decades of processing-security infrastructure that is expensive to replicate.

2. Why the model likes it / is it durable

b1_live_scores.csv shows V with an incomplete live-scoring row (composite, decile, live_rank all blank; mktcap blank) — a data conflict: Visa is unambiguously a >$650B mega-cap and should be scored. fam_Q 0.868 (very high quality percentile) and roe 0.624 are populated and consistent with a durable, high-return network business; mom_12_1 0.120 is unpopulated for value/earnings-momentum families. This looks like a pipeline gap for this name rather than a real quality signal — flagged for the quant team rather than treated as a fundamental red flag. The durability case (network effects, non-lending model, 51%+ net margin) is independently verifiable in filings below and does not depend on the model score.

TTM (FQ4 FY25–FQ3 FY26): revenue $44.4B, GAAP net income $22.6B, non-GAAP diluted EPS $12.78, GAAP diluted EPS $11.76*. Revenue growth has stepped up each of the last three quarters (12%→15%→17%) before moderating slightly to 14% in FQ3 FY26 on a tougher compare; processed transactions crossed 71.7B in FQ3 FY26 (+10% YoY) and payments volume topped $4 trillion in a single quarter for the first time. [1][2][3][4]

4. Guidance track record

Visa's 8-K earnings-release exhibits carry no numerical guidance; forward ranges are given verbally on the earnings call (secondary transcript sources, clearly marked as such below — never treated as filed facts). - FQ1 FY26 call (29-Jan-2026): no FY2026 range disclosed in the release itself. - FQ2 FY26 call (28-Apr-2026): management raised full-year FY2026 guidance to net revenue growth "low double-digit to low teens" and non-GAAP EPS growth "low teens" (per Motley Fool/Investing.com transcripts of the call) — this was itself a raise from the prior (FQ1) commentary, per secondary reporting. - FQ3 FY26 call (28-Jul-2026): management raised again to net revenue growth "low end of low teens", non-GAAP EPS growth "low end of mid-teens", opex growth "low end of low teens", tax rate 18.0–18.25% (Investing.com transcript quoting the CFO). CEO Ryan McInerney said results "exceeded the company's expectations." Two consecutive raises in the fiscal year, consistent with the acceleration seen in the filed quarterly numbers above. [5][6]

5. Moat, competitive position and secular drivers

  • Non-lending network model: Visa carries no consumer credit risk, so credit-cycle stress hits issuer banks, not Visa's income statement directly (though it can slow volume growth in a downturn).
  • Cross-border volume (ex.-intra-Europe) grew 11–12% in each of the last three quarters — a higher-take-rate segment than domestic, and the main reason margin has stayed >50%.
  • New growth vectors disclosed in filings/calls: Visa Stablecoin Platform (stablecoin minting/movement/management), an "Open Standard" partnership for OpenUSD issuance, tokenized-deposit work with Pismo, and an OpenAI partnership to enable Visa payments inside agentic-commerce flows. These are optionality, not yet revenue lines — treated as bull-case items, not base-case drivers.
  • Competitive risk: Mastercard is the direct scaled competitor; real-time/account-to-account rails (FedNow, Pix-style schemes, stablecoins) and large-merchant surcharging (post-MDL settlement, see §6) are the structural threats to take-rate over a 10-year horizon.

6. Earnings quality & balance sheet

Entity scope: all figures below are consolidated Visa Inc. (there is no separately reported bank/subsidiary segment balance sheet for Visa — unlike banks/insurers in this batch). - FY2025 (10-K for fiscal year ended 30-Sep-2025, filed 06-Nov-2025): operating cash flow $23,059M − capex (PaymentsToAcquireProductiveAssets) $1,482M = FCF $21,577M, FCF/GAAP-NI = 108% (favorable, no working-capital red flag). - TTM-through-31-Mar-2026 (derived: FY2025 10-K annual − six-month YTD ended 31-Mar-2025 [10-Q filed 30-Apr-2025] + six-month YTD ended 31-Mar-2026 [10-Q filed 29-Apr-2026]): OCF $22,756M, capex $1,571M, FCF ≈ $21.2B. This slightly understates the true trailing-twelve-month figure because the FQ3 FY26 quarter (Apr–Jun 2026) is not yet in the SEC bulk XBRL companyfacts feed as of this write-up (see §13 limitation) — GAAP net income for that quarter ($5.6B, per the earnings release) suggests TTM FCF is closer to $22–23B on the same conversion ratio. - Balance sheet, Condensed Consolidated Balance Sheet, Form 10-Q for the quarterly period ended 31-Mar-2026 (filed 29-Apr-2026), consolidated: cash and cash equivalents $12,404M; current maturities of long-term debt $1,559M; long-term debt (noncurrent) $22,417M; total debt $23,976M; total stockholders' equity (incl. non-controlling interest) $35,661M. Net debt ≈ $11.6B, against TTM EBITDA of roughly $32–33B — net leverage under 0.4x, a fortress balance sheet by any standard. - Share count: FQ1 FY26 buybacks $3.8B (11.0M shares @ $342.13); FQ2 FY26 $7.9B (~25M shares), plus a new $20B authorization; FQ3 FY26 $4.9B (14.5M shares @ $330.71), $28.4B authorization remaining. FY2025 full year: ~54M shares for $18.2B. Buybacks are a structural, multi-billion-dollar-per-quarter EPS tailwind. Dividend $0.670/quarter (~0.7% yield). - SBC not separately broken out in the release exhibits reviewed; not flagged as material based on Visa's historically low SBC/revenue ratio (<2%).

7. Valuation — reverse DCF (no V1 systematic valuation row for V)

v4/outputs/v1_valuation_table.csv and v1_valuation.json were checked: no row exists for V. v1_verdict is therefore set to null in the summary JSON, per instructions. [Corrected 2026-10-06: risk-free 4.2% is wrong (10-year Treasury 5.17% on 25 Sep 2026), FCF adds back about $0.9bn of stock compensation and the balance sheet is dated 31 Mar 2026; restated implied growth is about 11.0%/yr, see Correction section] Solving for the constant FCF growth rate that justifies the price: ≈8.9%/year for 10 years. [Corrected 2026-10-06: restated to about 11.0%/year on programme inputs (range 10.2-11.4%)] - Bear case (EPS/FCF growth ≈6%/yr): cross-border/travel volume growth normalizes to low-single-digit, real-time-rail and stablecoin disintermediation start taking measurable share, litigation costs stay elevated (see §11), multiple compresses to ~22x. - Base case (≈13%/yr): continuation of management's own "low-teens revenue / mid-teens EPS" FY2026 guide moderating slightly over the decade as cross-border normalizes, buybacks continue at the current $15–20B/yr pace, multiple holds near 27x. - Bull case (≈17%/yr): stablecoin/agentic-commerce initiatives add a genuine new volume vector on top of the base network, opex leverage continues, multiple re-rates to 30x. Implied vs. base: BELOW. [Corrected 2026-10-08 (DV41): implied 11.1% is aggregate FCF growth, the 13% base is per-share EPS growth including buyback accretion; like-for-like it is in line; verdict INCLUDE -> INCLUDE-SMALL] The reverse-DCF-implied 8.9% sits meaningfully below the 13% base case [Corrected 2026-10-06: restated: implied about 11.0% vs 13% base, still BELOW but by about 2 points, not 4] — the market is pricing Visa for something closer to its bear/base blend, not crediting it with sustaining its own guided mid-teens EPS growth for a decade. This is the basis for the INCLUDE verdict.

8. Bull case

  1. Two consecutive guidance raises within FY2026 (Apr and Jul 2026 calls) on real, filed acceleration in quarterly revenue growth (12%→17%).
  2. Reverse-DCF implied growth (8.9%) sits below both management's own guide and this analyst's base case (13%) — the stock is not priced for its own guidance to hold.
  3. Net-debt/EBITDA under 0.4x with $28.4B of buyback authorization remaining — capital return is a durable, self-funded EPS tailwind independent of volume growth.

9. Bear case

  1. Interchange MDL litigation costs have been large and recurring: $2.5B provisioned in FY2025 alone, plus $707M (FQ1 FY26), $311M (FQ2 FY26) and $237M (FQ3 FY26) — over $3.7B added across the last five reported quarters [Corrected 2026-10-06: the $3.7B is FQ1 FY25 to FQ3 FY26, seven quarters; the last four quarters total about $1.7B (FQ4 FY25 $434M + $707M + $311M + $237M)], a real and growing (not one-off) drag on reported margins.
  2. Real-time account-to-account rails and stablecoin payment rails are a genuine long-run disintermediation threat to card interchange economics — the same secular risk the company itself is now hedging via its own Stablecoin Platform.
  3. FQ3 FY26 revenue growth (14%) decelerated from FQ2's 17% — a single data point, but worth watching for whether the FQ2 print (aided by FIFA World Cup-related value-added-services demand per management) was a temporary pull-forward.

10. Key risks & kill criteria

  1. Net revenue growth falls below 8% YoY (constant-currency) for two consecutive fiscal quarters.
  2. Quarterly interchange-litigation provisions exceed $500M in any single quarter (vs. $237–707M range seen FQ1–FQ3 FY26) [Corrected 2026-10-08 (DV41): already exceeded in FQ4 FY25 ($899M) and FQ1 FY26 ($707M)], signalling the MDL settlement is deteriorating rather than resolving.
  3. Net debt/EBITDA rises above 1.5x (from ~0.4x today) without a offsetting acquisition-driven earnings step-up.
  4. Non-GAAP diluted EPS growth guidance is cut (vs. today's "low end of mid-teens" for FY2026) at any of the next two quarterly calls.
  5. Cross-border volume growth (ex.-intra-Europe) falls below 6% YoY for two consecutive quarters (from 11–12% today) — the highest-margin volume line decelerating structurally.

11. Catalysts & calendar

  • Next earnings: fiscal Q4/full-year FY2026, estimated late October 2026 (not yet confirmed as of this cutoff) — FY2025's equivalent release was 28-Oct-2025.
  • Interchange MDL: the district court granted preliminary approval of the amended/superseding settlement agreement in June 2026 (the agreement itself is dated 10-Nov-2025); final approval and the 90-day implementation window for merchant-surcharging changes are the next milestones to watch — a real catalyst/risk date, not yet reached as of 25-Sep-2026.

12. Red-flag scan

  • Litigation (the primary red flag): the interchange multidistrict litigation (In re Payment Card Interchange Fee and Merchant Discount Antitrust Litigation, E.D.N.Y.) is decades-old; Visa entered a superseding amended settlement agreement dated 10-Nov-2025, which received preliminary court approval in June 2026 (10bps reduction in the US combined average effective credit interchange rate for five years, expanded merchant surcharging rights). This is disclosed and provisioned for in the earnings releases cited in §9 — a known, sized, recurring cost, not a surprise, but large enough (>$3.7B across five quarters) to matter to margin trend.
  • No auditor changes, restatements, going-concern language, or SEC/DOJ investigations beyond the above found in sources reviewed.
  • Insider-selling pattern not independently re-checked at Form-4 level this pass (time-boxed); flagged as unverified rather than asserted clean.
  • Data conflict: b1_live_scores.csv shows V with a blank mktcap/composite/live_rank despite being a >$650B constituent — a data-pipeline gap, reported to the quant team, not evidence of any fundamental issue.

One-sentence reason: dominant, sticky, net-cash life-sciences cloud software (CRM/Vault) with four consecutive quarterly guidance raises and 16–18% revenue growth at 44–45% non-GAAP operating margin — a reverse DCF says the price requires only ~7% 10-year FCF growth, well below this analyst's 16% base case, with the company's one real legal overhang (the eight-year IQVIA dispute) already settled with no damages exchanged. [Corrected 5 Oct 2026: the '~7% implied growth' is not robust: it used FCF that adds back stock-based compensation (~$0.49bn a year) and includes interest income on the $7.2bn of cash that is also subtracted from EV (~$0.23bn after tax). On cash flow net of both, and a cost of equity consistent with the 25 Sep 2026 10-year Treasury (10.0%), the price implies ~16% 10-year FCF growth, above a restated 12-14% evidence-based base. Verdict restated to WATCH; see Correction section]

1. Business in plain English

Veeva sells cloud software to pharmaceutical and biotech companies: Vault CRM (managing interactions with doctors), Vault Clinical/Regulatory/Quality (managing drug development and compliance paperwork), and adjacent data/analytics products. Customers are pharma/biotech commercial and R&D organizations; revenue is subscription-based (84–87% of total) with the balance in professional services (implementation). The moat is high switching costs (life-sciences workflows are validated/regulated, so ripping out the system of record is expensive and risky) plus a purpose-built, life-sciences-specific product set that horizontal CRM/ERP vendors have not successfully replicated.

dossiers.VICI:
VICI Properties Inc. (VICI) — Diligence Dossier (F34, standard depth)

1. Verdict

INCLUDE-SMALL (half weight). Thesis horizon 12–36 months. One-sentence reason: as of the 2026-09-25 close, an 8x-forward-AFFO, ~7.7%-yielding, investment-grade-adjacent triple-net gaming REIT with a clean four-release guidance-raise streak (2025–2026) is priced for AFFO/share to shrink forever, which its own results and pipeline contradict — but two tenants still supply ~70% of rent per the Q2 2026 10-Q, which is why this is a starter, not a full, position.

Thesis (≤25 words): Owns irreplaceable Las Vegas Strip and regional casino real estate on long, CPI-linked leases, priced far below what its own steady growth and diversification deals justify.

2. Business in plain English

VICI Properties is a triple-net-lease REIT that owns the real estate under casino-resorts (Caesars Palace, MGM Grand, The Venetian, Mandalay Bay and dozens of regional properties) and leases it back to operators on long-term, CPI-linked leases, plus a growing book of experiential and leisure assets (bowling via Bowlero, golf via Cabot, and now a first Club Med Caribbean resort). It makes money on the spread between its cost of capital (debt + equity) and the yield it earns funding new acquisitions and mortgage/financing-receivable deals, so growth comes from rent escalators plus accretive external deal-making, not from operating the casinos itself. Competitive position: the largest gaming-focused net-lease REIT, with essentially no direct competitor of similar scale in single-purpose casino real estate.

3. Why the model likes it / durability

Triage (Q14_triage.json, as_of 2026-09-25) scored VICI quality 4, growth 3, price_vs_growth 5, no red flags, reasoning "8x NTM P/E with a 7.7% yield and high-teens revenue growth is a rare combination for an investment-grade landlord; main risk is tenant concentration (Caesars/MGM) rather than the real estate itself." The pre-registered quant composite (b1_live_scores.csv) is far less enthusiastic: live_rank 441/503, composite 0.113, driven by a very strong value percentile (fam_V 0.997 — cheapest-in-market on book/price and EBIT/EV) but a weak quality percentile (fam_Q 0.204, because REIT accruals/leverage/asset-growth inputs are largely NaN or penalize balance-sheet growth funded by debt) and near-bottom momentum/earnings-momentum (fam_M 0.088, fam_S 0.014). This is explainable, not a fundamental red flag: the composite's quality and momentum families are built for operating companies, not net-lease REITs whose "growth" is intentionally debt/equity-funded acquisition, and whose stock has simply been unloved (rate-sensitive sector) rather than fundamentally weak — the durable driver is the value/income combination triage flagged, which primary-source results below confirm is real and growing, not an artefact.

6. Earnings quality & balance sheet

FCF conversion: VICI's own AFFO (the REIT-appropriate cash-flow proxy) tracks operating cash flow closely — per the Q1 2026 10-Q (filed 2026-04-29), OCF $631.9M vs AFFO $650.9M, a clean relationship with no material one-off working-capital swings. Balance sheet: total debt $17.2bn at the Q2 2026 8-K (filed 2026-07-29), leverage ~4.9x annualized adjusted EBITDA, liquidity $2.5bn (cash $288M + $2.2bn revolver capacity), remaining below VICI's own target leverage range. Shares outstanding rose modestly from ~1.057bn (Q2 2025 10-Q) to ~1.101bn (Q2 2026 10-Q), consistent with ATM equity issuance funding accretive acquisitions rather than dilutive stock-based comp. Dividend: quarterly $0.4525+ (raised ~4% YoY per the Q3 2025 8-K declaration) [Corrected 2026-10-08: quarterly dividend is $0.45 per share (raised $0.0175, +4.0%), not $0.4525; source Q3 2025 8-K Ex-99.1, acc 0001705696-25-000130], trailing yield ~7.7–7.8% at the 2026-09-25 price; AFFO payout ratio ~73–75%, leaving a modest retained-cash cushion. Tenant concentration is the central balance-sheet-adjacent risk: per the Q1 2026 and Q2 2026 10-Qs, Caesars represented ~36–37% and MGM ~34–36% of total contractual rent in the most recent quarters (Q1 2026: MGM 36%/Caesars 37%, ~73% combined; Q2 2026: Caesars 36%/MGM 34%, ~70% combined) — a real, undiversified two-tenant credit exposure, though the trend is modestly improving as new deals (Golden Entertainment, Gamehost, Club Med) add other operators.

7. Valuation snapshot & reverse DCF

Price (2026-09-25 close) $23.51; NTM P/E ~8.0x (d4, calendarised); dividend yield ~7.7–7.8%; FY2026 P/AFFO on the guided midpoint ($2.46/sh) ≈9.6x. No V1 row exists for VICI (checked v1_valuation_table.csv — no row; VICI appears only as a peer-comparison sample inside FRT's V1 detail JSON, not as its own valuation) → v1_verdict = null; no systematic reconciliation is possible, so this dossier's valuation view is independently derived using a REIT-appropriate framework (AFFO yield / required-total-return), not a generic FCF DCF.

Reverse DCF (Gordon-growth on AFFO/share): Price = AFFO₁×(1+g)/(r−g). Using AFFO/share $2.46 (2026 guide midpoint) and a required total return r of 8.5–9.5% (a net-lease-REIT risk premium appropriate for VICI's leverage and two-tenant concentration — a pure CAPM beta-based WACC (β≈0.68) would imply an unrealistically low ~6–7% and is not used here because beta understates single-name lease-concentration risk), the price of $23.51 implies perpetual AFFO/share growth of roughly −0.9% to −1.8% across that discount-rate range — i.e. the market is pricing VICI as if AFFO per share will shrink indefinitely. My evidence-based base case is +3–4%/yr (embedded CPI-linked escalators, most capped at 2–3%/yr on the largest leases, plus the demonstrated pace of accretive third-party acquisitions — Golden Entertainment $1.16bn, Gamehost C$200.6M, Club Med $20.3M+$55.2M redevelopment — funded at a spread to VICI's cost of capital, consistent with the guided +3.4% for 2026 and the 4.6–5.7%/quarter AFFO/share growth actually delivered over the past two years). Implied growth is clearly below base case: the stock is priced more cheaply than a no-growth, in-perpetuity REIT. Bear case (AFFO/share growth slows to +1%/yr on tenant stress, exit multiple compresses to 7x from ~9.6x): 3-yr annualized total return ≈ +4% [Corrected 2026-10-08: recomputed bear (AFFO/share +1%/yr, exit 7x, dividend $1.80 growing 1%) is about -0.4%/yr, not +4%]. Base case (+3.5%/yr growth, multiple stable): ≈ +11%/yr. Bull case (+5%/yr growth on continued accretive/diversifying deal flow, multiple re-rates to ~9.5x as rate fears ease): ≈ +18–19%/yr [Corrected 2026-10-08: at the stated 9.5x exit and +5%/yr growth the bull return is about +12.9%/yr; +18-19% requires an exit near 11.5x (a re-rate from 9.6x, not 9.5x)].

8. Bull case / Bear case

Bull: (1) Rent escalators (CPI-linked, several uncapped in early lease years) plus an active, accretive acquisition pipeline (Golden Entertainment, Gamehost, Club Med) funded at a spread to cost of capital keep compounding AFFO/share even with zero cap-rate compression; (2) management is visibly diversifying away from the Caesars/MGM duopoly — combined concentration fell from ~73% (Q1'26) to ~70% (Q2'26) in one quarter, and the Club Med and Gamehost deals open entirely new verticals (leisure resorts, Canadian gaming); (3) at ~9.6x forward AFFO and a 7.7–7.8% yield, VICI is near the cheapest it has traded relative to its own multi-year history for a business generating long-duration, largely investment-grade-adjacent contracted cash flows. Bear: (1) Caesars + MGM still supply ~70% of contractual rent — an unusually concentrated exposure for a REIT this size; a material deterioration at either operator (regional gaming softness, a leveraged refinancing squeeze, new-supply competition) leaves VICI with limited ability to quickly re-lease single-purpose casino real estate; (2) higher-for-longer interest rates raise VICI's own refinancing cost on $17.2bn of debt faster than escalators grow rent, compressing the spread that funds accretive growth; (3) GAAP net income is highly volatile quarter to quarter (−39% YoY in Q2'26) on non-cash fair-value items in VICI's financing-receivable and preferred-equity book, which creates real headline/print-day risk (the Q2'26 print was reported as an "EPS miss" despite AFFO growth) even though the underlying cash-flow metric is steady.

9. Key risks & measurable kill criteria

Any of the following would break the thesis; each is a specific, observable, time-bound signpost to monitor at each earnings release, not a vague worry: 1. Combined Caesars + MGM share of total contractual rent stops declining and rises back above 75% for two consecutive quarters (from ~70% currently), signalling the diversification trend has reversed. 2. AFFO/share guidance is cut (any reduction to the low end of the then-current full-year range) at a subsequent release — track record is currently four-for-four raises/holds. 3. Net debt/adjusted EBITDA rises above 5.5x (from ~4.9x currently) without a stated deleveraging plan. 4. A monetary default, lease restructuring, or sub-investment-grade credit-rating downgrade (below B1/B+) at either Caesars or MGM. 5. Realized rent growth trails CPI by more than 100bps for two consecutive years, i.e. the escalator caps bind and erode real rental income (VICI's own disclosed risk).

10. Catalysts & calendar

Next earnings: 2026-10-29 (Q3'26, per d4 next_earnings_date). Watch for further tenant-diversification deal flow (following Golden Entertainment/Gamehost/Club Med) and any update on the Caesars/MGM concentration trend.

11. Red-flag scan

No auditor change, restatement, or going-concern language found in the filings reviewed. No SEC/DOJ investigation or short-seller report found in this cycle's search. Insider activity: routine Form 4 activity (RSU vesting/settlement and associated tax-related sales), no unusual pattern; short interest ~3.0% of float as of end-April 2026, up ~22% from the prior count but still a low absolute level. The only real, open item is the tenant concentration discussed throughout (§6, §8, §9) — it is disclosed, quantified, and the trend is (modestly) improving, not a hidden risk.

1. Verdict: WATCH (horizon 12-36 months). Best-in-class refiner with a strong balance sheet, but the $387.18 close (25 Sep 2026) prices a refining-margin spike (Q2 2026 margin $23.62/bbl vs $12.29/bbl for FY2025) as if it were durable. Agent: F37 · Standard depth · Prepared 2026-09-26 · Prices/market data as of 2026-09-25 close ($97.14; mkt cap ≈$23.68B)

Data quality note: all figures are consolidated (Veralto has no separately-reported standalone entity), in US dollars ($ = USD; m/mn = millions, bn = billions unless a per-share $ figure), sourced primarily from SEC EDGAR XBRL and company earnings releases as cited in Section 13; GAAP vs. non-GAAP/adjusted figures are labelled throughout; approximated (derived) figures are flagged where used.

1. Verdict

WATCH — not now; would revisit on a pullback toward the mid-$80s or on two consecutive quarters of Product Quality & Innovation (PQI) core growth back above ~4%. Veralto is a genuinely high-quality, Danaher-heritage compounder (34% ROE, 17.3% net margin, low leverage, recurring consumables/service revenue), but the reverse DCF shows the price already assumes roughly the growth rate the company can plausibly deliver given a soft PQI segment — this is the "great business priced for more than it can comfortably deliver" case the mandate explicitly asks to be honest about, not an INCLUDE. No V1 row exists for VLTO, so v1_verdict is null.

2. Business in plain English

Veralto (spun off from Danaher in September 2023) operates two segments: Water Quality (~57% of revenue — instruments, chemistries and services for testing/treating municipal and industrial water, brands including Hach and ChemTreat) and Product Quality & Innovation (~43% — marking/coding equipment (Videojet), and packaging/color-management software and hardware (X-Rite, Pantone, and the newly acquired GlobalVision packaging-compliance software)). Revenue is heavily recurring: consumables, service contracts and software subscriptions tied to installed equipment, inherited from Danaher's playbook of pricing the instrument to sell the annuity. The moat is regulatory-driven demand (water-quality testing is often legally mandated) plus high switching costs once an instrument/workflow is validated into a regulated process.

Sector routing note: none of the stock-analysis skill's sector playbooks fit cleanly. waste-environmental.md is explicitly about waste collection/disposal and landfill permits, which does not describe Veralto's analytical- instrumentation and marking/software business at all; Veralto is closer to a diversified, high-margin instrumentation/consumables business (the Danaher/Roper archetype). This dossier therefore uses the generic core-factor/DuPont framework rather than forcing an ill-fitting sector playbook, and says so explicitly per the skill's own instruction for when no playbook applies.

The quality (34% ROE, 17.3% margin, 1.1x leverage per the original triage) is real and durable — Danaher-system pricing discipline and consumables mix do not disappear on spin-off — but growth is genuinely modest: Water Quality core growth has been accelerating (3.8% Q1 2026 → 5.7% Q2 2026) while PQI has been soft (-1.0% Q1 2026 → +2.0% Q2 2026), and a $0.05/share Q2 EPS benefit came from one-off IEEPA tariff refunds, not operations.

Bull (3): 1. Water Quality core growth is genuinely accelerating (3.8% → 5.7% over two quarters) and is regulation-backed, recurring-revenue demand, not a cyclical bounce. 2. SBC at 1.3% of revenue and net debt/EBITDA of ~1.1x show real capital discipline — a Danaher-system business that compounds through bolt-on M&A (GlobalVision) and buybacks without diluting shareholders. 3. If PQI's Q1→Q2 2026 improvement (-1.0% → +2.0% core growth) continues into H2, the "soft segment" bear case weakens and the stock could re-rate off a currently fair, not cheap, multiple.

Bear (3): 1. The reverse DCF shows the price already assuming close to the growth rate a sober base case would forecast — there is little valuation cushion if PQI's recovery stalls or Water Quality decelerates. 2. Part of the FY2026 guidance raise is explicitly a one-off tariff refund ($0.05/share in Q2), not organic reacceleration; stripping it, the "raise" is smaller than headline. 3. A newly-issued $725M senior notes offering, even if framed as refinancing, modestly increases fixed obligations at a company whose PQI segment has been growing below the rate needed to comfortably grow into more leverage.

1. Verdict

WATCH — the underlying data/analytics moat is real and the price implies less growth than the base case, but a debt-funded buyback has pushed consolidated stockholders' equity into a deficit, management has now promised a growth "return to Investor Day targets" in two consecutive quarters without delivering it, and there is an active driver-data-sharing MDL. Horizon to revisit: 2–3 quarters (next 2 earnings releases), not 12–36 months.

2. Business in plain English

Verisk sells proprietary data, analytics, and software mainly to the global property & casualty insurance industry: "Underwriting" (forms/rules/loss-cost content that insurers are often contractually or regulatorily required to use) and "Claims" (anti-fraud analytics, property/restoration solutions). It makes money via high-margin subscriptions with strong renewal economics because its content (loss costs, rating rules, catastrophe models) is embedded in customers' regulatory filings and workflows — a genuine switching-cost moat, not merely a network effect.

Consolidated GAAP entity (Verisk Analytics, Inc. and subsidiaries; Verisk does not report a segment-level balance sheet), per the Q2'26 10-Q balance sheet (30 Jun 2026 vs 31 Dec 2025), accession 0001437749-26-024749: - Cash fell from $2,178.2m to $551.4m in six months (−75%). - Consolidated long-term debt rose from $3,228.3m to $4,215.8m (XBRL tag LongTermDebt, CIK0001442145, cross-checked at $4,217.2m for the same period -- a $1.4m/0.03% rounding difference against the press-release balance sheet figure used here, immaterial); total debt (long-term $4,215.8m + short-term/current portion $257.7m = $4,473.5m, arithmetic sum, not itself a single filed XBRL fact) fell from $4,737.2m (long-term $3,228.3m + current $1,508.9m) as the current portion was refinanced into a $999m senior-notes issuance plus a $500m term loan and $750m revolver draw/repay during H1'26 (cash-flow statement). - Total Verisk stockholders' equity (consolidated) went from +$309.0m (Dec 2025) to −$1,189.0m (Jun 2026) — a stockholders' deficit. 7. Valuation & reverse DCF

NTM P/E 20.1x, FCF yield ~4.8% (triage snapshot, consolidated basis). Reverse DCF (10-yr explicit + Gordon terminal, WACC 8.0%, terminal growth 3.0%, EV ≈$26.07bn [mkt cap $22.15bn + net debt $3.92bn], FY2025 FCF base $1.192bn): implied 10-year FCF growth ≈ 3.8% p.a. [Corrected 2026-10-08: method errors: the FY25 FCF base adds back SBC ($54.2M) and is after interest while the EV nets debt; unlevered FCF after SBC is about $1,214M, giving about 3.5% (EV method) or about 4.2% (levered FCF $1,138M vs market cap at 8.8% cost of equity); still well below the 7-8% base, so 'below' stands] Base case (mid-single-digit OCC revenue growth per management's own reiterated guidance quoted verbatim in Section 5, similar EBITDA growth, plus buyback-driven per-share accretion) is ~7–8%. Implied vs base: BELOW on a pure DCF-arithmetic basis. However, this reverse DCF uses today's EV, which already embeds the post-buyback debt load; if the buyback pace continues at the H1'26 rate ($1.57bn/half-year) funded further by debt, net debt/EBITDA will keep rising and WACC (cost of capital) should rise with it, which would raise the implied growth bar back toward or above base case. Net: the valuation looks attractive only if the current capital-structure trajectory does not continue — which is precisely the point of the WATCH verdict rather than INCLUDE.

8. Bull / bear

Bull: (1) genuine regulatory/contractual embedding of Verisk's underwriting content in customer workflows gives real pricing power (OCC underwriting revenue +5.6% in Q2'26 "primarily due to an annual increase in prices"); (2) claims/anti-fraud analytics growing faster (+6.1% OCC) as insurers invest in loss-cost control; (3) buyback-driven EPS accretion is real cash returned to shareholders, not merely financial engineering, if the debt is serviced comfortably (interest coverage still solid at ~7x EBITDA/interest based on guided figures). Bear: (1) consolidated stockholders' deficit and consolidated net debt/EBITDA trending toward or above 2.5–3x removes balance-sheet flexibility exactly when management wants to keep buying back stock; (2) growth-reacceleration has now been promised in three straight releases without a clear step-up in reported OCC growth (4.7% Q1'26 → 5.8% Q2'26 is directionally positive but still below what would be needed to justify "acceleration" framing over a full year); (3) the Telematics/driver-data class-action MDL is unresolved, actively adding to legal costs each quarter, and carries tail risk given the size of the certified/putative classes (see below).

  1. Full-year 2026 revenue or adjusted EBITDA guidance is cut below the unchanged range quoted in Section 5 above ("$3,190" to "$3,240" [million] revenue / "$1,790" to "$1,830" [million] Adjusted EBITDA) at the Q3 or Q4 2026 release (guidance has been flat for 2 quarters — any cut would be a first).
  2. Consolidated net debt/adjusted EBITDA exceeds 3.0x at any quarter-end (was ≈2.2x on run-rate guidance basis as of Jun'26, up from ≈1.7x implied at Dec'25 on the initial FY26 EBITDA guide).
  3. A material adverse ruling, class certification, or settlement in In re: Consumer Vehicle Driving Data Tracking Litigation (MDL No. 1:24-md-03115-TWT, N.D. Georgia) — the GM/OnStar/LexisNexis/Verisk telematics-data-sharing class actions — resulting in a disclosed reserve or payment exceeding, illustratively, $100m.
  4. Underlying/OCC subscription revenue growth fails to exceed 6% for two consecutive quarters despite two prior quarters of management guidance promising a "return to Investor Day targets."
  5. Any credit-rating agency downgrade of Verisk's consolidated debt, or Verisk's consolidated stockholders' equity remaining in deficit for more than four consecutive quarters without a clear path back to positive.

10. Catalysts & calendar

Next earnings: ~late Oct 2026 (Q3 2026), based on the Jul-2025/Jul-2026 release cadence — estimate only, not confirmed by a company release. Watch for: (a) the outcome of motions to dismiss in the Telematics MDL (fully briefed as of the last filing reviewed, April 2025, with a Sept–Oct 2025 follow-on suit still pending); (b) any update on remaining ASR settlement and further buyback authorization use ($800.0m remaining as of 30 Jun 2026).

dossiers.VRSN:
VRSN — Verisign, Inc. — Fundamental Diligence Dossier

1. Verdict

INCLUDE-SMALL — 24–36 month horizon. A durable, contractually-protected monopoly on .com/.net domain registry with real, exercised pricing power and an aggressive buyback program, but the current 27.3x NTM P/E is pricing in roughly 14.5%/yr growth for a decade against a delivered 5-year CAGR of just 5.8% — even generous credit for the newly-resumed price increases doesn't fully close that gap. [Corrected 2026-10-06: the 14.5% is the year-1 growth rate of a ten-year linear fade to 3% (average about 8.7%), not a constant rate, and it is not comparable with the 5.8% delivered CAGR; on free cash flow after SBC and a 9.24% WACC the constant-growth equivalent is 9.5% a year versus about 9-10% in the evidence-based base (price steps of up to 7% a year on .com to Nov 2029 plus 5% domain-base growth), so implied_vs_base is in_line; verdict unchanged] Named reservation: hold at reduced weight versus a full-conviction name; do not size this as if the bull case (25.8%/yr) were the base case.

2. Business in plain English

Verisign operates the authoritative registry for the .com and .net top-level internet domains under an exclusive agreement with ICANN (renewed in November 2024 through November 30, 2030) and a related Cooperative Agreement with the U.S. Department of Commerce. It sells wholesale registrations and renewals to domain registrars (GoDaddy, Namecheap, etc.), who in turn sell to end customers; Verisign itself does not sell to consumers. Because the marginal cost of adding or renewing a domain in an existing registry database is close to zero, incremental revenue converts to profit at very high margins (68.2% GAAP operating margin, Q2 2026). Its competitive position is not "market share" in the normal sense — it is a government-linked, contractually exclusive registry operator, with pricing capped by that same contract.

3. Why the model likes it — durable or artefact?

B1 ranks VRSN #53 (composite 89.4th percentile), driven by exceptionally strong Quality (gross-profit/assets 98.8th percentile — reflecting the registry's near-zero marginal cost — OCF/assets 96.9th percentile) and strong Value (FCF yield 79.4th percentile, EBIT/EV 64.8th percentile), with average Momentum and Earnings-momentum. This is durable, not an artefact — the underlying economics (near-100% incremental margin, contractual multi-year pricing rights, sole-source registry) are structural, not accounting-driven, and are directly confirmed in this review by the actual Q2 2026 operating margin (68.2%) and the just-announced Nov 2026 price increase. Data conflict flagged and resolved: V1's own valuation model flagged a conflict — "D3 TTM revenue implies an implausible EBIT margin (67.9%)" and substituted a Yahoo revenue figure to compute the DCF. Having independently confirmed the 67.9–68.2% operating margin directly from Verisign's own SEC filings and Q2 2026 earnings release, this is not a data error — it is a real, structural feature of the registry business and V1's "implausible" flag was a false positive that should not have triggered a data substitution. This is disclosed here as a data_conflict for the record, though it does not change any of V1's actual output values materially.

6. Earnings quality & balance sheet

  • Extremely capital-light: capex is consistently under 2% of revenue ($26.0M in H1 2026 vs. $434.6M Q2 revenue alone), so OCF converts to FCF almost fully.
  • OCF growing: FY2025 $1,091.1M vs. FY2024 $902.6M (+20.9%) vs. FY2023 $853.8M; H1 2026 $504.0M vs. H1 2025 $493.8M (+2.1% — a visible deceleration from the FY2025 pace worth watching, though could be timing/working-capital).
  • Negative equity from buybacks (use net debt/EBITDA, not ROE): stockholders' equity is −$2,254.1M at Q2 2026, deepening from −$1,977.0M at Q1 2025 — buybacks have exceeded net income in most recent years (FY2025 buybacks $881.6M vs. net income $825.7M = 107%; FY2024 buybacks $1,225.6M vs. NI $785.7M = 156%). On an OCF basis the coverage is healthier (FY2025 buybacks were 81% of OCF, not underwater). Debt: ~$1.785–1.79bn of senior notes, essentially flat for years. Net debt/EBITDA ≈1.1x (V1 net debt $1,306.2M ÷ TTM EBITDA ≈$1,186M) — modest leverage despite the negative book-equity headline.
  • June 2026 debt refinancing, fully closed before this review's cutoff: on 2026-06-26 Verisign issued $550M of 5.10% Senior Notes due 2031; on 2026-07-20 it used the proceeds to redeem the existing $550M 4.75% Senior Notes due 2027. Net effect: maturity extended from 2027 to 2031, coupon up ~35bps, no increase in principal — a maturity-extension refinancing, not incremental leverage for buybacks.
  • Share count down from 107.1M (Q3'22) to 91.1M (Q2'26), −14.9% over ~3.75 years (~3.9%/yr).

7. Valuation snapshot — reconciliation with V1

V1 verdict: fair (score −0.084). NTM P/E 27.3x — 39.5th percentile of its own ~14.75-year history (i.e. somewhat cheaper than its own historical average) but well above the peer median of 16.7x (peer set: AKAM, GDDY — only 2 true comparables, and neither is a close business-model match: AKAM is a CDN/security vendor, GDDY is a retail registrar, not a sole-source wholesale registry — peer-set quality is a real limitation on this comparison). WACC 8.85%. Implied 10-year growth from the current price: +14.5%/yr, vs. consensus FY1 growth +9.7%, delivered 5-year CAGR +5.8%, delivered 10-year CAGR +4.4%. [Corrected 2026-10-06: V1's 14.5% is a year-1 rate fading linearly to 3%, so comparing it with delivered CAGRs overstates the gap; constant-growth equivalent 9.5% at WACC 9.24% on FCF after SBC; V1's net debt of $1,306M matches the 30 Jun 2026 balance sheet (debt $2,334.4M incl. $549.3M current notes redeemed 20 Jul, less cash and marketable securities $1,034.1M)] Bear/base/bull 3-year annualised returns: −10.2% / +7.8% / +25.8%. The model's own base-case fair value ($359.70) already exceeds the single highest Wall Street 12-month price target ($355). My view: the "fair" verdict is right, and I would not push back on the base case (+7.8%/yr) — but the "implied 14.5%/yr growth" framing overstates how aggressive the pricing really is. VRSN can raise .com prices up to 7%/yr in years 3–6 of each 6-year ICANN term (no increases allowed in years 1–2) — it just exercised this, raising the wholesale price from $10.26 to $10.97 (+6.9%) effective November 1, 2026 — and domain-base growth guidance has just been raised to 5.2–6.0%. Price (~+7%) × base (~+5.5%) is a plausible ~12%/yr revenue tailwind in peak-pricing years, before the buyback-driven EPS uplift (~4%/yr from share-count reduction) — i.e., something in the low-to-mid-teens EPS growth is achievable in good years, which is close to, but still below, the 14.5%/yr the reverse-DCF requires every year for ten years. The bull case (25.8%/yr, requiring 34.9x exit multiple) is the scenario that needs the most scepticism, not the base case. dossier_view: fair; consistent with V1: yes (I agree with the verdict and the base case; I flag the "implied growth" framing and the thin peer set as nuances, not disagreements with the number itself).

8. Bull case / Bear case

Bull: 1. Contractually exclusive registry through Nov 2030 with demonstrated, exercised pricing power (7% max annual increase, just taken) flowing through at near-100% incremental margin. 2. Domain-base growth reaccelerating and guided up twice in 2026 (3.1–4.3% → 5.2–6.0%), with record new registrations, management attributing part of the strength to AI-related tailwinds rather than headwinds. 3. Extremely capital-light (capex <2% of revenue), funding a large, sustained buyback program (14.9% share-count reduction in ~4 years) against only ~1.1x net debt/EBITDA.

Bear: 1. The reverse-DCF's implied 14.5%/yr decade-long growth rate is well above anything VRSN has ever delivered (5-year CAGR 5.8%, 10-year CAGR 4.4%), and rests on a thin, imperfect 2-name peer comparison; the model's own base-case value already exceeds the Street's most bullish 12-month target. 2. Pricing power is not unlimited: no increases are allowed in years 1–2 of each 6-year ICANN cycle, and the whole framework is a negotiated, government-linked agreement (ICANN / U.S. Dept. of Commerce) that is renewed, not permanent. 3. Negative and deepening equity (−$2,254.1M, worsening ~$277M in 15 months) now funded partly by debt refinanced at a higher coupon (5.10% vs. 4.75%) — a modest but real increase in the cost of capital.

9. Key risks & measurable kill criteria

VRT — Vertiv Holdings Co

1. Verdict

WATCH — thesis horizon 12–36 months. Vertiv is a genuinely excellent business right now: the pure-play leader in power and liquid-cooling infrastructure for AI/hyperscaler data centers, growing net sales 24–30% YoY with margins expanding ~400+bps and free cash flow up 150–240% YoY, now sitting in a net-cash position with a record $15bn backlog. But the 25 September 2026 close (already down from a post-Q2-selloff level, after the stock fell as much as 26% on 29 July 2026 when reported net sales missed consensus by ~3%) still prices in continued strong growth on a reverse DCF (~14.3%/year for ten years) that is at or slightly above this dossier's own evidence-based base case (~11–12%/year, reflecting an expected deceleration from today's 30%+ organic growth as the current 2.9x book-to-bill normalizes). This is exactly the triage's own caution: "significant re-rating already happened; a hyperscaler capex pause is the key risk." A genuinely strong operating story, priced for more strength than a conservative base case can defend — WATCH, not INCLUDE, pending either a better entry price or firmer evidence that the current order/backlog surge is durable rather than a pull-forward.

2. Business in plain English

Vertiv makes the power and thermal-management ("cooling") equipment that keeps data centers running — uninterruptible power supplies, power distribution, switchgear, and (increasingly, as AI chips get hotter) liquid-cooling systems for the racks that house GPUs. It sells almost entirely to data-center owners and operators: hyperscalers (Microsoft, Amazon, Google, Meta and others building AI infrastructure), colocation providers, and enterprises. It does not own or operate any data centers itself — it is a picks-and-shovels equipment and services supplier to the AI buildout, competing with Schneider Electric and Eaton. Its revenue is driven by (a) new data-center construction and retrofits tied directly to hyperscaler capital-expenditure cycles, and (b) a growing recurring services/parts business on its large installed base. The backlog ($15bn, +109% YoY) and book-to-bill (2.9x as of the most recent quarter reviewed) [Corrected 2026-10-08: the ~2.9x book-to-bill and $15.0bn backlog are 31 Dec 2025 figures (Q4 2025 release, acc 0001674101-26-000006); the Q1 and Q2 2026 releases do not disclose book-to-bill or backlog, so they are not the 'most recent quarter'] reflect orders placed well ahead of installation — a genuine demand signal, but also a source of potential volatility if that order pace normalizes or hyperscalers pause spending.

3. Why the model likes it — and is it durable?

B1 composite is upper-mid (live_rank 177/~2,300, decile 7, quintile 4; composite 0.646). Family drivers: Momentum (fam_M ≈0.76, high) — the stock has rallied hard (12-month price return ≈+72%, mom_12_1 0.716); Quality (fam_Q ≈0.64, good) — strong gross-profit/assets and ROE (36.4%), though leverage/asset-growth metrics are elevated by the scale of the AI-infrastructure buildout; Earnings momentum (fam_S ≈0.59, above average); Value (fam_V ≈0.21, weak) — VRT screens expensive on every value sub-metric, the honest counterweight the triage itself flagged (57x trailing P/E).

Durability check: the underlying demand is real and evidenced in primary filings — revenue, backlog and margin all corroborate the AI-infrastructure narrative, and management's FY2026 guidance has been raised at every release this year (see §5). But two specific, dated facts temper the "durable" read: (1) Q2 2026 (reported 29 July 2026) missed analyst revenue estimates ($3.27bn vs. ~$3.38bn consensus) despite the guidance raise and EPS beat, with management attributing the shortfall to "minor timing shifts, primarily due to temporary supply chain congestion and multi-phased project execution" — a plausible but unverified explanation for a real, market-moving miss (the stock fell as much as 26% that day); (2) a 2.9x book-to-bill ratio is, by the company's own historical standards, extreme, and even a modest normalization toward a more typical 1.2–1.5x ratio (as seen as recently as Q3 2025) would mechanically slow reported backlog growth even if underlying demand stays strong.
